shelves.title: Herbs and dietary supplements Deposit #17 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: For the supplements patients actually take, what does the randomized evidence show about benefit?
shelves.balance: The shelf sorts into three piles: real but mostly modest benefits — potassium salt substitute cut stroke and death in a 21,000-person trial, vitamin E improved liver histology without improving fibrosis, and psyllium, creatine with training, melatonin, ginger, curcumin, and cranberry each show small, specific, replicated effects on surrogate or symptom endpoints — plus one lonely hard-outcome positive, CoQ10 in heart failure ( HR 0.50 ), unreplicated since 2014. And a harm pile every supplement conversation needs: vitamin E raised prostate cancer in SELECT ( HR 1.17 ), an annual mega-dose of vitamin D increased falls and fractures, and beta-carotene with vitamin A raised lung cancer in smokers (CARET, stopped early) — the pattern being that replacement-level uses behave, while pharmacologic mega-doses in healthy people are where the harm lives.

cards.headline: Liu 2026: natto red yeast rice for LDL cholesterol
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 1,136 randomized, 1,110 in the modified ITT analysis — LDL fell 21.02 mg/dL and 13.21% at 3 months with natto red yeast rice 1,950 mg/day (P<0.001).
cards.type: Multicenter, double-placebo, double-blind, four-arm randomized trial
cards.people: 1,136 adults were randomized; 1,110 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis across placebo, natto red yeast rice, simvastatin, and combination groups
cards.result: Natto red yeast rice 1,950 mg/day lowered LDL-C versus placebo by 21.02 mg/dL (95% CI 14.06–27.98 mg/dL) and by 13.21% (95% CI 8.54%–17.88%) at 3 months; both P<0.001. Adverse-event rates were similar across groups
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was only 3 months, LDL-C was a surrogate endpoint, and this defined Chinese product cannot be assumed equivalent to retail red yeast rice The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.search: liu 2026 natto red yeast rice ldl cholesterol randomized trial jacc asia pmid 42212982

cards.headline: Gholami 2025: psyllium and lipid levels
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 41 RCT reports, 2,049 adults — LDL −8.55 mg/dL (4.19–12.92) ; total cholesterol −9.05 mg/dL (4.40–13.71) ; I²=88.46%.
cards.type: Systematic review and random-effects dose-response meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
cards.people: 41 RCT reports with 2,049 adults: 1,124 assigned to psyllium and 925 to control
cards.result: Psyllium reduced LDL-C by 8.55 mg/dL (95% CI 4.19–12.92 mg/dL) and total cholesterol by 9.05 mg/dL (95% CI 4.40–13.71 mg/dL). LDL-C heterogeneity was high (I²=88.46%)
cards.watchOut: The trials were highly heterogeneous, and the outcomes were lipid surrogates rather than cardiovascular events The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.search: gholami 2025 psyllium lipid ldl cholesterol systematic review dose response meta-analysis randomized trials genes nutrition pmid 41366295

cards.headline: Feng 2022: curcuminoids for knee osteoarthritis
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 15 studies, 1,670 patients with knee OA — VAS pain WMD −1.77 (−2.44 to −1.09) ; WOMAC total −7.06 ; function −5.04 ; adverse events RR 1.03 .
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
cards.people: 15 studies with 1,670 patients with knee osteoarthritis
cards.result: Versus placebo, curcuminoids improved VAS pain by WMD −1.77 (95% CI −2.44 to −1.09), WOMAC total score by WMD −7.06 (95% CI −12.27 to −1.84), and WOMAC function by WMD −5.04 (95% CI −7.65 to −2.43). Adverse events were not increased (RR 1.03 , 95% CI 0.69–1.53)
cards.watchOut: Formulations, doses, and bioavailability systems differed, most trials were short, and the evidence does not establish disease modification
cards.source: Feng J et al., BMC Complement Med Ther 2022;22:276, DOI 10.1186/s12906-022-03740-9, PMID 36261810
cards.search: feng 2022 curcuminoids knee osteoarthritis pain function vas womac systematic review meta-analysis bmc complementary medicine therapies pmid 36261810

shelves.title: Psyllium Deposit #23 · Oct 24, 2026
shelves.question: Does psyllium supplementation improve lipid profiles in adults?
shelves.balance: Three LDL sources, one consistent direction — Gholami 2025 pooled LDL −8.55 mg/dL , Anderson 2000 pooled −7% vs placebo, and Anderson’s 26-week trial −6.7% — but heterogeneity is very high (I² 88% in Gholami), and lipid changes are not cardiovascular events: a surrogate win, not an outcome win. Bonus side fact: psyllium also lowered fasting glucose ( −37.0 mg/dL ) and HbA1c ( −0.97% ) in treated type 2 diabetes (Gibb 2015) — noted here only as a bonus; the full glycemic evidence is reserved for its own shelf.

cards.type: Systematic review and random-effects dose-response meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
cards.people: 41 RCT reports with 2,049 adults: 1,124 assigned to psyllium and 925 to control
cards.result: Psyllium reduced LDL-C by 8.55 mg/dL (95% CI 4.19–12.92 mg/dL) and total cholesterol by 9.05 mg/dL (95% CI 4.40–13.71 mg/dL). LDL-C heterogeneity was high (I²=88.46%)
cards.watchOut: The trials were highly heterogeneous, and the outcomes were lipid surrogates rather than cardiovascular events The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Anderson 2000: psyllium meta-analysis
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 8 trials, 656 participants — psyllium 10.2 g/day added to a low-fat diet: LDL −7% , total cholesterol −4% vs placebo (both P<0.0001 ).
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Am J Clin Nutr 2000
cards.people: 8 trials with 656 participants: 384 assigned to psyllium and 272 to placebo
cards.result: Psyllium 10.2 g/day added to a low-fat diet lowered LDL cholesterol by 7% and total cholesterol by 4% vs placebo (both P<0.0001)
cards.watchOut: Percent reductions on a low-fat diet background; the outcomes were lipid surrogates rather than cardiovascular events
cards.source: Anderson JW et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2000;71:472–479
cards.search: anderson 2000 psyllium meta-analysis cholesterol low-fat diet ldl total cholesterol american journal clinical nutrition 71 472

cards.headline: Anderson 2000: psyllium, 26-week randomized trial
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 26 weeks , psyllium 5.1 g twice daily — LDL −6.7% , total cholesterol −4.7% vs placebo ( P<0.001 ).
cards.type: Long-term randomized controlled trial (26 weeks), Am J Clin Nutr 2000
cards.people: Adults randomized to psyllium or placebo for 26 weeks
cards.result: Psyllium 5.1 g twice daily lowered LDL cholesterol by 6.7% and total cholesterol by 4.7% vs placebo (P<0.001)
cards.watchOut: A single long-term trial; the outcomes were lipid surrogates rather than cardiovascular events
cards.source: Anderson JW et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2000;71:1433–1438
cards.search: anderson 2000 psyllium long-term randomized trial 26 weeks cholesterol ldl american journal clinical nutrition 71 1433

cards.headline: Gibb 2015: psyllium and glycemic control
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 35 randomized controlled studies — in patients being treated for type 2 diabetes, psyllium dosed before meals lowered fasting glucose −37.0 mg/dL and HbA1c −0.97% .
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled clinical studies (35 studies assessed in 8 meta-analyses covering euglycemic subjects, patients at risk of type 2 diabetes, and patients being treated for type 2 diabetes)
cards.people: 35 randomized, controlled clinical studies spanning three decades and three continents
cards.result: In patients being treated for type 2 diabetes, multiweek studies with psyllium dosed before meals showed fasting blood glucose −37.0 mg/dL (P<0.001) and HbA1c −0.97% (−10.6 mmol/mol; P=0.048). No significant glucose lowering in euglycemic subjects and only a modest improvement in pre-diabetes; the glycemic effect was proportional to baseline fasting glucose
cards.watchOut: Three of the authors — Gibb, McRorie and Russell — worked for Procter & Gamble, which sells psyllium (Metamucil), and the analysis drew on P&G’s own stored clinical records alongside the published literature. Glycemic surrogates, not clinical outcomes The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.search: gibb 2015 psyllium glycemic control fasting glucose hba1c type 2 diabetes meta-analysis randomized controlled procter gamble metamucil american journal clinical nutrition pmid 26561625

shelves.title: Peppermint oil and adverse events (Ingrosso 2022)
shelves.question: Does peppermint oil cause adverse events in IBS — and do they outweigh the benefit?
shelves.balance: In 10 trials of 1,030 patients, peppermint oil helped global IBS symptoms (RR 0.65, NNT 4) and pain (RR 0.76, NNT 7) — but any adverse event was more common (RR 1.57: 17.1% vs 12.1%), driven partly by reflux symptoms (RR 1.67), on very-low-certainty evidence. A modest benefit with a real, if uncertain, adverse-event cost.

cards.headline: Ingrosso 2022: peppermint oil in IBS — benefit and adverse events
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 10 RCTs, 1,030 IBS patients — global symptoms not improving RR 0.65 (NNT 4 ), abdominal pain RR 0.76 (NNT 7 ); but any adverse event RR 1.57 ( 17.1% vs 12.1% ) and reflux symptoms RR 1.67 , on very-low-certainty evidence.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2022
cards.people: 1,030 patients with irritable bowel syndrome in 10 eligible RCTs
cards.result: Peppermint oil vs placebo: global IBS symptoms not improving RR 0.65 (95% CI 0.43–0.98; NNT 4 ); abdominal pain not improving RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.62–0.93; NNT 7 ). Adverse events were significantly higher with peppermint oil: any adverse event RR 1.57 (95% CI 1.04–2.37), 58/340 (17.1%) vs 46/380 (12.1%) , 7 RCTs; gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms RR 1.67 (95% CI 1.18–2.38), 83/465 (17.9%) vs 34/444 (7.7%) , 8 RCTs. The authors rated the quality of evidence very low
cards.watchOut: The evidence is very-low certainty, and the adverse-event analyses rest on subsets of the trials (7 of 10 for any adverse event, 8 of 10 for reflux) The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Ingrosso MR, Ianiro G, Nee J, et al., Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2022;56(6):932–941, DOI 10.1111/apt.17179, PMID 35942669
cards.search: ingrosso 2022 peppermint oil irritable bowel syndrome ibs adverse events reflux herb harm systematic review meta-analysis randomized trials alimentary pharmacology therapeutics pmid 35942669

shelves.title: Oral arginine and blood pressure: a modest, temporary fall
shelves.question: Does oral L-arginine, taken in moderation, lower blood pressure in humans?
shelves.balance: Oral arginine lowers blood pressure — about 6 systolic and 3 diastolic across 22 trials — and the effect holds in healthy and hypertensive people alike. But it is modest, it needs at least 4 grams a day, it doesn't grow past 9 grams, and it fades: in the developer's own crossover, pressure fell within two hours and was back within an hour of stopping. The responder pattern runs through the whole story — only the people whose citrulline rose got the full metabolic effect — and the biggest drops of all came in a handful of dialysis patients starting at 171 systolic.

cards.headline: 22 oral trials: systolic −6.4, diastolic −2.6 mmHg — but no benefit past 9 g a day or past 24 days.
cards.summary: Pooled systolic −6.40 mmHg , diastolic −2.64 mmHg across 22 oral trials — effective at ≥4 g/day, no added benefit past 9 g/day.
cards.type: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials (oral L-arginine only; infusion and acute interventions excluded).
cards.people: 22 RCTs, 30 effect sizes; adults; intervention duration ≥4 days; searched to April 2021.
cards.result: Pooled SBP WMD −6.40 mmHg (95% CI −8.74, −4.05; P<0.001); DBP WMD −2.64 mmHg (−3.94, −1.40; P<0.001). Significant reductions regardless of baseline BP category (normotensive, hypertensive), study duration (≤24 days, >24 days), sex, health status, and BMI. No significant changes with dosages >9 g/day, trial duration >24 days, or in obese individuals. DBP fell more effectively in females. Dose-response: effective dosage ≥4 g/day for SBP (P=0.034).
cards.watchOut: Pooled small trials with heterogeneity; no hard outcomes (events, mortality) — blood pressure only; the long-duration and high-dose nulls cut against a bigger-is-better story. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Shiraseb F, Bagheri R, Mirzaei K, Asbaghi O. Adv Nutr. 2022. PMID 34967840. PMCID PMC9340976. DOI 10.1093/advances/nmab155.
cards.search: shiraseb 2022 oral l-arginine blood pressure systolic diastolic meta-analysis dose-response randomized placebo-controlled trials advances nutrition pmid 34967840 pmcid pmc9340976 doi 10.1093/advances/nmab155 hypertension normotensive dose

cards.headline: The first meta-analysis, a decade earlier: 11 trials, 387 people, −5.4/−2.7 mmHg.
cards.summary: Systolic −5.39 mmHg , diastolic −2.66 mmHg vs placebo — 11 trials, 387 participants, oral L-arginine 4–24 g/day.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials.
cards.people: 11 trials, 387 participants; oral L-arginine 4–24 g/day.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, SBP −5.39 mmHg (95% CI −8.54 to −2.25, P=0.001); DBP −2.66 mmHg (−3.77 to −1.54, P<0.001). Sensitivity analyses restricted to trials ≥4 weeks and to trials without antihypertensive medications yielded similar results.
cards.watchOut: Small, older trial set, superseded in size by the 2022 analysis — kept here as the decade-apart replication of the same numbers, not as independent evidence.
cards.source: Dong JY, Qin LQ, Zhang Z, Zhao Y, Wang J, Arigoni F, Zhang W. Am Heart J. 2011;162(6):959–965. DOI 10.1016/j.ahj.2011.09.012.
cards.search: dong 2011 oral l-arginine blood pressure meta-analysis randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials american heart journal doi 10.1016/j.ahj.2011.09.012 systolic diastolic

cards.headline: In type 2 diabetes with mild hypertension, oral arginine drops blood pressure for as long as you give it — then it stops.
cards.summary: Systolic 135 → 123 mmHg , diastolic 86.9 → 80.7 mmHg on arginine — 6 patients; pressure back to baseline within an hour of stopping.
cards.people: 6 patients with type 2 diabetes and mild hypertension, 3-day GCRC stay; 3 g oral arginine per hour for 10 h on day 2 or day 3, BP monitored 5 am–4 pm.
cards.result: Citrulline 31.3 ± 6.0 to 41.5 ± 6.0 µmol/L (P<0.05). Systolic BP 135 ± 7 to 123 ± 8 mmHg (P<0.05); diastolic 86.9 ± 1.7 to 80.7 ± 2.4 mmHg (P<0.05). BP fall noted 2 h after starting; BP returned to baseline within 1 h of stopping. No effect on C-peptide, insulin, or other hormones.
cards.watchOut: n=6, single-day acute crossover, no placebo arm on the BP days (each patient crossed over between arginine day and control day); a 12/6 mmHg fall that vanishes within an hour of stopping is a proof of mechanism, not a treatment result — no chronic-dosing data on this shelf. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Huynh NT, Tayek JA. J Am Coll Nutr. 2002;21(5):422–7. PMID 12356784.
cards.search: huynh tayek 2002 oral arginine blood pressure type 2 diabetes mild hypertension crossover gcrc citrulline journal american college nutrition pmid 12356784 founder acute

cards.headline: The biggest drops were in dialysis and transplant patients: 172 to 143 systolic — but tiny numbers.
cards.summary: Hemodialysis systolic 171.5 → 142.8 mmHg ; transplant crossover systolic 155.9 → 143.2 — small pilot and crossover studies.
cards.type: Prospective pilot study plus randomized crossover study.
cards.people: Pilot: 6 normotensive volunteers and 10 kidney-transplant patients (arginine 9.0 g/day × 9 days, then 18.0 g/day × 9 days); 6 hemodialysis and 4 peritoneal dialysis patients (same doses × 14 days). Crossover: 20 hypertensive kidney-transplant patients, arginine-only or arginine + canola oil, two 2-month periods with a month off between.
cards.result: Pilot: systolic pressure in hemodialysis patients fell 171.5 ± 7.5 to 142.8 ± 8.3 mmHg (P=0.028). Crossover: systolic 155.9 ± 5.0 at baseline to 143.2 ± 3.2 after the first 2 months (P=0.03) and 143.3 ± 2.5 after the second 2 months (P=0.014); diastolic also fell. Renal function did not change. Canola oil had no effect. Arginine was well tolerated for up to 60 consecutive days.
cards.watchOut: Small pilot plus small crossover; the pilot phase had no placebo arm; the largest drops were in a handful of dialysis patients starting at 171 systolic — regression to the mean and small numbers both apply. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Kelly BS, Alexander JW, Dreyer D, et al. J Parenter Enteral Nutr. 2001;25(4):194–202. PMID 11434650. DOI 10.1177/0148607101025004194.
cards.search: kelly 2001 oral arginine blood pressure kidney transplant dialysis hemodialysis peritoneal canola oil crossover pilot journal parenteral enteral nutrition pmid 11434650 doi 10.1177/0148607101025004194 renal

cards.headline: Oral arginine cuts glucose production — but only in the people whose citrulline rises.
cards.summary: Glucose production fell 16.2% on arginine vs 9.7% on alanine — but only in the 10 volunteers whose citrulline rose ≥30%.
cards.type: Acute physiology study, arginine vs L-alanine control.
cards.people: 15 normal-weight volunteers, 3 g freebase arginine or alanine hourly 4 am–2 pm, 3-day GCRC stay; neither changed C-peptide or insulin.
cards.result: Arginine group glucose-production fall 16.2% ± 1.9% vs alanine 9.7% ± 3.6% (P<0.05). Split by citrulline response: 10 volunteers with ≥30% citrulline rise (29 ± 2 to 49 ± 4 µmol/L, P<0.05) cut glucose production 18.2% ± 1.9% over the final 4 h (2.00 ± 0.08 to 1.64 ± 0.07 mg/kg/min, P<0.01); 5 with <30% rise (26 ± 2 to 32 ± 2 µmol/L) cut it only 12.4% ± 3.9% (1.97 ± 0.13 to 1.73 ± 0.13 mg/kg/min, NS) — indistinguishable from alanine controls.
cards.watchOut: n=15, single-day acute dosing in healthy volunteers; the responder split is post-hoc by citrulline rise, and citrulline is only an indirect marker of nitric-oxide generation — no NO was measured directly. This is a mechanism card (oral arginine engages the NO pathway), not a blood-pressure outcome. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.search: apostol tayek 2003 oral arginine glucose production citrulline nitric oxide alanine metabolism pmid 14624416 doi 10.1016/s0026-0495(03)00323-8 responder founder acute physiology

shelves.title: Cranberry for recurrent urinary tract infection
shelves.question: Does cranberry prevent recurrent urinary tract infection in women?
shelves.balance: A defined product at a defined dose — 500 mg a day of whole cranberry fruit powder — halved recurrence in one good trial. Across 50 trials of mixed products the average is about 30% fewer UTIs. Product and dose are the whole story: juice and mixed products vary, and the pooled number is an average over unlike products.

cards.headline: Across 50 trials, cranberry products cut symptomatic UTI risk by about 30%.
cards.summary: Cranberry products reduced the risk of symptomatic urinary tract infection, risk ratio 0.70 .
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
cards.people: 50 trials, 8,857 participants; cranberry products (juice, tablets, capsules) vs placebo, no treatment, or other interventions.
cards.result: Cranberry products reduced the risk of symptomatic urinary tract infection, risk ratio 0.70 .
cards.watchOut: Pooled across unlike products and doses — juice, tablets, capsules, mixed formulations; the pooled RR is an average, not the effect of any one product at any one dose; heterogeneity in product and dose is the main limitation.
cards.source: Williams G, Hahn D, Stephens JH, Craig JC, Hodson EM. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023;(4):CD001321. (PMID to confirm from the PubMed record before build.)
cards.search: cochrane 2023 cranberry urinary tract infection uti prevention women systematic review meta-analysis williams cd001321

cards.headline: Stonehouse 2025: cranberry for recurrent UTI
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 150 women with recurrent UTI, 145 analyzed — culture-confirmed UTI adjusted RR 0.48 (0.26–0.87) with cranberry 500 mg/day; first UTI adjusted HR 0.36 .
cards.people: 150 women aged 18–65 years with recurrent uncomplicated UTI were randomized; 145 were included in the primary full-analysis set
cards.result: Whole cranberry powder (Pacran) 500 mg/day reduced culture-confirmed UTI risk versus placebo (adjusted RR 0.48 , 95% CI 0.26–0.87; P=0.01), delayed the first UTI (adjusted HR 0.36 , 95% CI 0.18–0.74), and reduced total UTIs per participant (adjusted IRR 0.41 , 95% CI 0.21–0.79)
cards.watchOut: Only half of the planned 300 participants were enrolled, and the sponsor and raw-material supplier helped design and monitor this specific proprietary-product trial The tested product was Pacran (Givaudan Flavors Corp.), marketed as the Swisse cranberry supplement; the study was sponsored by Swisse Wellness Pty Ltd.
cards.source: Stonehouse W et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2025;121:932–941, DOI 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2025.01.022, PMID 39863114
cards.search: stonehouse 2025 cranberry recurrent urinary tract infection women randomized double blind american journal clinical nutrition pmid 39863114

shelves.title: Creatine monohydrate in older adults
shelves.question: Does creatine monohydrate help older adults — and what does it do to the creatinine?
shelves.balance: Creatine adds a small strength increment on top of resistance training in healthy older adults — g 0.31 — while muscle mass and physical function show no significant additional benefit. And it reliably raises serum creatinine while true kidney filtration stays put. Know both before you prescribe it or interpret the labs.

cards.headline: Creatine plus training adds a small strength effect in adults over 60 — g 0.31 — but mass and function do not move.
cards.summary: Muscle strength significantly improved, small effect (Hedges g 0.31, 95% CI 0.18–0.45 ), moderate certainty of evidence. Pooled effects on muscle mass (g 0.35, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.78 ) and physical function (g 0.47, 95% CI −0.08 to 1.03; p=0.086 ) were not statistically significant, with low and very low certainty respectively. No moderator — creatine dose, loading phase, intervention duration, training frequency, training intensity, sex, or testing site — explained the variation.
cards.type: Systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
cards.people: 11 RCTs; adults aged 60 years and older; creatine plus resistance training vs resistance training alone or placebo plus resistance training.
cards.result: Muscle strength significantly improved, small effect (Hedges g 0.31, 95% CI 0.18–0.45 ), moderate certainty of evidence. Pooled effects on muscle mass (g 0.35, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.78 ) and physical function (g 0.47, 95% CI −0.08 to 1.03; p=0.086 ) were not statistically significant, with low and very low certainty respectively. No moderator — creatine dose, loading phase, intervention duration, training frequency, training intensity, sex, or testing site — explained the variation.
cards.watchOut: The strength effect is small and on top of training, not instead of it; mass and function nulls; findings should not be extrapolated to frail, sarcopenic, or functionally limited older adults.
cards.source: Yao L, Yang D, Gao J. Front Nutr. 2026;13:1919884. DOI 10.3389/fnut.2026.1919884. PROSPERO CRD420261417231.
cards.search: yao 2026 creatine resistance training older adults strength muscle mass physical function three-level meta-analysis hedges frontiers nutrition 1919884

cards.headline: Creatine raises serum creatinine by 0.14 mg/dL — but measured kidney filtration does not change.
cards.summary: Serum creatinine rose 0.14 mg/dL (95% CI 0.05–0.22, P=0.002) ; creatinine-based eGFR fell 10.75 mL/min/1.73 m² . Measured GFR (chromium-EDTA) did not change significantly (mean difference +5.89, P=0.06 ).
cards.people: 26 studies, 1,036 participants.
cards.result: Serum creatinine rose 0.14 mg/dL (95% CI 0.05–0.22, P=0.002) ; creatinine-based eGFR fell 10.75 mL/min/1.73 m² . Measured GFR (chromium-EDTA) did not change significantly (mean difference +5.89, P=0.06 ).
cards.watchOut: The creatinine rise is the artifact — creatine is metabolized to creatinine, so the lab value rises while true filtration is unchanged; read cystatin C or a measured GFR, not the creatinine-based eGFR, in someone taking creatine. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: de Souza Almeida et al. Int Urol Nephrol. 2026. PMID 42507286. DOI 10.1007/s11255-026-05287-x.
cards.search: de souza almeida 2026 creatine creatinine kidney gfr egfr chromium-edta meta-analysis international urology nephrology pmid 42507286 doi 10.1007/s11255-026-05287-x

cards.headline: Chilibeck 2017: creatine with resistance training in older adults
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 22 trials, 721 older adults — lean mass +1.37 kg (0.97–1.76) with creatine plus training; chest-press SMD 0.35 , leg-press SMD 0.24 .
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
cards.people: 22 trials with 721 men and women; mean ages across studies ranged from 57 to 70 years
cards.result: Creatine plus resistance training increased lean tissue mass by 1.37 kg more than placebo plus training (95% CI 0.97–1.76). Chest-press strength improved by SMD 0.35 (95% CI 0.16–0.53), and leg-press strength by SMD 0.24 (95% CI 0.05–0.43)
cards.watchOut: Most trials were small and short, and they measured lean mass and strength rather than disability, falls, fractures, or independence The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Chilibeck PD et al., Open Access J Sports Med 2017;8:213–226, DOI 10.2147/OAJSM.S123529, PMID 29138605
cards.search: chilibeck 2017 creatine resistance training older adults lean mass strength systematic review meta-analysis open access journal sports medicine pmid 29138605

shelves.title: Standardized red yeast rice
shelves.question: Does standardized red yeast rice prevent cardiovascular events?
shelves.balance: One hard-outcome trial in post-MI patients — 45% fewer coronary events — plus a modern LDL trial. But both are standardized products, and the supplement-market version is not the trial product: Xuezhikang is a prescription-grade extract in China, and over-the-counter red yeast rice varies in monacolin content.

cards.headline: In post-MI patients, a standardized red yeast rice extract cut major coronary events by 45%.
cards.summary: Primary endpoint (major coronary events: nonfatal MI and death from coronary heart disease) 5.7% with Xuezhikang vs 10.4% with placebo — a 45% relative reduction. Cardiovascular death 30% lower; total death 33% lower.
cards.people: ~4,870 patients with previous myocardial infarction; mean follow-up 4.5 years.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (major coronary events: nonfatal MI and death from coronary heart disease) 5.7% with Xuezhikang vs 10.4% with placebo — a 45% relative reduction. Cardiovascular death 30% lower; total death 33% lower.
cards.watchOut: Chinese post-MI secondary-prevention population; Xuezhikang is a standardized extract containing naturally occurring monacolin K (lovastatin-like) — it is a prescription-grade product in China, not the variable over-the-counter red yeast rice sold as a supplement elsewhere.
cards.search: lu 2008 xuezhikang red yeast rice myocardial infarction coronary events secondary prevention monacolin china american journal cardiology pmid 18549841

cards.headline: Natto red yeast rice 1,950 mg a day cut LDL by 21 mg/dL — 13% — vs placebo.
cards.summary: LDL-C −21.02 mg/dL (−13.21%) vs placebo (P<0.001).
cards.people: 1,110 participants; natto red yeast rice 1,950 mg/day vs placebo.
cards.result: LDL-C −21.02 mg/dL (−13.21%) vs placebo (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Surrogate endpoint (LDL-C), not events; the event benefit on this shelf is carried by Lu 2008, not this trial. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Coenzyme Q10 in heart failure (Q-SYMBIO)
shelves.question: Does coenzyme Q10 improve outcomes in chronic heart failure?
shelves.balance: One trial says CoQ10 halves events in heart failure; everything around it says handle with care — the earlier literature was 395 patients of short-term surrogate data (ejection fraction +3.67% , Fotino 2013), and the pooled mortality benefit ( RR 0.69 , Lei & Liu 2017; Cochrane 2021: probably reduces mortality and hospitalisation) appears only when Q-SYMBIO is in the pool. The honest statement is not “CoQ10 works” but “one good trial, never replicated, carries the entire outcome claim.”

cards.headline: Fotino 2013: before Q-SYMBIO, the evidence was 395 patients and a surrogate — ejection fraction +3.67%
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 13 randomized trials, 395 participants, all small and short (2–28 weeks) — net ejection fraction change +3.67% (1.60–5.74) ; NYHA class change −0.30 (−0.66 to 0.06) , not significant. No mortality data existed to pool.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized trials, Am J Clin Nutr 2013
cards.people: 13 randomized trials, 395 participants — all small and short (2–28 weeks)
cards.result: Net ejection fraction change +3.67% (95% CI 1.60–5.74); NYHA class change −0.30 (−0.66 to 0.06), not significant
cards.watchOut: Surrogate endpoints only — no mortality data existed to pool; this was the entire evidence base when Q-SYMBIO reported The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Fotino AD et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2013;97(2):268–275. DOI 10.3945/ajcn.112.040741. PMID 23221577
cards.search: fotino 2013 coenzyme q10 heart failure meta-analysis ejection fraction nyha american journal clinical nutrition pmid 23221577 doi 10.3945/ajcn.112.040741 pre q-symbio

cards.headline: Al Saadi 2021 (Cochrane): probably reduces mortality and hospitalisation — yet “no convincing evidence to support or refute”
cards.summary: Cochrane review 2021 — moderate-quality evidence that CoQ10 probably reduces all-cause mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation (hospitalisation RR 0.62 (0.49–0.78) ; 2 studies, 1,061 participants); ejection fraction +1.77 on very low-quality evidence. The authors still conclude there is no convincing evidence to support or refute CoQ10 for heart failure.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021
cards.people: Randomized trials of CoQ10 in heart failure; the hospitalisation estimate pools 2 studies with 1,061 participants
cards.result: Moderate-quality evidence that CoQ10 probably reduces all-cause mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation (hospitalisation RR 0.62 , 95% CI 0.49–0.78; 2 studies, 1,061 participants); ejection fraction mean difference +1.77 (0.09–3.44) on very low-quality evidence. The authors’ conclusion: “no convincing evidence to support or refute the use of coenzyme Q10 for heart failure”
cards.watchOut: Contrast the 2014 Cochrane review (7 RCTs, 914 participants, before Q-SYMBIO), which found no mortality effect — adding the one trial moved the pooled answer

cards.headline: Lei & Liu 2017: pooled mortality RR 0.69 — a signal that exists only with Q-SYMBIO in the pool
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 14 trials, 2,149 participants including Q-SYMBIO — mortality RR 0.69 (0.50–0.95) and improved exercise capacity; the authors call for further trials.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2017
cards.people: 14 trials, 2,149 participants, including Q-SYMBIO
cards.result: Mortality RR 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.95) and improved exercise capacity; the authors call for further trials
cards.watchOut: The pooled mortality signal appears only in analyses that include Q-SYMBIO — remove the one trial and the outcome claim goes with it
cards.source: Lei L, Liu Y. BMC Cardiovasc Disord 2017

cards.headline: Mortensen 2014 (Q-SYMBIO): CoQ10 in chronic heart failure
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 420 patients with NYHA III/IV heart failure — major adverse CV events 30/202 (15%) vs 57/218 (26%) , HR 0.50 (0.32–0.80) at 106 weeks.
cards.people: 420 patients with chronic NYHA class III or IV heart failure; 202 received CoQ10 100 mg three times daily and 218 received placebo
cards.result: At 106 weeks, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 30/202 (15%) with CoQ10 versus 57/218 (26%) with placebo ( HR 0.50 , 95% CI 0.32–0.80; P=0.003). Cardiovascular death was 18/202 (9%) versus 34/218 (16%) (HR 0.51), and all-cause death was 21/202 (10%) versus 39/218 (18%) (HR 0.51)

shelves.title: Oat beta-glucan and LDL cholesterol
shelves.question: Does oat beta-glucan lower LDL cholesterol?
shelves.balance: The pooled trials say about 10 mg/dL off LDL (0.25 mmol/L) at 3 grams a day or more; the newest feeding trial points the same way but doesn't reach significance on its own. A food, not a pill — the dose is a bowl of oats.

cards.headline: Oat beta-glucan at 3 grams a day or more: LDL down about 10 mg/dL across 28 trials.
cards.summary: LDL-C −10 mg/dL (the paper reports −0.25 mmol/L; 95% CI ≈8–12 mg/dL, converted from 0.20–0.30 mmol/L); total cholesterol −12 mg/dL (−0.30 mmol/L).
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
cards.people: 28 RCTs; oat beta-glucan ≥3 g/day.
cards.result: LDL-C −10 mg/dL (the paper reports −0.25 mmol/L; 95% CI ≈8–12 mg/dL, converted from 0.20–0.30 mmol/L); total cholesterol −12 mg/dL (−0.30 mmol/L).
cards.watchOut: Surrogate endpoint (LDL-C), not events; dose threshold ≥3 g/day — below that, no effect shown; the effect is modest and food-based. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.result: LDL-C −11.2 mg/dL with the oat diet vs control (p=0.0638 across diets).

shelves.title: Alpha-lipoic acid in diabetic neuropathy
shelves.question: Does alpha-lipoic acid ease diabetic neuropathy?
shelves.balance: Alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg eases neuropathic symptoms in five weeks, and the 2026 pool agrees on symptoms while the objective nerve measures stay flat. Symptom relief, not disease modification — and 600 mg is the dose; higher doses add side effects without added benefit.

cards.headline: 600 mg a day for 5 weeks: symptom score down 51%, response 62% vs 26% on placebo.
cards.summary: Total Symptom Score fell 4.9 points (51%) at 600 mg vs 2.9 points (32%) on placebo; clinical response 62% vs 26% . Higher doses did not add benefit and added side effects.
cards.people: 181 patients with diabetic polyneuropathy; alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg, 1,200 mg, or 1,800 mg daily vs placebo for 5 weeks.
cards.result: Total Symptom Score fell 4.9 points (51%) at 600 mg vs 2.9 points (32%) on placebo; clinical response 62% vs 26% . Higher doses did not add benefit and added side effects.
cards.watchOut: 5 weeks — short; symptom score, not nerve conduction or hard outcomes; the 600 mg dose is the effective one. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Ziegler D et al. Diabetes Care. 2006;29(11):2365–2370. PMID 17065669.

shelves.title: Beni-kōji (red yeast rice) supplement outbreak, Japan 2024 — a contamination event
shelves.question: What happened when a mold toxin contaminated beni-kōji supplements in Japan in 2024?
shelves.balance: This shelf documents a manufacturing contamination failure, not a pharmacological harm of red yeast rice — the deaths and kidney injuries trace to puberulic acid from mold contamination of specific 2023 batches, not to monacolin K or to beni-kōji as an ingredient. It sits next to Shelf #52 (red yeast rice LDL evidence) as the product-safety record for the same ingredient class, and as a case study in the risks of a lightly regulated supplement category (Japan’s “foods with function claims”).

cards.headline: The official record: three supplements recalled, 5 deaths confirmed — and 76 more under investigation as suspected.
cards.summary: On March 22, 2024, Kobayashi Pharmaceutical recalled three beni-kōji supplements after consumers developed kidney injury; about 300,000 units were recalled. By the end of April 2024, 5 deaths were confirmed in people who had taken the supplements and more than 240 people had been hospitalized ; on June 28, 2024 the health ministry announced 76 further deaths were under investigation as suspected to be related. The cause identified was puberulic acid , a toxic compound produced by blue mold (Penicillium) in the implicated products.
cards.type: Official outbreak record — recall and investigation announcements (Kobayashi Pharmaceutical; Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare), 2024.
cards.people: Consumers of Kobayashi Pharmaceutical beni-kōji supplements in Japan; the ingredient had also been supplied to dozens of other companies (later tallies ~170), spreading recalls to foods and to Taiwan.
cards.result: On March 22, 2024, Kobayashi Pharmaceutical recalled three beni-kōji (red yeast rice) supplements — Benikoji CholesteHelp (“Red Koji Cholesterol Help”), Naishi Help Plus Cholesterol, and Natto-kinase Sarasara Tsubu GOLD — after consumers developed kidney injury; about 300,000 units were recalled. By the end of April 2024, 5 deaths were confirmed in people who had taken the supplements, and more than 240 people had been hospitalized . On June 28, 2024, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare announced 76 further deaths were under investigation as suspected to be related — reported totals must therefore always be split confirmed vs suspected. On March 29, 2024 the ministry announced detection of puberulic acid , a toxic compound produced by blue mold (Penicillium), in the implicated products; rat studies later showed the implicated product and puberulic acid alone caused renal tubular degeneration and necrosis, and two further unexpected mold-derived compounds were found. Kobayashi discontinued beni-kōji production on August 8, 2024.
cards.watchOut: This is a contamination event, not a trial result and not evidence about beni-kōji itself: the harm traces to puberulic acid in specific 2023 batches, not to monacolin K. Death totals moved during the investigation — only the 5 are confirmed; the 76 were under investigation as suspected, not established as caused by the products.
cards.source: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (Japan) and Kobayashi Pharmaceutical announcements, 2024: recall, March 22; puberulic acid detection, March 29; suspected deaths under investigation, June 28; production discontinued, August 8.
cards.search: beni-koji red yeast rice kobayashi pharmaceutical recall japan 2024 puberulic acid penicillium mold contamination kidney injury ministry of health labour welfare outbreak cholestehelp

cards.headline: The clinical syndrome: Fanconi syndrome from acute proximal tubular injury — and kidney function often did not fully come back.
cards.summary: The renal lesion was acute proximal tubular injury producing Fanconi syndrome — phosphate, glucose, amino-acid and bicarbonate wasting. Kidney biopsies showed acute tubular injury / tubulointerstitial nephritis with normal glomeruli. Most patients did not fully recover kidney function after stopping the supplement, though electrolytes and urine abnormalities improved with discontinuation, fluids, and electrolyte correction.
cards.type: Case series report compiling the published cases.
cards.people: Patients who developed kidney injury after taking a beni-kōji supplement — the published cases (Murata, Takeuchi, Oda, Maiguma, Miyazaki, Chikasue 2024) plus the authors’ two cases.
cards.result: The renal lesion was acute proximal tubular injury producing Fanconi syndrome (phosphate, glucose, amino-acid and bicarbonate wasting). Kidney biopsies showed acute tubular injury / tubulointerstitial nephritis with normal glomeruli. Most patients did not fully recover kidney function after stopping the supplement, though electrolytes and urine abnormalities improved with discontinuation, fluids, and electrolyte correction.
cards.watchOut: A case series describes the syndrome and its course in the published cases — it cannot give the frequency of injury among all users; the exposure side of the record is Card 1. Incomplete recovery is the pattern in these reported cases, which are the more severe end of the outbreak.
cards.source: “Fanconi syndrome with acute proximal tubular injury induced by a dietary supplement containing beni-koji: a case series report.” BMC Nephrol. 2024. DOI 10.1186/s12882-024-03903-5.

shelves.title: Nigella sativa (black seed) — safety: no harm signal found
shelves.question: What harm, if any, does oral Nigella sativa (black seed) cause at the doses used in trials?
shelves.balance: Across two decades of reviews and the trial record, no severe harm signal for oral Nigella sativa at customary doses (1–3 g/day seeds, 5 mL/day oil) has been found — the documented items are minor gastrointestinal effects, rare skin reactions (mostly topical), a hypoglycemia note in hepatitis C patients, and a CYP-interaction flag at 5 g/day. This shelf exists so the negative is on the record: examined, not overlooked.

cards.headline: Mashayekhi-Sardoo 2020: no severe adverse effects in the clinical trial record
cards.summary: Narrative safety review — clinical trials report no severe adverse effects ; the oil at 5 mL/day for 26 days and seeds at 1–3 g/day for 3 months produced no significant hepatic, renal, or gastrointestinal harm, and pooled analyses show no significant change in liver or kidney biochemistry.
cards.people: Patients in the clinical trials reviewed — including diabetic and centrally obese patients taking seeds, and hepatitis C patients taking seed-oil capsules
cards.result: Clinical trials report no severe adverse effects . The oil at 5 mL/day for 26 days produced no significant hepatic, renal, or gastrointestinal adverse effects; seeds at 1–3 g/day for 3 months in diabetic and centrally obese patients produced no significant alterations in renal or hepatic function; pooled analyses likewise show no significant change in liver or kidney biochemistry. Items that do appear in the record: epigastric pain and hypoglycemia in hepatitis C patients taking seed-oil capsules; one study reporting increased AST/ALT and γ-GT/ALP activities with the oil; inhibition of CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 by seeds at 5 g/day (a drug-interaction flag, shown in microsomes and volunteers); and case reports of allergic contact dermatitis after topical use and one case of erythema multiforme with capsules
cards.watchOut: A narrative review of a small, heterogeneous trial record — no severe signal found is not proof of safety at higher doses or over longer use, and the CYP2D6/CYP3A4 inhibition at 5 g/day is a real interaction flag for drugs cleared by those enzymes
cards.source: Mashayekhi-Sardoo H et al., Asian Biomedicine 2020;14(4):127–137; PMID 37551386; DOI 10.1515/abm-2020-0020
cards.search: nigella sativa black seed safety review mashayekhi-sardoo 2020 asian biomedicine adverse effects hepatic renal gastrointestinal cyp2d6 cyp3a4 inhibition contact dermatitis erythema multiforme hypoglycemia hepatitis c pmid 37551386

cards.headline: Ali & Blunden 2003: “a very low degree of toxicity”
cards.summary: The classic pharmacology and toxicology review — the seeds are characterized by “a very low degree of toxicity” ; seed extract or oil has not induced significant adverse effects on liver or kidney function, and the human harm reports it records are two cases of contact dermatitis after topical use.
cards.type: Pharmacology and toxicology review, Phytotherapy Research 2003
cards.people: The human reports in the literature reviewed, alongside laboratory toxicology of seed extract and oil
cards.result: The seeds are characterized by “a very low degree of toxicity” ; administration of seed extract or oil has not induced significant adverse effects on liver or kidney function; two cases of contact dermatitis after topical use are the human harm reports the review records
cards.watchOut: A 2003 review — it predates much of the modern trial record; read with Card 1 (2020), which reaches the same conclusion two decades later The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Ali BH, Blunden G, Phytotherapy Research 2003; PMID 12722128; DOI 10.1002/ptr.1309

shelves.title: Glucosamine (± chondroitin) and warfarin — the INR interaction
shelves.question: Does glucosamine, with or without chondroitin, raise the INR in patients taking warfarin?
shelves.balance: In randomized trials glucosamine and chondroitin are as benign as placebo; the one consistent post-marketing signal is INR elevation in patients on warfarin — case-report grade and mechanism unknown, but noted by the FDA, WHO, and EFSA, and clinically actionable: a patient on warfarin who starts glucosamine needs INR monitoring. (Not carded: three liver-injury cases on multi-ingredient glucosamine products in the LiverTox record — the products contained other potentially hepatotoxic herbals and were never characterized, so attribution is not possible.)

cards.headline: Knudsen & Sokol 2008: INR rose after glucosamine/chondroitin was started — in one case only after the dose was tripled
cards.summary: Case report and database review — patients previously stabilized on warfarin showed significant INR increases after starting glucosamine/chondroitin; in one case the INR rose only after the dose was tripled, from 500 mg/400 mg to 1,500 mg/1,200 mg daily . MedWatch held about 20 reports linking the combination to increased INR, bruising, or bleeding, and the WHO database about 20 further reports for glucosamine alone.
cards.type: Case report and review of the literature and the FDA MedWatch database, Pharmacotherapy 2008
cards.people: Patients previously stabilized on warfarin who started glucosamine/chondroitin, plus spontaneous reports in the MedWatch and WHO databases
cards.result: Patients previously stabilized on warfarin showed significant INR increases after starting glucosamine/chondroitin; in one case the INR rose only after the glucosamine/chondroitin dose was tripled (from 500 mg/400 mg to 1,500 mg/1,200 mg daily ). The MedWatch review found about 20 reports linking glucosamine plus chondroitin to increased INR, bruising, or bleeding in warfarin patients, and the WHO database holds about 20 further reports for glucosamine alone; the European Food Safety Authority has noted roughly 40 cases with coumarin anticoagulants
cards.watchOut: Mechanism unknown; all evidence is case-report grade — no controlled study has tested the interaction. Spontaneous reports cannot give a rate, but the signal recurs across independent databases (FDA, WHO, EFSA)
cards.source: Knudsen JF, Sokol GH, “Potential glucosamine-warfarin interaction resulting in increased international normalized ratio: case report and review of the literature and MedWatch database,” Pharmacotherapy 2008
cards.search: glucosamine chondroitin warfarin interaction inr international normalized ratio knudsen sokol 2008 pharmacotherapy case report medwatch fda who efsa coumarin bleeding bruising

cards.headline: Sawitzke 2010 (GAIT): two years of glucosamine/chondroitin, adverse events no different from placebo
cards.summary: GAIT 2-year results — 662 patients with knee osteoarthritis on glucosamine, chondroitin, both, celecoxib, or placebo: adverse-event rates were similar across all groups and no liver-related serious adverse event occurred. Miller & Clegg 2011 conclude that other than a possible interaction with warfarin, no serious adverse events have been linked to long-term use.
cards.type: Randomized trial safety results (GAIT, 2-year), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 2010; with a review conclusion, Rheumatic Disease Clinics of North America 2011
cards.people: 662 patients with knee osteoarthritis randomized to glucosamine, chondroitin, both, celecoxib, or placebo for 2 years
cards.result: Adverse-event rates were similar across all groups and no liver-related serious adverse event occurred . Miller & Clegg 2011 conclude that other than a possible interaction with warfarin, no serious adverse events have been linked to long-term use of glucosamine and chondroitin
cards.watchOut: A trial population screened for a knee-osteoarthritis study — patients on warfarin are exactly the group a trial like this underrepresents, so the trial’s clean record does not answer Card 1’s interaction question The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Sawitzke AD et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2010;69:1459–1464; PMID 20525840 · Miller KL, Clegg DO, Rheum Dis Clin North Am 2011; PMID 21220090

shelves.title: Turmeric/curcumin liver injury — the bioavailability-enhanced product problem
shelves.question: Can turmeric or curcumin supplements injure the liver — and is the injury tied to the modern high-absorption formulations?
shelves.balance: Culinary turmeric and plain curcumin show a flat adverse-event record in trials (pooled RR ~1.03) — the liver injury belongs to bioavailability-enhanced products (piperine combinations, phytosome and similar formulations engineered to defeat curcumin’s poor absorption). Three independent literatures converge: US DILIN clinical cases (10, one fatal), Italian phytovigilance (7 cases plus 23 in review; mandatory warning labels followed), and a US pathology series (11 cases). The injury is hepatocellular, appears 1–4 months in, and concentrates in HLA-B*35:01 carriers; NIH LiverTox now rates turmeric/curcumin a well-documented cause of clinically apparent liver injury, and Australia’s TGA issued a 2023 alert (9 assessable reports, one death). Rare, idiosyncratic, occasionally fatal — and invisible to the trial adverse-event pooling.

cards.headline: Halegoua-DeMarzio 2023 (DILIN): 10 adjudicated turmeric liver-injury cases — 5 hospitalized, 1 death
cards.summary: US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network — 10 adjudicated cases of turmeric-associated liver injury enrolled 2004–2022, all since 2011 and six since 2017; 8 women , median age 56 ; injury hepatocellular in 9 of 10 , latency 1–4 months ; 5 hospitalized and 1 died of acute liver failure. 7 of 10 patients carried HLA-B*35:01.
cards.type: Adjudicated case series, US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network (DILIN), American Journal of Medicine 2023
cards.people: 10 patients with turmeric-associated liver injury enrolled 2004–2022 — all since 2011, six since 2017; 8 women, median age 56
cards.result: Injury was hepatocellular in 9 of 10 cases, with latency of 1–4 months ; 5 patients were hospitalized and 1 died of acute liver failure . Chemical analysis confirmed turmeric in all 7 products tested , 3 of which also contained piperine (black pepper). 7 of 10 patients carried HLA-B*35:01 (allele frequency 0.45 vs ~0.06 in population controls)
cards.watchOut: A case series has no exposure denominator, so it cannot give an incidence rate — it establishes that the injury occurs and what it looks like, not how often. The products were supplements, not culinary turmeric; the HLA association rests on 10 patients The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Halegoua-DeMarzio D et al., Am J Med 2023;136(2):200–206; PMID 36252717
cards.search: turmeric curcumin liver injury dilin drug induced liver injury network halegoua-demarzio 2023 american journal of medicine hepatocellular hla-b*35:01 piperine black pepper acute liver failure pmid 36252717

cards.headline: Lombardi 2021: 7 Tuscan cases — every one a high-bioavailability, high-dose curcumin formulation
cards.summary: Italian Phytovigilance database — 7 Tuscan cases of acute cholestatic hepatitis on Curcuma longa supplements, in every case a high-bioavailability, high-dose curcumin formulation, with causality supported by positive dechallenge in most; the paper’s systematic review identified 23 further published cases . Italy’s case cluster led to a mandatory liver-warning label on curcuma supplements from January 2020.
cards.type: Phytovigilance case series with systematic review, British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology 2021
cards.people: 7 patients in Tuscany with acute cholestatic hepatitis while taking Curcuma longa supplements, reported to the Italian Phytovigilance database
cards.result: In every case the product was a high-bioavailability, high-dose curcumin formulation ; causality was supported by positive dechallenge in most cases. The accompanying systematic review identified 23 further published cases of curcuma-associated liver injury. Italy’s case cluster led to a mandatory liver-warning label on curcuma supplements from January 2020
cards.watchOut: Spontaneous reports cannot give a rate, and reporting may be stimulated by publicity. The pattern here was cholestatic, against hepatocellular in the US DILIN series (Reference 1) — the injury pattern may vary by formulation
cards.source: Lombardi N et al., Br J Clin Pharmacol 2021;87:741–753; DOI 10.1111/bcp.14460
cards.search: turmeric curcuma longa curcumin liver injury lombardi 2021 british journal clinical pharmacology italian phytovigilance tuscany cholestatic hepatitis high bioavailability piperine warning label doi 10.1111/bcp.14460

cards.headline: Papke 2025: 11 pathology cases — panlobular and zone 3 injury under the microscope
cards.summary: Pathology-archive series from 5 US medical centers — 11 cases of turmeric supplement–associated hepatitis showing panlobular and zone 3 (centrilobular) injury; 7 patients symptomatic , 5 jaundiced , none died . Independent tissue-level corroboration of the DILIN clinical series.
cards.type: Pathology-archive case series, 5 US medical centers, Histopathology 2025
cards.people: 11 patients with turmeric supplement–associated hepatitis identified in pathology archives
cards.result: Biopsies showed panlobular and zone 3 (centrilobular) injury; 7 patients were symptomatic and 5 jaundiced ; none died . The series independently corroborates the DILIN clinical cases (Reference 1) at tissue level
cards.watchOut: Pathology-archive cases are selected for having had a biopsy, which skews toward more severe or diagnostically uncertain presentations; no exposure denominator, so no rate can be derived The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Papke DJ et al., Histopathology 2025;86:410–422; PMID 39381846

shelves.title: Melatonin for sleep onset
shelves.question: Does melatonin improve sleep onset, total sleep time, or sleep quality in primary sleep disorders?
shelves.balance: Melatonin shortens the time to fall asleep by minutes, on average — a real, small, replicated effect on a symptom, not a treatment for any disease.

cards.headline: Ferracioli-Oda 2013: melatonin for primary sleep disorders
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 19 trials, 1,683 adults and children — sleep latency −7.06 minutes (4.37–9.75) ; total sleep +8.25 minutes ; quality SMD 0.22 .
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized, placebo-controlled trials
cards.people: 19 trials with 1,683 adults and children with primary sleep disorders
cards.result: Melatonin reduced sleep latency by 7.06 minutes (95% CI 4.37–9.75), increased total sleep time by 8.25 minutes (95% CI 1.74–14.75), and improved sleep quality by SMD 0.22 (95% CI 0.12–0.32)
cards.watchOut: Populations and sleep disorders varied, and the absolute improvements in sleep onset and duration were small The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Ferracioli-Oda E et al., PLoS One 2013;8:e63773, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0063773, PMID 23691095

shelves.title: Peppermint oil for irritable bowel syndrome
shelves.question: Does peppermint oil relieve the pain and global symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome — and does the answer survive a large, rigorous trial with regulator-defined endpoints?
shelves.balance: Peppermint oil is the supplement shelf’s small-trial parable: a dozen small trials pool into a large, tidy benefit (RR 2.39) — and then the largest, most rigorous trial (PERSUADE) misses its primary endpoint while its secondaries nod yes. The effect on IBS pain and global symptoms is probably real and probably smaller than the pooled number; formulation and release site may decide who gets it. Symptom relief is the entire claim — there are no disease outcomes in IBS to win.

cards.headline: Alammar 2019: twelve small trials pooled — peppermint oil more than doubled global IBS improvement (RR 2.39) and improved abdominal pain (RR 1.78), with no significant excess of adverse events.
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 12 RCTs, 835 patients — global symptom improvement RR 2.39 (1.93–2.97) across 7 trials; abdominal pain RR 1.78 (1.43–2.20) across 6 trials; number needed to treat 3 for global symptoms and 4 for pain; adverse events 9.3% vs 6.1% (RR 1.40, P=0.16).
cards.type: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (protocol registered on PROSPERO)
cards.people: 12 randomized trials with 835 patients with IBS. The global-improvement pool covered 7 trials (253 patients on peppermint oil vs 254 on placebo) and the abdominal-pain pool 6 trials (278 vs 278)
cards.result: Global symptom improvement: risk ratio 2.39 (95% CI 1.93–2.97; I²=0%; P<0.00001). Abdominal pain: risk ratio 1.78 (95% CI 1.43–2.20; I²=0%; P<0.00001). The number needed to treat to prevent one patient from having persistent symptoms was 3 for global symptoms and 4 for abdominal pain. Adverse events, pooled across 8 trials, did not differ: 32 events in 344 patients (9.3%) on peppermint oil vs 20 in 327 (6.1%) on placebo (RR 1.40 , 95% CI 0.87–2.26; P=0.16)
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and short, the endpoints are subjective symptom reports, and an I² of 0% across trials this small says as much about their size as about their agreement. Treat the pooled RR 2.39 as this literature’s optimistic bound: the largest and most rigorous trial (Reference 3) did not reproduce a benefit on its prespecified primary endpoint The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Alammar N, Wang L, Saberi B, Nanavati J, Holtmann G, Shinohara RT, Mullin GE. The impact of peppermint oil on the irritable bowel syndrome: a meta-analysis of the pooled clinical data. BMC Complement Altern Med. 2019;19(1):21. DOI 10.1186/s12906-018-2409-0. PMID 30654773.
cards.search: alammar 2019 peppermint oil irritable bowel syndrome ibs meta-analysis pooled clinical data global improvement abdominal pain bmc complementary alternative medicine pmid 30654773

cards.headline: Cash 2016 (IBSREST): a proprietary triple-coated peppermint oil cut total IBS symptom scores by 40% vs 24.3% on placebo at 4 weeks (P=0.0246) — in 72 patients, testing the manufacturer’s own formulation.
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 72 patients with Rome III IBS-M or IBS-D, 4 weeks — Total IBS Symptom Score fell 40% on peppermint oil (mean change −1.16) vs 24.3% on placebo (−0.70), P=0.0246 ; the separation was already present at 24 hours ( 19.6% vs 10.3% , P=0.0092). Peppermint oil was well tolerated, with few adverse events.
cards.people: 72 patients fulfilling Rome III criteria for IBS-M or IBS-D (mean age 40.7 years, 75% female); 35 received peppermint oil three times daily and 37 received placebo. The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in the Total IBS Symptom Score (TISS) at 4 weeks
cards.result: At 4 weeks the Total IBS Symptom Score had fallen 40% from baseline on peppermint oil (mean change −1.16 , SD 0.807) versus 24.3% on placebo (mean change −0.70 , SD 0.737); P=0.0246 . At 24 hours the reduction was already larger on peppermint oil ( 19.6% , mean change −0.55) than on placebo ( 10.3% , −0.27); P=0.0092. The peppermint oil group also improved more on multiple individual gastrointestinal symptoms and on severe or unbearable symptoms. Peppermint oil was well tolerated with few adverse events
cards.watchOut: Two cautions travel with this card. First, manufacturer involvement: the tested product is a proprietary triple-coated, site-specific formulation (PO-SST) and a co-author is an employee of IM HealthScience LLC, the company behind that formulation — this is the maker testing its own product. Second, formulation-specificity: the result belongs to this sustained small-intestinal-release product and its dosing, and does not transfer to ordinary peppermint oil capsules. Beyond both: 72 patients, 4 weeks, one symptom score The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Cash BD, Epstein MS, Shah SM. A novel delivery system of peppermint oil is an effective therapy for irritable bowel syndrome symptoms. Dig Dis Sci. 2016;61(2):560–571. DOI 10.1007/s10620-015-3858-7. PMID 26319955.
cards.search: cash 2016 ibsrest peppermint oil novel delivery system site specific technology triple coated sustained release small intestine irritable bowel syndrome ibs-m ibs-d total ibs symptom score digestive diseases sciences pmid 26319955 manufacturer im healthscience

cards.headline: Weerts 2020 (PERSUADE): the largest, most rigorous peppermint oil trial missed its primary endpoint — FDA pain response 46.8% vs 34.4% on placebo (P=0.17) — while its secondary outcomes leaned positive.
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 189 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis (Rome IV IBS), 8 weeks — abdominal pain response: small-intestinal-release peppermint oil 29/62 (46.8%) , P=0.170 vs placebo; ileocolonic-release 26/63 (41.3%) , P=0.385; placebo 22/64 (34.4%) . Overall relief also not significant. Secondary outcomes favored small-intestinal release — abdominal pain (P=0.016), discomfort (P=0.020), IBS severity (P=0.020) — and mild adverse events were more common on peppermint oil (P<0.005).
cards.type: Multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PERSUADE) at 4 hospitals in the Netherlands, 8 weeks
cards.people: 190 patients with IBS by Rome IV criteria were enrolled; 189 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (mean age 34.0 years, 77.8% female, 57.7% recruited in primary care) and 178 completed the study. Patients received 182 mg small-intestinal-release peppermint oil, 182 mg ileocolonic-release peppermint oil, or placebo. The primary endpoint was the FDA abdominal pain response: at least a 30% decrease in the weekly average of worst daily abdominal pain, in at least 4 weeks; the co-primary endpoint was overall relief of IBS symptoms as defined by the EMA
cards.result: Abdominal pain response did not differ significantly from placebo: small-intestinal-release 29/62 (46.8%) , P=0.170; ileocolonic-release 26/63 (41.3%) , P=0.385; placebo 22/64 (34.4%) . Overall relief likewise did not differ (9.7%, P=0.317, and 1.6%, P=0.351, vs 4.7% on placebo). The small-intestinal formulation did produce greater improvements than placebo on the secondary outcomes of abdominal pain (P=0.016), discomfort (P=0.020), and IBS severity (P=0.020). Adverse events, although mild, were more common in both peppermint oil groups (P<0.005). The authors’ conclusions: neither formulation produced statistically significant reductions in abdominal pain response or overall symptom relief on the regulatory endpoints, and the findings do not support further development of ileocolonic-release peppermint oil for IBS
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint is a missed primary endpoint: the secondary positives were not the trial’s prespecified test of success, and relief rates this low on the EMA endpoint (under 10% in every arm) show how much stricter regulator-defined outcomes are than the symptom scales of the older trials. Note also the placebo arm’s 34.4% pain response — the background against which every small positive trial on this shelf was measured The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Weerts ZZRM, Masclee AAM, Witteman BJM, et al. Efficacy and safety of peppermint oil in a randomized, double-blind trial of patients with irritable bowel syndrome. Gastroenterology. 2020;158(1):123–136. DOI 10.1053/j.gastro.2019.08.026. PMID 31470006.

shelves.title: Cranberry products for UTI prevention: the 2023 Cochrane reversal, and the primary trials that explain it
shelves.question: Do cranberry products prevent urinary tract infections — and in whom?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Tract Infections · Vaccinium macrocarpon · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts · Beverages · Recurrence · Nursing Homes · Female · Humans
shelves.balance: The headline lives on Shelf #50 and is pointed to, not re-carded: the 2023 Cochrane update (Williams; 50 studies, 8,857 participants) reversed the review's earlier no-benefit position, finding cranberry products reduced symptomatic, culture-verified UTI (RR 0.70 [95% CI 0.58–0.84], moderate certainty) — with benefit concentrated in women with recurrent UTI (RR 0.74), children (RR 0.46) and people susceptible after an intervention (RR 0.47), and little or no benefit in elderly institutionalised people (RR 0.93), pregnant women (RR 1.06) or adults with neuromuscular bladder dysfunction (RR 0.97). This shelf cards the primary trials underneath that pattern: Kontiokari 2001 (open trial; first recurrence at 6 months 16% cranberry-lingonberry vs 36% control), Maki 2016 (clinical UTI episodes cut, IRR 0.61 — while culture-confirmed time-to-UTI was null, HR 0.97), Barbosa-Cesnik 2011 (blinded juice trial in college women: recurrence 20.0% cranberry vs 14.0% placebo — null, in the wrong direction), and Juthani-Mehta 2016 (nursing-home women: bacteriuria-plus-pyuria 29.1% vs 29.0%, OR 1.01 — null, matching Cochrane's elderly subgroup). Product, dose and population are the whole story, exactly as Shelf #50's balance warns. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Kontiokari 2001 (BMJ): cranberry-lingonberry juice cut first recurrence — 16% vs 36% at 6 months (absolute reduction 20 points, NNT 5) — in an open trial
cards.summary: Open, randomised, 12-month trial in 150 women with an E. coli UTI, allocated to cranberry-lingonberry juice concentrate 50 mL daily for 6 months, a Lactobacillus GG drink, or no intervention. First recurrence of symptomatic UTI by 6 months: 8 (16%) in the cranberry group, 19 (39%) lactobacillus, 18 (36%) control — a 20% absolute risk reduction versus control [95% CI 3–36], P=0.023, NNT 5 [3–34]. Cumulative first-recurrence rates differed between groups over 12 months (P=0.048).
cards.type: Open, randomised controlled trial, BMJ 2001. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 150 women with urinary tract infection caused by Escherichia coli, from university-student health centres and a university hospital staff population, Finland. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: At 6 months, at least one recurrence: cranberry-lingonberry 16% (8 women), lactobacillus 39% (19), control 36% (18). Absolute risk reduction cranberry vs control 20% (95% CI 3% to 36%; P=0.023); NNT 5 (95% CI 3 to 34).
cards.watchOut: Open trial, no placebo, a cranberry-lingonberry mixture (not cranberry alone), and a young, healthy population — the most favourable setting in this literature. It supports the 'women with recurrent UTI' subgroup of the Cochrane analysis; it cannot be generalised to juice products, older women or catheterised patients. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Kontiokari T et al. Randomised trial of cranberry-lingonberry juice and Lactobacillus GG drink for the prevention of urinary tract infections in women. BMJ. 2001;322(7302):1571. PMID 11431298

cards.headline: Barbosa-Cesnik 2011: blinded cranberry juice was null in college women — recurrence 20.0% on cranberry vs 14.0% on placebo
cards.summary: Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 319 college women presenting with an acute UTI, drinking 8 oz of 27% cranberry juice or placebo twice daily, followed to a second UTI or 6 months. Overall recurrence was 16.9% [95% CI 12.8–21.0] and was slightly higher on cranberry (20.0%) than placebo (14.0%); urinary-symptom presence at 3 days, 1–2 weeks and ≥1 month did not differ markedly. The trial was designed to detect the two-fold difference reported by earlier unblinded trials and did not find it.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Clin Infect Dis 2011. The record's databank carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 319 college women with an acute urinary tract infection. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Recurrence of UTI within 6 months: 20.0% on cranberry juice vs 14.0% on placebo (overall recurrence 16.9%, 95% CI 12.8% to 21.0%). No marked between-group differences in urinary symptoms at any follow-up point.
cards.watchOut: The necessary counterweight on this shelf: in the same broad population as Kontiokari (young women with recurrent UTI), a blinded juice trial found nothing — directionally worse on cranberry. Formulation and dose differ (27% juice twice daily versus concentrate), which is the product-heterogeneity problem in one pair of cards. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Barbosa-Cesnik C et al. Cranberry juice fails to prevent recurrent urinary tract infection: results from a randomized placebo-controlled trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2011;52(1):23-30. PMID 21148516

cards.headline: Maki 2016: a cranberry beverage cut clinical UTI episodes (IRR 0.61) — while the culture-confirmed endpoint was null (HR 0.97)
cards.summary: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial: 373 women with a recent UTI drank one 240-mL cranberry beverage (n=185) or placebo (n=188) daily for 24 weeks; mean age 40.9 years. Investigator-diagnosed clinical UTI episodes: 39 on cranberry vs 67 on placebo (antibiotic-use-adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.61 [95% CI 0.41–0.91], P=0.016); clinical UTI with pyuria also reduced (IRR 0.63 [0.40–0.97]). But time to UTI with culture positivity did not differ (HR 0.97 [0.56–1.67], P=0.914). One clinical event was prevented per 3.2 woman-years of treatment.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, Am J Clin Nutr 2016. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01776021.
cards.people: 373 women with a history of a recent urinary tract infection (185 cranberry, 188 placebo); mean age 40.9 years; 86% completed the 24-week treatment period in both groups.
cards.result: Clinical UTI episodes: 39 (cranberry) vs 67 (placebo); adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.91; P=0.016). Clinical UTI with pyuria: IRR 0.63 (0.40 to 0.97; P=0.037). Time to culture-positive UTI: HR 0.97 (0.56 to 1.67; P=0.914) — no difference.
cards.watchOut: Read the two endpoints together: the episodes clinicians diagnosed and treated fell; the culture-confirmed events did not. A symptom-endpoint benefit with a null microbiological endpoint can reflect reporting or prescribing behaviour as easily as antibacterial action — and this was an industry-formulated beverage trial of one specific product. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Maki KC et al. Consumption of a cranberry juice beverage lowered the number of clinical urinary tract infection episodes in women with a recent history of urinary tract infection. Am J Clin Nutr. 2016;103(6):1434-42. PMID 27251185 · NCT01776021

cards.headline: Juthani-Mehta 2016 (JAMA): cranberry capsules null in nursing-home women — bacteriuria-plus-pyuria 29.1% vs 29.0% (OR 1.01)
cards.summary: Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 185 women aged ≥65 in 21 nursing homes (mean age 86.4 years), given two cranberry capsules daily (72 mg proanthocyanidin total) or placebo for 1 year. Primary outcome (bacteriuria plus pyuria, assessed every 2 months): adjusted 29.1% vs 29.0% (OR 1.01 [95% CI 0.61–1.66], P=0.98). No significant differences in symptomatic UTI (10 vs 12 episodes), deaths (17 vs 16), hospitalisations, resistant organisms, or antibiotic use.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, JAMA 2016. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01691430.
cards.people: 185 women aged 65 years or older residing in 21 nursing homes near New Haven, Connecticut (92 cranberry, 93 placebo); mean age 86.4 years (SD 8.2); 147 completed the study.
cards.result: Presence of bacteriuria plus pyuria over 1 year (adjusted): 29.1% cranberry vs 29.0% placebo (OR 1.01; 95% CI 0.61 to 1.66; P=0.98). Symptomatic UTIs: 10 vs 12 episodes. Deaths 17 vs 16; hospitalisations 33 vs 50 admissions (rate ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.32 to 1.40) — none significant.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a laboratory composite (bacteriuria plus pyuria), not symptomatic infection — asymptomatic bacteriuria in this population should not be treated in any case, so the trial's null on its own endpoint and its null on symptomatic episodes (10 vs 12) are the two facts to carry. It matches the Cochrane elderly-institutionalised subgroup (RR 0.93) almost exactly. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the Cochrane reversal and the primary trials tell one story — benefit, where real, is for younger women with recurrent UTI and specific products
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–4 with the pointer to the synthesis home: the Cochrane 2023 review itself (Williams, PMID 37068952; RR 0.70 for symptomatic, culture-verified UTI) is carded on Shelf #50 and is not re-carded here; its subgroup pattern — benefit in women with recurrent UTI, children and post-intervention susceptibility; none in institutionalised elderly, pregnancy or neuromuscular bladder dysfunction — is exactly what the primary trials on this shelf show one by one. The 2025 Stonehouse whole-fruit-powder trial (PMID 39863114) is likewise already carded on Shelf #50. Needed evidence: an independently funded, blinded trial of a defined-PAC-dose product in women with recurrent UTI, powered on culture-verified symptomatic recurrence — the gap Maki's split endpoints leave open.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–4 together with the Shelf #50 pointer stated in the summary.
cards.people: 150 + 319 + 373 + 185 women across Cards 1–4; 8,857 participants across the 50 Cochrane trials on Shelf #50.
cards.result: Positive: Kontiokari (16% vs 36% first recurrence, open), Maki clinical episodes (IRR 0.61, culture endpoint null). Null: Barbosa-Cesnik (20.0% vs 14.0%), Juthani-Mehta (OR 1.01). Pooled (Shelf #50): RR 0.70 [0.58–0.84] overall; RR 0.93 in institutionalised elderly.
cards.watchOut: Never quote the pooled RR 0.70 without its population: it averages products and groups among whom the effect ranges from RR 0.46 (children) to RR 1.06 (pregnancy).

shelves.title: Glucosamine ± chondroitin for knee osteoarthritis pain
shelves.question: Do glucosamine and chondroitin, alone or combined, relieve knee osteoarthritis pain more than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Celecoxib · Chondroitin Sulfates/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucosamine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Osteoarthritis, Knee/classification/complications/drug therapy · Pain/classification/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — the treatment made no difference is the finding for the overall population: in GAIT (1,583 patients) glucosamine, chondroitin and their combination were not significantly better than placebo on the primary pain response, and a network meta-analysis of 10 large trials (3,803 patients) found pain differences of only -0.3 to -0.5 cm on a 10 cm scale, none reaching the prespecified clinically important difference. MOVES found the combination non-inferior to celecoxib in severe pain, but with no placebo arm it cannot show the combination beats placebo. The one positive signal — GAIT's exploratory moderate-to-severe subgroup — is a subgroup finding, not the trial's primary result. The warfarin-interaction question for these products is a different question, home on Shelf #65, and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: GAIT: glucosamine and chondroitin did not beat placebo overall in 1,583 patients with knee osteoarthritis
cards.summary: GAIT (1,583 patients): response differences vs placebo (60.1%) were +3.9 points (glucosamine), +5.3 (chondroitin) and +6.5 (combination) — none significant .
cards.people: 1,583 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (mild pain n=1,229; moderate to severe n=354); mean age 59 years, 64% women.
cards.result: The primary outcome was a 20% decrease in knee pain at 24 weeks. Response rates versus placebo (60.1%) were 3.9 percentage points higher with glucosamine (P=0.30), 5.3 points higher with chondroitin sulfate (P=0.17) and 6.5 points higher with combined treatment (P=0.09) — none significant — while the celecoxib control was 10.0 points higher (P=0.008). In the exploratory moderate-to-severe subgroup, combined therapy responded more than placebo (79.2% vs 54.3%, P=0.002). Adverse events were mild, infrequent and evenly distributed.
cards.watchOut: The moderate-to-severe subgroup result is exploratory and was not the trial's overall primary finding; the overall-group result is null. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Clegg DO et al. Glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, and the two in combination for painful knee osteoarthritis. N Engl J Med. 2006;354(8):795-808. PMID: 16495392. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00032890, from the record's databank.
