cards.headline: MOVES: the combination matched celecoxib in severe knee pain — but there was no placebo group
cards.summary: MOVES: the combination matched celecoxib on WOMAC pain (−185.7 vs −186.8; difference −1.11) — with no placebo group , so it cannot show either beat placebo.
cards.people: 606 patients with Kellgren and Lawrence grades 2-3 knee osteoarthritis and moderate-to-severe pain (WOMAC score ≥301 on a 0-500 scale) in France, Germany, Poland and Spain; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months the adjusted mean change in WOMAC pain was -185.7 (95% CI -200.3 to -171.1) with chondroitin sulfate plus glucosamine hydrochloride and -186.8 (-201.7 to -171.9) with celecoxib, a difference of -1.11 (-22.0 to 19.8; p=0.92), meeting the non-inferiority margin of -40. OMERACT-OARSI response criteria were met by 79.7% (combination) and 79.2% (celecoxib); adverse events were low and similarly distributed.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to celecoxib without a placebo arm cannot distinguish drug efficacy from natural history and placebo response — both groups improved by about 50%. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis of 10 large trials: pain effects too small to be clinically important
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis (10 large trials): pain differences of −0.3 to −0.5 cm on a 10 cm scale — below the −0.9 cm prespecified clinically important threshold.
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 10 trials in 3,803 patients with osteoarthritis of the knee or hip, each trial larger than 200 patients; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: On a 10 cm visual analogue pain scale, differences versus placebo were -0.4 cm (95% credible interval -0.7 to -0.1) for glucosamine, -0.3 cm (-0.7 to 0.0) for chondroitin and -0.5 cm (-0.9 to 0.0) for the combination; for none did the credible interval cross the prespecified minimal clinically important difference of -0.9 cm. Differences in joint-space narrowing were minute, with intervals overlapping zero, and industry-independent trials showed smaller effects than commercially funded trials (P=0.02 for interaction).
cards.watchOut: The authors' conclusion was that health authorities and insurers should not cover these preparations; effects, if any, are below what patients can feel. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.result: Against placebo, the evidence is null at clinically important size: GAIT's primary response differences were non-significant (+3.9 to +6.5 percentage points) and the network meta-analysis found -0.3 to -0.5 cm on a 10 cm scale, below the -0.9 cm clinically important threshold. MOVES shows the combination performs like celecoxib over 6 months in severe pain, which is compatible with both treatments riding on placebo response and natural history. This shelf is stamped LIKELY — the null: routine use for knee osteoarthritis pain is not supported, and the GAIT moderate-to-severe subgroup finding (79.2% vs 54.3%) remains exploratory. cards.watchOut: Do not present the GAIT subgroup or the MOVES non-inferiority result as proof of efficacy; neither was a placebo-controlled primary win.

shelves.title: Saw palmetto for benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms
shelves.question: Does saw palmetto extract improve urinary symptoms in BPH more than placebo, at standard or escalating doses?
shelves.mesh: Androgen Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Prostate/pathology · Prostatic Hyperplasia/drug therapy/pathology/physiopathology · Serenoa/adverse effects · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY — the treatment made no difference is the finding: two large, well-blinded placebo-controlled trials found no benefit at the standard dose for a year (STEP, n=225) or at up to three times the standard dose for 72 weeks (CAMUS, n=369, where placebo improved slightly more), and the Cochrane review of 32 trials (5,666 men) reaches the same conclusion on symptom scores, responder rates, flow and prostate size. This is one of the cleaner supplement nulls in the library.

cards.headline: STEP: one year of saw palmetto did not improve symptoms or flow versus placebo
cards.summary: STEP: one year of saw palmetto vs placebo — symptom-score difference 0.04 points [−0.93 to 1.01]; flow difference 0.43 mL/min, also null.
cards.people: 225 men over the age of 49 years with moderate-to-severe symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: After one year of saw palmetto extract 160 mg twice daily versus placebo, there was no significant difference in change in American Urological Association Symptom Index scores (mean difference 0.04 point; 95% CI -0.93 to 1.01), maximal urinary flow rate (mean difference 0.43 ml per minute; 95% CI -0.52 to 1.38), prostate size, residual volume after voiding, quality of life or serum PSA. The incidence of side effects was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: A single extract at the standard dose; the escalating-dose question is answered by CAMUS, carded next in programme order below. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Bent S et al. Saw palmetto for benign prostatic hyperplasia. N Engl J Med. 2006;354(6):557-66. PMID: 16467543. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00037154, from the record's databank.

cards.headline: CAMUS: even triple-dose saw palmetto did not beat placebo over 72 weeks
cards.summary: CAMUS: even at triple dose over 72 weeks, scores fell −2.20 vs −2.99 points — numerically favouring placebo .
cards.people: 369 men aged 45 years or older with an AUASI score between 8 and 24 at 11 North American sites; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Doses were escalated at 24 and 48 weeks to one, two and then three times the standard 320 mg/day dose. Between baseline and 72 weeks, mean AUASI scores decreased by -2.20 points (95% CI -3.04 to -1.36) with saw palmetto and by -2.99 points (-3.81 to -2.17) with placebo; the group mean difference was 0.79 points favouring placebo (upper bound of the 1-sided 95% CI most favourable to saw palmetto 1.77 points; 1-sided P=.91). Saw palmetto was no more effective than placebo for any secondary outcome, and no clearly attributable adverse effects were identified.
cards.watchOut: The dose-escalation design answers the 'the dose was too low' objection directly — the null persists at three times the standard dose. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Cochrane: across 32 trials and 5,666 men, Serenoa repens was not superior to placebo
cards.summary: Cochrane (32 trials, 5,666 men): long-term pooled difference 0.25 points [−0.58 to 1.07]; responders 42.6% vs 44.2%.
cards.people: 5,666 men assessed in 32 randomised controlled trials of 4 to 72 weeks; 27 trials were double-blinded. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In a meta-analysis of two high-quality long-term trials (n=582), Serenoa repens was not superior to placebo on the AUA symptom score (mean difference 0.25 points; 95% CI -0.58 to 1.07). In the 72-week trial, clinical responders (≥3-point improvement) were 42.6% on Serenoa repens and 44.2% on placebo (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.22); peak urine flow was not improved in the three high-quality moderate-to-long-term trials (MD 0.40 mL/s; 95% CI -0.30 to 1.09), and one 12-month trial (n=225) found no significant difference in prostate size (MD -1.22 cc; 95% CI -3.91 to 1.47).
cards.watchOut: The review pools many preparations and shorter, lower-quality trials alongside STEP and CAMUS; the high-quality long-term subset is the part that carries the conclusion.

shelves.title: St John's wort for major depression
shelves.question: Does St John's wort (hypericum) treat major depression as well as standard antidepressants, and better than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Major Depressive Disorder/diagnosis/drug therapy · Hypericum · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Regression Analysis · Sertraline/therapeutic use · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: the Cochrane synthesis of 29 trials (5,489 patients) found hypericum extracts superior to placebo (response rate ratio 1.28 in the nine larger trials) and statistically similar to standard antidepressants (rate ratios 1.02 vs tricyclics and 1.00 vs SSRIs), with fewer dropouts for adverse effects — but placebo-controlled results were markedly heterogeneous, trials from German-speaking countries reported more favourable findings, and the largest US trial (n=340) found neither hypericum nor sertraline significantly better than placebo on its primary outcomes. Extracts differ between products, so a class-level POSSIBLE is the honest ceiling.

cards.headline: The large US trial: neither St John's wort nor sertraline beat placebo on the primary outcomes
cards.summary: The large US trial: HAM-D change −9.20 (placebo) vs −8.68 (St John's wort) vs −10.53 (sertraline) — neither active treatment beat placebo on the primary outcomes.
cards.people: 340 adult outpatients with major depression and a baseline Hamilton Depression Scale (HAM-D) score of at least 20, at 12 US academic and community clinics; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Over 8 weeks, mean change in HAM-D total score was -9.20 (placebo) vs -8.68 for Hypericum perforatum extract LI-160 (P=.59 vs placebo) and -10.53 for sertraline (P=.18 vs placebo) — neither active treatment was significantly different from placebo on the primary measures. Full response occurred in 31.9% of placebo patients vs 23.9% on hypericum (P=.21) and 24.8% on sertraline (P=.26); sertraline was better than placebo only on the secondary CGI improvement scale (P=.02).
cards.watchOut: Because the sertraline comparator also failed on the primary outcomes, the trial may have had low assay sensitivity — but the authors note the complete absence of trends favouring hypericum.
cards.source: Hypericum Depression Trial Study Group (Davidson JR et al.). Effect of Hypericum perforatum (St John's wort) in major depressive disorder: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002;287(14):1807-14. PMID: 11939866. Registry ID: no registry ID appears in the record's databank.

cards.headline: Cochrane: hypericum beat placebo and matched standard antidepressants across 29 trials — with marked heterogeneity
cards.summary: Cochrane (29 trials): response rate ratio 1.28 [1.10 to 1.49] vs placebo in larger trials, and parity with standard antidepressants ( 1.02 ) — with marked heterogeneity.
cards.people: 29 trials with 5,489 patients with major depression (18 comparisons with placebo, 17 with synthetic standard antidepressants); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In nine larger placebo-controlled trials the combined response rate ratio for hypericum extracts versus placebo was 1.28 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.49), and 1.87 (1.22 to 2.87) in nine smaller trials. Versus standard antidepressants, response rate ratios were 1.02 (0.90 to 1.15; 5 trials) against tri- or tetracyclic antidepressants and 1.00 (0.90 to 1.11; 12 trials) against SSRIs. Patients on hypericum dropped out for adverse effects less often than those on older antidepressants (OR 0.24; 0.13 to 0.46) or SSRIs (OR 0.53; 0.34-0.83). Trials from German-speaking countries reported findings more favourable to hypericum, in both placebo and antidepressant comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Placebo-controlled results showed marked heterogeneity and a country-of-origin pattern; 'hypericum extract' is not one product — the tested extracts differ, and results may not transfer between preparations. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Kasper 2006: extract WS 5570 beat placebo in mild-to-moderate major depression
cards.summary: Kasper 2006: HAM-D falls of 11.6 and 10.8 points on extract WS 5570 vs 6.0 on placebo in mild-to-moderate depression.
cards.people: 332 male and female adult outpatients with a mild or moderate major depressive episode (123 on WS 5570 600 mg/day, 127 on 1200 mg/day, 82 on placebo); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix numerically.
cards.result: After 6 weeks, mean decreases in HAM-D total score were 11.6 ± 6.4 points (600 mg/day) and 10.8 ± 7.3 points (1200 mg/day) versus 6.0 ± 8.1 points on placebo, with both hypericum groups statistically superior to placebo on the primary and secondary efficacy measures, and significantly more responders and remissions than placebo. The incidence of adverse events was low in all groups.
cards.watchOut: A single-extract, 6-week trial in mild-to-moderate depression — the population in which placebo response and extract effects are hardest to separate, and not the moderately severe population of the null US trial. The WS 5570 tablets were manufactured by Dr. Willmar Schwabe Pharmaceuticals, Karlsruhe, Germany, as named in the publication's full text.
cards.source: Kasper S et al. Superior efficacy of St John's wort extract WS 5570 compared to placebo in patients with major depression: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center trial. BMC Med. 2006;4:14. PMID: 16796730. Registry ID: ISRCTN77277298, from the record's databank.

shelves.title: Echinacea for preventing and treating colds
shelves.question: Does echinacea prevent colds, or shorten them, versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Common Cold/drug therapy/immunology · Echinacea/adverse effects · Interleukin-8/blood · Leukocyte Count · Neutrophils · Patient Compliance · Physician-Patient Relations
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): the largest rigorous treatment trial (Barrett 2010, n=719) found illness duration and severity not statistically significant versus placebo (a 0.53-day trend), the Cochrane review of 24 trials (4,631 participants) found no individual prevention comparison significant and only one of seven treatment trials significant for duration, and concluded echinacea products have not been shown to provide benefits for treating colds, with at most a possible weak benefit from some products. One large prevention trial (Jawad 2012, n=755) reported fewer episodes on a single extract, but its abstract reports no episode counts. Products differ appreciably in composition, which further weakens any class claim.

cards.headline: Barrett 2010: echinacea did not significantly shorten or soften colds in 719 patients
cards.summary: Barrett 2010 (719 patients): severity 236 vs 264 and duration 6.34 vs 6.87 days — a trend only (P=0.089), not significant .
cards.people: 719 patients aged 12 to 80 years with new-onset common cold in Dane County, Wisconsin (713 completed); mean age 33.7 years, 64% female, 88% white.
cards.result: Mean global severity was 236 in the blinded echinacea group and 264 in the blinded placebo group, a 28-point trend toward benefit (95% CI -69 to 13 points; P=0.089) that was not statistically significant. Mean illness duration was 6.34 days (blinded echinacea) versus 6.87 days (blinded placebo), a non-significant 0.53-day benefit (CI -1.25 to 0.19 days; P=0.075). Changes in interleukin-8 levels and neutrophil counts were also not statistically significant. The authors conclude the results do not support an ability of this dose and formulation to substantively change the course of the common cold.
cards.watchOut: Higher-than-expected variability limited power to detect small benefits — a small effect is not excluded, but none was shown.
cards.source: Barrett B et al. Echinacea for treating the common cold: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2010;153(12):769-77. PMID: 21173411. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00065715, from the record's databank.

cards.headline: Cochrane: no prevention comparison was significant; only one of seven treatment trials shortened colds
cards.summary: Cochrane: none of 12 prevention comparisons was significant; only one of seven treatment trials shortened colds.
cards.people: 24 double-blind trials with 4,631 participants, totalling 33 comparisons of echinacea preparations and placebo (10 trials investigated prevention, 15 treatment); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: None of the 12 prevention comparisons reporting the number of patients with at least one cold episode found a statistically significant difference, although a post hoc pooling suggested a relative risk reduction of 10% to 20%. Of the seven treatment trials reporting cold duration, only one showed a significant effect over placebo. Dropouts and adverse effects did not differ significantly between groups. The authors conclude echinacea products have not here been shown to provide benefits for treating colds, although a weak benefit from some products is possible, and that positive trends in prophylaxis trials are of questionable clinical relevance.
cards.watchOut: Preparations differed appreciably in species, plant part and extraction, and the reviewers refrained from pooling the main analysis because of strong clinical heterogeneity; the 10-20% relative figure is post hoc.

cards.headline: Jawad 2012: one large prevention trial reported fewer colds on a single Echinacea purpurea extract
cards.summary: Jawad 2012: one large prevention trial reported fewer colds on a single extract — but its abstract reports no episode counts , and the card says so.

shelves.title: Coenzyme Q10 for statin-associated muscle symptoms
shelves.question: Does CoQ10 relieve muscle symptoms in people taking statins?
shelves.mesh: Dietary Supplements · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects · Muscular Diseases/chemically induced/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Ubiquinone/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Vitamins/therapeutic use · Activities of Daily Living
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): an updated meta-analysis of 12 small randomised trials (575 patients) found CoQ10 lowered symptom scores for pain, weakness, cramp and tiredness versus placebo, with no effect on creatine kinase — but the most rigorous primary trial, which first confirmed true statin myalgia by blinded statin-versus-placebo cross-over (only 36% of complainers reproduced symptoms), found CoQ10 600 mg/day did not reduce muscle pain at all. The positive pool rests on small, short trials like Caso 2007 (n=32, vitamin E comparator, 30 days). Q-SYMBIO, the heart-failure outcomes trial, is a different question and stays home on Shelf #53; it is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Updated meta-analysis: CoQ10 lowered muscle symptom scores across 12 small trials, but not creatine kinase
cards.summary: Pooled small trials: symptom scores favoured CoQ10 (pain weighted mean difference −1.60 ) — with no effect on creatine kinase .
cards.people: 12 randomised controlled trials with 575 patients in total (294 in CoQ10 groups, 281 in placebo groups); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, CoQ10 supplementation ameliorated statin-associated muscle symptoms: muscle pain (weighted mean difference -1.60; 95% CI -1.75 to -1.44; P<0.001), muscle weakness (-2.28; -2.79 to -1.77), muscle cramp (-1.78; -2.31 to -1.24) and muscle tiredness (-1.75; -2.31 to -1.19). No reduction in plasma creatine kinase was observed (weighted mean difference 0.09; -0.06 to 0.24; P=0.23). The authors conclude CoQ10 may be a complementary approach to manage statin-induced myopathy.
cards.watchOut: The pooled symptom-score differences come from small trials with differing scales and short follow-up; the objective marker (creatine kinase) did not move, and the largest rigorous trial (carded below) is null. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Caso 2007: pain fell 40% on CoQ10 in a 32-patient, 30-day trial — against vitamin E, not placebo
cards.summary: Caso 2007: pain fell 40% within the CoQ10 group — a 32-patient, 30-day trial against vitamin E, not placebo , with within-group changes.
cards.people: 32 patients with myopathic symptoms on statins, randomly assigned to coenzyme Q10 100 mg/day (n=18) or vitamin E 400 IU/day (n=14) for 30 days; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 30 days, pain severity decreased by 40% (p<0.001) and pain interference with daily activities decreased by 38% (p<0.02) in the CoQ10 group (within-group changes). In the vitamin E group, pain severity changed by +9% (not significant) and pain interference by -11% (not significant). The authors suggest CoQ10 supplementation may decrease muscle pain associated with statin treatment.
cards.watchOut: Very small, very short, and the comparator is vitamin E rather than placebo — within-group percentage falls cannot separate a CoQ10 effect from regression to the mean and expectation. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Taylor 2015: in confirmed statin myalgia, CoQ10 did not reduce muscle pain
cards.summary: Taylor 2015: in confirmed statin myalgia, CoQ10 did not reduce pain (p=0.53) despite blood levels rising 1.3 → 5.2 mcg/mL.
cards.people: 120 patients with prior statin myalgia symptoms entered an 8-week randomised double-blind cross-over confirmation phase (simvastatin 20 mg/day vs placebo); 41 developed muscle pain with simvastatin but not placebo and were randomised to simvastatin with CoQ10 (600 mg/day ubiquinol) or placebo for 8 weeks, with 24 then crossing to the alternative treatment. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Serum CoQ10 rose from 1.3 ± 0.4 to 5.2 ± 2.3 mcg/mL on CoQ10 but not on placebo, confirming exposure. Brief Pain Inventory pain severity and interference scores increased with simvastatin irrespective of CoQ10 assignment (p=0.53 and 0.56 for the CoQ10 comparison); there were no changes in muscle strength or maximal oxygen uptake, and no difference in time to pain onset (3.0 ± 2.0 vs 2.4 ± 2.1 weeks; p=0.55). More subjects reported pain with CoQ10 (14 of 20 vs 7 of 18; p=0.05). The authors note only 36% of patients complaining of statin myalgia develop symptoms during blinded statin-versus-placebo cross-over.
cards.watchOut: Small numbers of confirmed cases (41 randomised) — but this is the only carded trial that first proved the symptoms were statin-caused before testing the remedy, which is why its null weighs heavily. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: A positive small-trial pool against a null confirmation-first trial — MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the updated meta-analysis (12 trials, 575 patients), Caso 2007 (32 patients) and Taylor 2015 (41 patients with confirmed statin myalgia).
cards.result: The meta-analysis pools favourable symptom-score differences (pain weighted mean difference -1.60) with no creatine kinase effect, while the trial with the strongest design — blinded confirmation that symptoms were truly statin-induced, then high-dose CoQ10 with verified blood levels — found no pain benefit. shelves.title: DHEA supplementation in older adults
shelves.question: Does DHEA improve body composition, strength, metabolism or wellbeing in older men and women?
shelves.mesh: Aging/drug effects · Body Composition/drug effects · Bone Density/drug effects · Dehydroepiandrosterone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/blood · Estradiol/blood · Hormone Replacement Therapy/adverse effects · Insulin Resistance
shelves.balance: LIKELY the null: In the rigorous two-year Nair trial, DHEA had no significant effect on body composition, peak oxygen consumption, muscle strength, insulin sensitivity or quality of life in elderly men or women. The earlier one-year DHEAge study restored 'young' DHEAS concentrations and reported selective findings — improved bone turnover and most libido parameters in women over 70, and improved skin status particularly in women — without harmful accumulation of steroids. Those selective positives do not overturn the null on the outcomes this shelf's question asks about: composition, strength, metabolism and wellbeing.

cards.headline: Nair 2006: two years of DHEA in elderly men and women — no effect on body composition, strength, insulin sensitivity or quality of life
cards.summary: Nair 2006: two years of DHEA restored DHEAS levels — with no effect on body composition, strength, insulin sensitivity or quality of life.
cards.people: 87 elderly men with low sulfated DHEA and bioavailable testosterone (29 DHEA, 27 testosterone, 31 placebo) and 57 elderly women with low sulfated DHEA (27 DHEA, 30 placebo); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Over two years, DHEA raised plasma sulfated DHEA by a median of 3.4 micrograms/mL in men and 3.8 micrograms/mL in women versus the placebo change, yet a separate analysis of men and women showed no significant effect of DHEA on body-composition measurements. Neither DHEA nor testosterone altered peak oxygen consumption, muscle strength or insulin sensitivity. Men in both treatment groups had an increase in bone mineral density at the femoral neck, and women on DHEA had an increase at the ultradistal radius. Neither treatment improved quality of life or had major adverse effects. The authors conclude neither DHEA nor low-dose testosterone has physiologically relevant beneficial effects on body composition, physical performance, insulin sensitivity or quality of life in elderly people.
cards.watchOut: The trial was sized for physiological endpoints, not fractures or events; its bone-density findings are site-specific secondary results, not fracture protection. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Nair KS et al. DHEA in elderly women and DHEA or testosterone in elderly men. N Engl J Med. 2006 Oct 19;355(16):1647-1659. PMID: 17050889. Registry ID: NCT00254371, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DHEAge (Baulieu 2000): one year of DHEA 50 mg restored young DHEAS levels; benefits were selective — bone turnover and libido in women over 70, skin in women
cards.summary: DHEAge 2000: young DHEAS levels restored; benefits were selective (bone turnover, libido in older women) and small.
cards.people: 280 healthy individuals, women and men aged 60–79 years, given DHEA 50 mg orally or placebo daily for one year; the abstract does not state the sex split or mean age.
cards.result: No potentially harmful accumulation of DHEAS or active steroids was recorded. DHEA re-established a 'young' concentration of DHEAS, with a small increase in testosterone and estradiol, particularly in women. Bone turnover improved selectively in women over 70 years old, assessed by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and decreased osteoclastic activity. A significant increase in most libido parameters was also found in these older women, and skin status improved, particularly in women, in hydration, epidermal thickness, sebum production and pigmentation. The authors describe replacement that normalised some effects of aging without creating 'supermen/women'.
cards.watchOut: DHEAge's positives are subgroup- and domain-specific (women over 70; skin; libido) inside a report that predates modern trial reporting; it measured no strength, body-composition benefit or clinical event, and its framing is a narrative review-style report of the trial rather than a CONSORT-style results paper. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Baulieu EE et al. Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), DHEA sulfate, and aging: contribution of the DHEAge Study to a sociobiomedical issue. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2000 Apr 11;97(8):4279-4284. PMID: 10760294. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Synthesis: DHEA normalises a blood level, not a body — LIKELY the null on composition, strength, metabolism and wellbeing
cards.summary: DHEA normalises a blood level, not a body — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Nair 2006 (144 elderly men and women, 2 years) and DHEAge (280 healthy adults aged 60–79, 1 year).
cards.result: Both trials agree that a year or two of DHEA safely restores youthful DHEAS concentrations; they disagree only in emphasis. On the outcomes in this shelf's question, the larger, longer, more rigorously reported trial is null across the board — body composition, physical performance, insulin sensitivity and quality of life. DHEAge's selective findings in women over 70 (bone turnover, libido) and in skin are kept on their card, labelled selective, and do not lift the stamp. This shelf is stamped LIKELY the null.
cards.watchOut: Do not present DHEAge's subgroup findings as general anti-ageing benefit, and do not present the null as proof of harm: neither trial found major adverse effects.

shelves.title: Curcuma longa (turmeric) extract for knee osteoarthritis pain
shelves.question: Does a Curcuma longa / curcumin extract reduce knee pain in symptomatic knee osteoarthritis versus placebo (Wang's Tasmanian RCT; the Curcugen trial)?
shelves.mesh: Arthralgia/drug therapy,etiology · Curcuma · Knee Joint/diagnostic imaging,drug effects · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Osteoarthritis, Knee/complications,diagnostic imaging,drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Phytotherapy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small, short, double-blind placebo-controlled trials of two different extracts both favour turmeric/curcumin on pain scores. Wang 2021 (70 participants with effusion-synovitis, 12 weeks) found knee pain on a visual analogue scale improved by −9.1 mm versus placebo (95% CI −17.8 to −0.4; P=0.039) and WOMAC pain by −47.2 mm (−81.2 to −13.2; P=0.006), but no change in effusion-synovitis volume (3.2 mL, −0.3 to 6.8) or cartilage composition. Lopresti 2021 (101 adults, 8 weeks) found significantly better KOOS pain (p=0.009) and numeric pain ratings (p=0.001) on a curcumin extract, with pain-relief medication reduced in 37% versus 13%. Small samples, different proprietary extracts, pain-only outcomes and no structural effect — POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Turmeric liver-injury harm is a separate question, home on Shelf #66, cross-referenced and not re-carded here. NOTE: the topic file's printed anchor (PMID 33511486) is a systematic review, not Wang's trial; the real Wang RCT (PMID 32926799) is carded instead — see summary.md.

cards.headline: Wang 2021: Curcuma longa extract improved knee pain by −9.1 mm on a visual analogue scale versus placebo — and did not shrink effusion-synovitis
cards.summary: Wang 2021: Curcuma longa extract improved knee pain by −9.1 mm on a visual analogue scale vs placebo — and did not shrink effusion-synovitis. (The topic file's printed anchor was a systematic review; rejected at the gate and the real RCT re-pinned.)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (12 weeks, single centre)
cards.people: 70 participants with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis and ultrasonography-defined effusion-synovitis, from southern Tasmania, Australia, randomised to 2 capsules daily of Curcuma longa extract (36) or matched placebo (34) for 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Curcuma longa improved visual-analogue-scale knee pain compared with placebo by −9.1 mm (95% CI −17.8 to −0.4; P=0.039) but did not change effusion-synovitis volume (3.2 mL [CI −0.3 to 6.8]). It also improved WOMAC knee pain (−47.2 mm [CI −81.2 to −13.2]; P=0.006) but not lateral femoral cartilage T2 relaxation time (−0.4 ms [CI −1.1 to 0.3]). Adverse events occurred in 14 (39%) on extract and 18 (53%) on placebo (P=0.16); 2 events in the extract group and 5 in the placebo group may have been treatment related.
cards.watchOut: Seventy participants, one centre, 12 weeks, and the pain confidence interval (−17.8 to −0.4 mm) reaches almost to zero: a real but fragile pain signal with no effect on the imaging target the trial was built around. The trial's own stated limitation is its modest sample size and short duration. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Wang Z et al. Effectiveness of Curcuma longa Extract for the Treatment of Symptoms and Effusion-Synovitis of Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Trial. Ann Intern Med. 2021;173(11):861-869. PMID: 32926799. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12618000080224, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Lopresti 2021 (Curcugen): curcumin extract improved KOOS pain (p=0.009); 37% vs 13% reduced pain-relief medication
cards.summary: Lopresti 2021 (Curcugen): curcumin extract improved KOOS pain (p=0.009); 37% vs 13% reduced pain-relief medication. Its abstract reports p-values without effect sizes — the card says so.
cards.people: 101 adults with knee osteoarthritis randomised to a standardised curcumin extract (Curcugen) 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 8 weeks. The abstract does not state the arm sizes, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, curcumin significantly reduced the KOOS knee pain score (p=0.009) and numeric knee pain ratings (p=0.001), and was associated with greater improvements (p≤0.05) on the timed up-and-go test, the 6-minute walk test and the Japanese Orthopaedic Association total score, but not the 30-second chair stand test or the 40-m fast-paced walk test. Pain-relieving medication was reduced in 37% of participants on curcumin compared with 13% on placebo. The abstract reports p-values without the underlying score differences, so no effect sizes are printed here.
cards.watchOut: An 8-week trial of one proprietary extract, reported in its abstract as p-values without effect sizes: it corroborates the direction of Wang's result but cannot add precision to it, and its extract is not Wang's extract. The Curcugen extract was supplied by DolCas Biotech, LLC, as named in the publication's full text.

shelves.title: Chamomile extract for generalised anxiety: a modest benefit in the first controlled trial; continuation kept symptoms lower, relapse difference not significant
shelves.question: In adults with generalised anxiety disorder, does pharmaceutical-grade chamomile extract reduce anxiety symptoms compared with placebo — and does continuing it keep responders well?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anti-Anxiety Agents/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Anxiety Disorders/drug therapy, psychology · Capsules · Chamomile · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Chamomile tea is a folk anxiolytic; the extract has been through two randomised tests from one research group. In the first controlled trial (57 outpatients with mild-to-moderate generalised anxiety disorder, 8 weeks), chamomile extract produced a significantly greater reduction in Hamilton Anxiety scores than placebo (p=0.047), with tolerability no worse than placebo. In the continuation study, responders with moderate-to-severe GAD who kept taking chamomile for 26 weeks relapsed less often than those switched to placebo (15.2% vs 25.5%; HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.20–1.33 — not significant), while maintaining significantly lower symptom scores. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest effect in small single-centre trials, awaiting independent replication.

cards.headline: First controlled trial: chamomile beat placebo on Hamilton Anxiety scores over 8 weeks (p=0.047)
cards.summary: First controlled trial: chamomile beat placebo on Hamilton Anxiety scores over 8 weeks (p=0.047)
cards.people: 61 outpatients with mild-to-moderate generalised anxiety disorder enrolled, 57 randomised to pharmaceutical-grade chamomile extract (n=28) or placebo (n=29) for 8 weeks; primary outcome change in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale total score.
cards.result: The reduction in mean total HAM-A score was significantly greater on chamomile than placebo (p=0.047). Secondary outcomes (Beck Anxiety Inventory, Psychological Well Being, Clinical Global Impression) all moved in the same direction, though the study was not powered for them. One patient in each group stopped for adverse events; the distribution of adverse events did not differ (p=0.417).
cards.watchOut: Small and single-centre, from the group that developed the extract's trial programme; the p-value sits just under 0.05, so the finding needs the replication the authors themselves call for. The trial used a standardised chamomile extract; the publication names no commercial brand. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Continuation study: relapse 15.2% on continued chamomile vs 25.5% after switch to placebo (HR 0.52, not significant); symptoms stayed significantly lower
cards.summary: Continuation study: relapse 15.2% on continued chamomile vs 25.5% after switch to placebo (HR 0.52, not significant); symptoms stayed significantly lower
cards.people: 179 patients with moderate-to-severe generalised anxiety disorder received 12 weeks of open-label chamomile extract 1,500 mg/day; 93 responders entered a 26-week double-blind phase, randomised to continue chamomile or switch to placebo.
cards.result: Relapse occurred in 7/46 (15.2%) on chamomile vs 12/47 (25.5%) on placebo; mean time to relapse 11.4 vs 6.3 weeks; hazard ratio 0.52 (95% CI 0.20–1.33; p=0.16 — not significant). Chamomile participants maintained significantly lower GAD symptoms (p=0.0032), with small significant reductions in body weight and mean arterial pressure. Adverse event rates were similarly low.
cards.watchOut: The primary relapse outcome was not significant — the trial was underpowered for it because fewer placebo patients relapsed than expected. The honest claim is symptom maintenance, not proven relapse prevention. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Lavender oil (Silexan) for anxiety: beat placebo in a 539-patient GAD trial, in the same range as paroxetine in that trial
shelves.question: In adults with anxiety disorders, does the oral lavender-oil preparation Silexan reduce anxiety compared with placebo — and how does it compare with standard anxiolytics?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anti-Anxiety Agents/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Antidepressive Agents/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Anxiety Disorders/drug therapy, psychology · Depression/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Germany · Humans · Lavandula · Male · Middle Aged · Oils, Volatile/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Paroxetine/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Plant Oils/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Quality of Life · Remission Induction · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Silexan is a standardised oral lavender-oil preparation (named here because lavender products are not interchangeable, and only this preparation has this trial record). Its largest trial randomised 539 adults with generalised anxiety disorder to Silexan 160 mg, Silexan 80 mg, paroxetine 20 mg, or placebo for 10 weeks: Hamilton Anxiety scores fell 14.1 and 12.8 points on Silexan versus 9.5 on placebo (both doses p<0.01), while paroxetine's 11.3-point fall was only a trend in the full analysis set (p=0.10). Response rates were 60.3% and 51.9% on Silexan versus 37.8% on placebo, and adverse-event rates were comparable to placebo. The earlier programme — subsyndromal anxiety versus placebo, GAD versus lorazepam (comparable score reductions), restlessness versus placebo — is summarised in the 2010 review carded beside it, labelled as the review it is. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Silexan 160 mg and 80 mg beat placebo on Hamilton Anxiety scores in 539 GAD patients; paroxetine showed only a trend in the full analysis set
cards.summary: Silexan 160 mg and 80 mg beat placebo on Hamilton Anxiety scores in 539 GAD patients; paroxetine showed only a trend in the full analysis set
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo- and active-controlled trial (Kasper 2014)
cards.people: 539 adults with generalised anxiety disorder (DSM-5 criteria, HAM-A ≥18) in a randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial of Silexan 160 mg/day, Silexan 80 mg/day, paroxetine 20 mg/day, or placebo for 10 weeks.
cards.result: HAM-A reductions: 14.1±9.3 points (Silexan 160), 12.8±8.7 (Silexan 80), 11.3±8.0 (paroxetine), 9.5±9.0 (placebo). Both Silexan doses were superior to placebo (p<0.01); paroxetine showed a trend (p=0.10) in the full analysis set and was significant in observed cases. Response (≥50% HAM-A reduction): 60.3% and 51.9% vs 43.2% (paroxetine) vs 37.8% (placebo). Adverse-event incidence density was lowest on Silexan 160 mg (0.006/day) and similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The trial was manufacturer-supported and the paroxetine comparison flatters Silexan partly because paroxetine itself underperformed in the full analysis set; the clean claim is superiority to placebo, not superiority to an SSRI. Product tested: Silexan, Dr Willmar Schwabe's proprietary oral lavender-oil preparation — named because lavender products are not interchangeable.

The international journal of neuropsychopharmacology. 2014. PMID: 24456909. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. shelves.title: Ashwagandha for stress and anxiety: two small, short trials of two different extracts, both positive — weak evidence
shelves.question: In adults under stress, do standardised ashwagandha root extracts reduce stress and anxiety scores compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Anxiety Agents/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Anxiety/drug therapy, metabolism · Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulfate/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hydrocortisone/metabolism · Male · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Stress, Psychological/drug therapy, metabolism · Testosterone/metabolism · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Ashwagandha is marketed as an adaptogen for stress, and the randomised record is two small, short, single-centre trials — each of a different proprietary extract. Chandrasekhar (64 adults with chronic stress, 60 days) gave a high-concentration full-spectrum root extract 300 mg twice daily and reported significant reductions on all stress-assessment scales and in serum cortisol versus placebo. Lopresti (60 stressed adults, 60 days) gave a different extract (Shoden, 240 mg/day) and found a significant Hamilton Anxiety reduction (p=0.040), a near-significant DASS-21 result (p=0.096), and greater falls in morning cortisol. Effects of this size from trials of this size are exactly what MAYBE (weak evidence) is for — and 'ashwagandha' on a shop shelf is not one standardised thing, so the tested extracts are named. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Full-spectrum root extract 300 mg twice daily for 60 days significantly reduced all stress-scale scores and serum cortisol vs placebo (n=64)
cards.summary: Full-spectrum root extract 300 mg twice daily for 60 days significantly reduced all stress-scale scores and serum cortisol vs placebo (n=64)
cards.people: 64 adults with a history of chronic stress at a single centre, randomised to a high-concentration full-spectrum ashwagandha root extract (300 mg capsules twice daily) or placebo for 60 days, with serum cortisol and standard stress questionnaires.
cards.result: The ashwagandha group showed significant reductions (p<0.0001) on all stress-assessment scales at day 60 relative to placebo, and serum cortisol was substantially reduced (p=0.0006). Adverse effects were mild and comparable between groups; no serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Very small, single-centre, short, with uniformly large effects — a pattern that usually shrinks on replication. The PubMed record for this paper carries no MeSH list (noted on the source line rather than filled in). Product tested: the KSM-66 Ashwagandha root extract, provided by Ixoreal BioMed — named in the publication itself. Other ashwagandha extracts are not this product. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: Shoden extract 240 mg/day: HAM-A significantly lower (p=0.040), DASS-21 near-significant, morning cortisol reduced (n=60)
cards.people: 60 stressed, healthy adults randomised to a standardised ashwagandha extract (Shoden) 240 mg once daily or placebo for 60 days; outcomes Hamilton Anxiety Scale, DASS-21, cortisol, DHEA-S and testosterone.
cards.result: All participants completed the trial with no adverse events reported. Versus placebo: HAM-A reduction statistically significant (p=0.040); DASS-21 reduction near-significant (p=0.096); morning cortisol (p<0.001) and DHEA-S (p=0.004) fell more on ashwagandha. Testosterone rose in men over time but not significantly versus placebo (p=0.158).
cards.watchOut: A different extract from the 2012 trial's, so the two trials do not replicate each other so much as rhyme; the authors themselves call for larger, more diverse trials. Product tested: Shoden, a standardised ashwagandha extract (Arjuna Natural Ltd) named in the publication — a different proprietary extract from the KSM-66 used in the Chandrasekhar trial.
cards.source: Lopresti AL et al.. An investigation into the stress-relieving and pharmacological actions of an ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) extract: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31517876. Registry ID: CTRI/2017/08/009449 (Clinical Trials Registry-India, as recorded in the record). cards.summary: Synthesis: two small positive trials, two different extracts — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Ashwagandha root extracts for stress/anxiety: 124 participants across two 60-day placebo-controlled trials, each testing a different standardised extract.
cards.result: Both trials favoured the extract on stress/anxiety scores and cortisol; one primary scale in the second trial missed significance (p=0.096). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

shelves.title: Saffron for depression: matched fluoxetine in one small pilot and beat placebo in diabetic patients' comorbid symptoms — small, short trials only
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate major depression, does saffron (Crocus sativus) extract improve depressive symptoms compared with placebo or a standard antidepressant?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Crocus · Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluoxetine/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/adverse effects, therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Saffron has a traditional reputation in Persian medicine as a mood treatment, and its modern trial record is small, short and single-country. Noorbala randomised 40 outpatients with mild-to-moderate depression to saffron 30 mg/day or fluoxetine 20 mg/day for 6 weeks and found the two statistically indistinguishable (p=0.71 for the group comparison) — but with no placebo arm, 'as good as fluoxetine in a pilot' cannot show either drug worked. Milajerdi's placebo-controlled trial (54 patients with type 2 diabetes and comorbid mild-to-moderate depression–anxiety) found saffron significantly relieved the combined symptom measure, anxiety and sleep disturbance, though not depression alone. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the signal is consistent, the trials are tiny, and nothing here supports saffron as a substitute for standard care.

cards.headline: Pilot: saffron 30 mg/day was statistically indistinguishable from fluoxetine 20 mg/day over 6 weeks (n=40) — with no placebo group
cards.summary: Pilot: saffron 30 mg/day was statistically indistinguishable from fluoxetine 20 mg/day over 6 weeks (n=40) — with no placebo group
cards.people: 40 adult outpatients meeting DSM-IV criteria for mild-to-moderate major depression in a single-centre double-blind randomised trial of saffron capsules 30 mg/day versus fluoxetine 20 mg/day for 6 weeks.
cards.result: Saffron was 'effective similar to fluoxetine' on depression scores (F=0.13, df=1, p=0.71); side-effect profiles did not differ significantly. The authors conclude a large-scale trial is justified.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm: in mild-to-moderate depression, spontaneous improvement and placebo response are large, so equivalence with fluoxetine in 40 patients cannot establish that saffron itself works. Carded as the comparison it is. The publication does not name a commercial saffron product.
cards.source: Noorbala AA et al.. Hydro-alcoholic extract of Crocus sativus L. versus fluoxetine in the treatment of mild to moderate depression: a double-blind, randomized pilot trial. Journal of ethnopharmacology. 2005. PMID: 15707766. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. cards.headline: Placebo-controlled: saffron relieved comorbid depression–anxiety symptoms, anxiety and sleep in type 2 diabetes — depression alone not significant
cards.summary: Placebo-controlled: saffron relieved comorbid depression–anxiety symptoms, anxiety and sleep in type 2 diabetes — depression alone not significant
cards.people: 54 outpatients with type 2 diabetes and mild-to-moderate comorbid depression–anxiety, randomised to saffron alcoholic extract 30 mg/day or placebo capsules for 8 weeks; outcomes included Hamilton depression and anxiety scales, sleep quality and life satisfaction.
cards.result: After 8 weeks, the combined depression–anxiety measure, anxiety, and sleep disturbance were significantly relieved in the saffron group (p<0.05) while changes on placebo were not significant; depression alone did not reach significance, and life satisfaction, anthropometrics and blood pressure did not change in either group.
cards.watchOut: A diabetic population with comorbid symptoms is not the same question as major depression in general; the depression-specific endpoint missed significance even here. The publication does not name a commercial saffron product. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: UC-II collagen for knee osteoarthritis: one 191-patient trial beat placebo and glucosamine–chondroitin on WOMAC — a single manufacturer's programme
shelves.question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does undenatured type II collagen (UC-II, 40 mg/day) improve pain and function compared with placebo or with glucosamine plus chondroitin?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Biomarkers/blood · Body Mass Index · Body Weight · C-Reactive Protein/metabolism · Cartilage Oligomeric Matrix Protein/blood · Collagen Type II/administration & dosage · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Interleukin-6/blood · Male · Matrix Metalloproteinase 3/blood · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Collagen powders and capsules are sold for joint pain in many forms; the one with a real osteoarthritis trial behind it is UC-II, a specific undenatured type II collagen preparation (named because the evidence belongs to this preparation, not to collagen in general). In its 191-patient, 180-day trial, UC-II improved total WOMAC scores significantly more than placebo (p=0.002) and more than glucosamine hydrochloride plus chondroitin sulfate (p=0.04), with pain, stiffness and function subscales all concordant and no safety separation. The programme's earlier trial was in 55 healthy volunteers with exercise-induced knee discomfort — knee extension and time to pain on exertion improved — which supports plausibility but is not osteoarthritis evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one adequate trial, from a manufacturer-linked programme, awaiting independent replication.

cards.headline: UC-II beat placebo (p=0.002) and glucosamine–chondroitin (p=0.04) on total WOMAC at 180 days in 191 knee-OA patients
cards.summary: UC-II beat placebo (p=0.002) and glucosamine–chondroitin (p=0.04) on total WOMAC at 180 days in 191 knee-OA patients
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled trial (Lugo 2016)
cards.people: 191 volunteers with knee osteoarthritis randomised to UC-II 40 mg/day, glucosamine hydrochloride 1,500 mg plus chondroitin sulfate 1,200 mg/day, or placebo for 180 days; primary endpoint change in total WOMAC.
cards.result: At day 180 the UC-II group showed a significantly greater reduction in total WOMAC than placebo (p=0.002) and than glucosamine–chondroitin (p=0.04). All three WOMAC subscales favoured UC-II: pain (p=0.0003 vs placebo; p=0.016 vs GC), stiffness (p=0.004; p=0.044), physical function (p=0.007 vs placebo). Safety outcomes did not differ among groups.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports p-values rather than the size of the WOMAC difference, so the clinical magnitude cannot be judged from the record carded; the trial sits inside the manufacturer's development programme. Product tested: UC-II, InterHealth Nutraceuticals' undenatured type II collagen ingredient; the publication's authors include InterHealth staff.

Nutrition journal. 2016. PMID: 26822714. Registry ID: CTRI/2013/05/003663 and CTRI/2013/02/003348 (Clinical Trials Registry-India, as recorded in the record). cards.headline: Earlier trial in healthy volunteers (not OA): UC-II improved knee extension and lengthened pain-free exertion after 120 days
cards.summary: Earlier trial in healthy volunteers (not OA): UC-II improved knee extension and lengthened pain-free exertion after 120 days
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in healthy volunteers (Lugo 2013)
cards.people: 55 healthy subjects with no arthritis or resting joint pain who developed knee discomfort on a standardised stepmill test, randomised to UC-II 40 mg/day or placebo for 120 days.
cards.result: Average knee extension improved to 81.0° on UC-II vs 74.0° on placebo at day 120 (p=0.011); the UC-II group exercised longer before first discomfort (2.8 vs 1.4 minutes from baseline, p=0.019), and 5 UC-II subjects vs 1 placebo subject reported no pain during or after exertion. No product-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A healthy-volunteer exertion study — it cannot substitute for osteoarthritis evidence and is carded as background only. Its PubMed record carries no MeSH list (noted on the source line rather than filled in). Both study materials were provided by InterHealth Nutraceuticals, Inc. (Benicia, CA), as named in the publication's full text.

shelves.title: Milk thistle (silymarin): the modern JAMA trial was null on every measure — against a 1989 trial claiming a survival benefit in cirrhosis
shelves.question: In chronic liver disease, does silymarin (milk-thistle extract) improve liver biochemistry, viral measures, or survival compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Alanine Transaminase/blood, drug effects · Antioxidants/administration & dosage, adverse effects · DNA, Viral/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis C, Chronic/drug therapy, enzymology · Humans · Interferons/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Silymarin/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Milk thistle is the liver supplement patients reach for most, and its record contains the starkest disagreement in this slate. The rigorous modern trial (SyNCH; 154 patients with chronic hepatitis C who had failed interferon therapy) tested silymarin at two and three times customary doses for 24 weeks: the primary ALT outcome was met by about 4% of patients in every arm including placebo, and ALT decline, HCV RNA and quality of life did not differ. Against that stands a 1989 trial in 170 patients with cirrhosis reporting 4-year survival of 58% on silymarin versus 39% on placebo (p=0.036), driven by alcoholic cirrhosis and Child A subgroups — a mortality claim this shelf prints plainly rather than burying. Tier C, because a survival claim sits in the balance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large blinded trial's null across every measured outcome outweighs a smaller older trial's subgroup-driven survival signal, but the disagreement belongs to the developer's judgement, not the shelf's silence.

cards.headline: SyNCH: high-dose silymarin matched placebo on the ALT primary outcome (~4% in every arm) and on HCV RNA and quality of life
cards.summary: SyNCH: high-dose silymarin matched placebo on the ALT primary outcome (~4% in every arm) and on HCV RNA and quality of life
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Fried 2012, SyNCH)
cards.people: 154 persons with chronic hepatitis C and ALT ≥65 U/L previously unsuccessfully treated with interferon, at four US centres, randomised to silymarin 420 mg or 700 mg three times daily or placebo for 24 weeks; primary outcome ALT ≤45 U/L, or <65 with a ≥50% fall from baseline.
cards.result: Only 2 participants per group met the primary outcome (3.8% placebo, 4.0% at 420 mg, 3.8% at 700 mg; p≥0.99). Mean ALT decline did not differ (p=0.75), nor did HCV RNA change (p=0.54) or quality-of-life measures. The adverse-event profile was comparable to placebo.
cards.watchOut: A hepatitis C population in the pre-direct-acting-antiviral era, with a biochemical primary outcome; the trial cannot speak to cirrhosis survival — which is precisely the claim the older trial makes, and why both are carded. Product tested: Legalon 140 (Rottapharm | Madaus), the standardised silymarin product donated by its maker for this trial, as stated in the publication. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Fried MW et al.. Effect of silymarin (milk thistle) on liver disease in patients with chronic hepatitis C unsuccessfully treated with interferon therapy: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 22797645. Registry ID: NCT00680342. cards.headline: Ferenci 1989: 4-year survival 58% on silymarin vs 39% on placebo (p=0.036) in 170 patients with cirrhosis
cards.summary: Ferenci 1989: 4-year survival 58% on silymarin vs 39% on placebo (p=0.036) in 170 patients with cirrhosis
cards.people: 170 patients with cirrhosis (alcoholic and non-alcoholic; Child classes A–C) randomised to silymarin 140 mg three times daily (n=87) or placebo (n=83), treated until the last entrant completed 2 years; mean observation 41 months. Non-compliant patients and non-attenders were classed as dropouts and withdrawn.
cards.result: Deaths: 24 (+4 dropouts) on silymarin vs 37 (+2 dropouts) on placebo; liver-related deaths 18 vs 31. Four-year survival was 58±9% vs 39±9% (p=0.036). Subgroup analyses suggested benefit in alcoholic cirrhosis (p=0.01) and in patients initially rated Child A (p=0.03). No drug side effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: Pre-modern trial conduct by current standards: dropouts withdrawn rather than analysed intention-to-treat, and the headline rests partly on subgroups. Its survival claim has never been retested at scale — the honest position is 'unreplicated', not 'refuted', and not 'shown'. Product identity: published reviews tabulating this trial identify its silymarin as Legalon (Madaus), 140 mg three times daily — the same standardised product family as the modern trial. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Ferenci P et al.. Randomized controlled trial of silymarin treatment in patients with cirrhosis of the liver. Journal of hepatology. 1989. PMID: 2671116. shelves.title: Pelargonium extract (EPs 7630) eased bronchitis in its maker's trials
shelves.question: In adults with acute bronchitis, does the Pelargonium sidoides root extract EPs 7630 shorten or soften the illness compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Pelargonium · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts · Bronchitis · Anti-Infective Agents · Severity of Illness Index · Humans
shelves.balance: In its own trials, yes: the Pelargonium sidoides root extract EPs 7630 beat placebo on bronchitis symptom scores in three randomised, double-blind trials totalling 998 adults. The Bronchitis Severity Score fell by 5.9 versus 3.2 points over 7 days in 468 patients, with 16% versus 43% still unable to work at day 7 (Matthys 2003); by 7.2 versus 4.9 points in 124 patients (Chuchalin 2005); and in dose-finding, by 4.3, 6.1 and 6.3 points at 30, 60 and 90 mg/day versus 2.7 on placebo in 406 patients — a dose-response (Matthys 2010). The tested product is named for clarification: EPs 7630, a registered trademark of Dr. Willmar Schwabe GmbH & Co. KG, Karlsruhe, Germany. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the results are consistent and dose-responsive, but every trial is the single manufacturer's programme, the endpoint is a symptom score in a self-limiting illness, and there is no independent replication.

cards.headline: Matthys 2003: EPs 7630 cut the Bronchitis Severity Score by 5.9 points versus 3.2 on placebo, and only 16% were still unable to work at day 7 versus 43%
cards.summary: Matthys 2003: EPs 7630 cut the Bronchitis Severity Score by 5.9 points versus 3.2 on placebo, and only 16% were still unable to work at day 7 versus 43%
cards.people: 468 adults with acute bronchitis present for 48 hours or less and a Bronchitis Severity Score (BSS) of 5 points or more, seen by 36 primary care physicians in the outpatient setting, randomised to EPs 7630, a Pelargonium sidoides root extract, or placebo — 30 drops three times daily for 7 days (233 EPs 7630, 235 placebo).
cards.result: The decrease in BSS from baseline to day 7 was 5.9 ± 2.9 points on EPs 7630 versus 3.2 ± 4.1 points on placebo; the 95% confidence interval for the difference was −3.36 to −2.06, showing significant superiority of EPs 7630 (p<0.0001). Working inability decreased to 16% in the EPs 7630 group compared with 43% in the placebo group (p<0.0001), illness duration was significantly shorter (p<0.001), and onset of effect within the first four days was recognised by 53.6% versus 36.2% (p<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 20/233 on EPs 7630 and 16/235 on placebo, all non-serious.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a symptom score (BSS), not a hard outcome, in a self-limiting illness; the multi-stage adaptive design and the manufacturer's trial programme (see synthesis) frame how much weight a single large positive trial can carry. The tested product is the specific extract EPs 7630, not any pelargonium preparation.
cards.source: Matthys H et al.. Efficacy and safety of an extract of Pelargonium sidoides (EPs 7630) in adults with acute bronchitis. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Phytomedicine. 2003. PMID: 12807337. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Chuchalin 2005: EPs 7630 beat placebo again — BSS fell 7.2 versus 4.9 points (P<.0001), with faster onset and better quality of life
cards.summary: Chuchalin 2005: EPs 7630 beat placebo again — BSS fell 7.2 versus 4.9 points (P<.0001), with faster onset and better quality of life
cards.people: 124 adults with acute bronchitis present for 48 hours or less and a Bronchitis Severity Score of 5 points or more, at six outpatient clinics, randomised to EPs 7630 or placebo — 30 drops three times daily for seven days (64 EPs 7630, 60 placebo). The publication names the tested product: EPs 7630, a registered trademark of Dr. Willmar Schwabe GmbH & Co. KG, Karlsruhe, Germany.
cards.result: The decrease in BSS from baseline to day seven was 7.2 ± 3.1 points with EPs 7630 versus 4.9 ± 2.7 points with placebo (P<.0001; 95% CI for the difference 1.21 to 3.56 as printed). For each of the five individual symptoms, rates of complete recovery were considerably higher in the EPs 7630 group; onset of effect within the first four days was recognised in 68.8% versus 33.3% (P<.0001), and health-related quality of life improved more with EPs 7630. Adverse events occurred in 15/64 on EPs 7630 and 10/60 on placebo, all non-serious.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the three trials (n=124) and part of the same manufacturer's programme as the other two — a replication by the maker, not independent replication. EPs 7630 is a defined extract of one company (Dr. Willmar Schwabe GmbH & Co. KG, named here for clarification, not promotion); results do not transfer to other pelargonium products, which are not FDA-regulated and may differ.

cards.headline: Matthys 2010: dose-finding in 406 patients — BSS fell 4.3, 6.1 and 6.3 points at 30, 60 and 90 mg/day versus 2.7 on placebo, a dose-response
cards.summary: Matthys 2010: dose-finding in 406 patients — BSS fell 4.3, 6.1 and 6.3 points at 30, 60 and 90 mg/day versus 2.7 on placebo, a dose-response
cards.people: 406 adults with acute bronchitis outside the strict indication for antibiotics, in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre dose-finding trial, assigned to EPs 7630 tablets 10 mg three times a day (30 mg/day), 20 mg three times a day (60 mg/day), 30 mg three times a day (90 mg/day) or placebo three times a day, for 7 days.
cards.result: Between day 0 and day 7, mean BSS decreased by 2.7 ± 2.3 points on placebo, 4.3 ± 1.9 at 30 mg/day, 6.1 ± 2.1 at 60 mg/day and 6.3 ± 2.0 at 90 mg/day; the differences between each EPs 7630 group and placebo were statistically significant (p<0.0001 each), and secondary endpoints showed comparable results. All documented adverse events were mild to moderate, their frequency was dose-dependent, and no serious adverse events were reported; the authors identify 20 mg tablets three times daily as the optimal dose for benefit–risk.
cards.watchOut: A dose-response on a symptom score strengthens the case that something pharmacological is happening — but this is still the same manufacturer's programme, the same BSS endpoint, and a 7-day horizon in a self-limiting illness; adverse-event frequency rose with dose.
cards.source: Matthys H et al.. shelves.title: Elderberry for flu: early small trials said yes, the best trial said no
shelves.question: In people with influenza or the common cold, does black elderberry extract shorten the illness or soften symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Common Cold · Dietary Supplements · Humans · Influenza, Human · Plant Extracts · Sambucus · Sambucus nigra
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Two early trials pointed to benefit — symptoms relieved on average 4 days earlier in a 60-patient influenza trial (Zakay-Rones 2004), and fewer cold-episode days (57 versus 117, p = 0.02) in 312 air travellers (Tiralongo 2016), though cold episodes themselves were not significantly fewer there (12 versus 17, p = 0.4). The most rigorous test went the other way: in 87 emergency-department patients with PCR-confirmed influenza, elderberry was no better than placebo on the primary outcome (5.3 versus 4.9 days, p = 0.57), in a trial reported as powered over 0.90 to detect a 2-day benefit (Macknin 2020). Small early positive trials plus one well-powered null do not add up to proof. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the early small trials said yes, but the best trial said no, so any benefit remains unproven.

cards.headline: Zakay-Rones 2004: symptoms relieved on average 4 days earlier on elderberry syrup — in 60 patients in a single flu season
cards.summary: Zakay-Rones 2004: symptoms relieved on average 4 days earlier on elderberry syrup — in 60 patients in a single flu season
cards.people: 60 patients aged 18–54 years suffering from influenza-like symptoms for 48 hours or less, enrolled during the influenza season of 1999–2000 in Norway in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
cards.result: Patients received 15 mL of elderberry or placebo syrup four times a day for 5 days and recorded symptoms on a visual analogue scale. Symptoms were relieved on average 4 days earlier and use of rescue medication was significantly less in those receiving elderberry extract compared with placebo.
cards.watchOut: Small (n = 60) and single-season, and the authors themselves said the findings needed confirmation in a larger study. The abstract does not name a retail brand — the trial used a commercial elderberry syrup, and no brand is named here.
cards.source: Zakay-Rones Z et al.. Randomized study of the efficacy and safety of oral elderberry extract in the treatment of influenza A and B virus infections. The Journal of International Medical Research. 2004. PMID: 15080016. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Tiralongo 2016: fewer cold-episode days in air travellers (57 versus 117, p = 0.02), but episodes were not significantly fewer (12 versus 17)
cards.summary: Tiralongo 2016: fewer cold-episode days in air travellers (57 versus 117, p = 0.02), but episodes were not significantly fewer (12 versus 17)
cards.people: 312 economy-class passengers travelling from Australia to an overseas destination, in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a standardised membrane-filtered elderberry (Sambucus nigra L.) extract, with cold episodes, duration and symptoms recorded in a daily diary and assessed using the Jackson score.
cards.result: Most cold episodes occurred in the placebo group (17 versus 12), but the difference was not significant (p = 0.4). Placebo-group participants had a significantly longer duration of cold-episode days (117 versus 57, p = 0.02) and the average symptom score over these days was also significantly higher (583 versus 247, p = 0.05).

cards.headline: Macknin 2020: no benefit in PCR-confirmed influenza — 5.3 versus 4.9 days to the primary outcome (p = 0.57)
cards.summary: Macknin 2020: no benefit in PCR-confirmed influenza — 5.3 versus 4.9 days to the primary outcome (p = 0.57)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (FDA-approved, investigator-initiated, Investigational New Drug trial)
cards.people: 87 consecutive consenting patients over age four (43 randomised to elderberry, 44 to placebo; average age 25 years, 56% male) with under 48 hours of at least two moderate-severity influenza symptoms and a positive polymerase chain reaction influenza test, in three emergency rooms (two suburban, one urban) in a Midwestern US health system; patients could also choose to receive the standard dosage of oseltamivir.
cards.result: The primary outcome — days until all symptoms were none or mild for 21.5 hours — was 5.3 ± 3.6 days on elderberry compared with 4.9 ± 2.8 days on placebo (p = 0.57); days to complete symptom resolution were 8.6 versus 8.7 (p = 0.87). Patients aged 5–12 years received 15 mL elderberry extract twice a day for 5 days and those over 12 received it four times a day. The authors report a small sample size but power over 0.90 to detect a 2-day benefit of elderberry versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc analysis suggested primary outcomes with elderberry taken alone (without oseltamivir) were 2 days worse than with placebo taken alone — post-hoc and hypothesis-generating only, not a proven harm. The small n cuts both ways, but the reported power over 0.90 for a 2-day benefit argues against dismissing the null as merely 'too small to tell'. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: small early trials said yes, the well-powered PCR-confirmed trial said no — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: small early trials said yes, the well-powered PCR-confirmed trial said no — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: 459 people across the three randomised trials above: 60 with influenza-like illness, 312 air travellers, and 87 emergency-department patients with PCR-confirmed influenza.
cards.result: Elderberry relieved symptoms about 4 days earlier in one small single-season trial and cut cold-episode days in air travellers, but in PCR-confirmed influenza it did not beat placebo (5.3 versus 4.9 days to the primary outcome). The preparations and populations differed, and the only trial that confirmed influenza by PCR was null. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: No trial names a retail brand a reader can match to a shop product, and the preparations differ between trials, so one trial's extract cannot stand in for another's. The post-hoc signal of worse outcomes without oseltamivir in Macknin 2020 is hypothesis-generating only.

shelves.title: Aged garlic extract for blood pressure: two positive trials of one product from one research group — promising, not yet independently confirmed
shelves.question: In adults with hypertension, does aged garlic extract (the Kyolic preparation) lower blood pressure compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/chemistry/*therapeutic use · Capsules · Combined Modality Therapy/adverse effects · Cysteine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/analysis/therapeutic use · *Dietary Supplements/adverse effects/analysis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Garlic/*chemistry · Humans · Hypertension/*diet therapy/drug therapy · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Patient Dropouts · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage/adverse effects/chemistry/*therapeutic use · Plant Roots/*chemistry
shelves.balance: Garlic is one of the most-bought supplements for blood pressure, and the trial evidence comes almost entirely from one Australian research group testing one product — Kyolic aged garlic extract. In a dose-response trial (79 hypertensive patients, 12 weeks), 480 mg/day lowered systolic pressure by 11.8 mmHg against placebo (p=0.006); the higher 960 mg dose looked borderline at 8 weeks. In the group's AGE at Heart trial (88 completers, 1.2 g/day, 12 weeks), systolic pressure fell 5.0 mmHg on average (p=0.016), and the half of patients who responded fell by 11.5/6.3 mmHg. A 5 mmHg average systolic fall is clinically worthwhile if real — but two trials from a single programme, on a surrogate endpoint, with no independent replication, is exactly the profile that earns a moderate stamp rather than a strong one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine-looking blood-pressure effect for the tested aged garlic extract, awaiting confirmation by independent groups.

cards.headline: Aged garlic extract 480 mg/day cut systolic pressure 11.8 mmHg versus placebo at 12 weeks
cards.summary: Aged garlic extract 480 mg/day cut systolic pressure 11.8 mmHg versus placebo at 12 weeks
cards.people: 79 patients with hypertension randomised double-blind to aged garlic extract capsules (240, 480 or 960 mg/day) or placebo for 12 weeks in a dose-response trial.
cards.result: Systolic blood pressure fell 11.8 ± 5.4 mmHg more on 480 mg than on placebo (p=0.006); the 960 mg dose showed a borderline effect at 8 weeks and the 240 mg dose none. The extract tested was Kyolic aged garlic extract — the publication names the product; garlic powders and oils are different preparations and were not tested here.
cards.watchOut: Single research programme and a blood-pressure surrogate; the result applies to the tested aged extract, not to culinary garlic or other garlic products. The Kyolic preparation was Wakunaga's (printed 'Wakunaga/Wagner' in the publication's full text); trial capsules were provided by Vitaco Health Ltd.
cards.source: Ried K et al.. Aged garlic extract reduces blood pressure in hypertensives: a dose-response trial. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2013. PMID: 23169470. shelves.title: Boswellia for knee osteoarthritis: three small trials agree — two test one company's named extracts (5-Loxin, Aflapin)
shelves.question: Does Boswellia serrata extract (frankincense) relieve the pain of knee osteoarthritis?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Boswellia · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Edema · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Pain Measurement · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three small double-blind trials of Boswellia serrata extracts (n = 30, 60, 60) all favour the extract over placebo for knee osteoarthritis pain and function, with the two modern trials testing named commercial preparations (5-Loxin, Aflapin) and reporting benefit within 5–7 days. All three trials are small and short, two share authors and products from a single development programme, and the oldest reports no effect sizes — enough for POSSIBLE, no more.

cards.headline: Crossover trial in 30 patients: less pain, more knee flexion and walking distance on Boswellia extract
cards.summary: Crossover trial in 30 patients: less pain, more knee flexion and walking distance on Boswellia extract
cards.people: 30 patients with knee osteoarthritis; Boswellia serrata extract or placebo for 8 weeks, then washout and crossover to the opposite treatment for 8 weeks, double-blind
cards.result: On the extract, patients reported decreased knee pain, increased knee flexion and increased walking distance, and the frequency of knee swelling decreased; radiology did not change. Differences versus placebo were statistically significant (the abstract reports no effect sizes). The extract was well tolerated apart from minor gastrointestinal effects.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients, no numbers in the abstract, and the extract is not characterised beyond 'Boswellia serrata extract' — this card supports the class weakly, not any product. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: 5-Loxin and Aflapin both beat placebo over 90 days in 60 patients — Aflapin worked within 7 days
cards.people: 60 patients with knee osteoarthritis randomised to 100 mg 5-Loxin (n = 20), 100 mg Aflapin (n = 20) or placebo (n = 20) daily for 90 days, double-blind; pain and function by visual analogue scale, Lequesne index and WOMAC

cards.headline: Synthesis: a plausible short-term pain reliever, proven only in small developer-run trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: a plausible short-term pain reliever, proven only in small developer-run trials
cards.people: 150 patients across the three randomised trials carded
cards.result: Boswellia serrata extracts — generically in 2003, and as the named preparations 5-Loxin and Aflapin in 2010–2011 — consistently beat placebo on knee pain and function over 1–3 months, with minor gastrointestinal effects the main harm reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
