shelves.title: Arnica for bruising: homeopathic arnica matched placebo; the gel matched ibuprofen — with no placebo to beat
shelves.question: Does arnica (homeopathic tablets or topical gel) reduce bruising, post-surgical swelling or joint pain?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Arnica · Carpal Tunnel Syndrome · Contusions · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hand · Homeopathy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Pain · Phytotherapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — homeopathic arnica, the form most people take for bruising, was no better than placebo for pain or bruising after hand surgery, and across three knee-surgery trials only the smallest comparison reached significance. Topical arnica gel matched ibuprofen gel for hand osteoarthritis in a 204-patient trial — but with no placebo arm, that trial cannot show either gel beats doing nothing. The bruising claim people actually buy arnica for remains unproven.

cards.headline: Three knee-surgery trials of homeopathic arnica: significant in one of three (the cruciate trial, P = 0.019)
cards.summary: Three knee-surgery trials of homeopathic arnica: significant in one of three (the cruciate trial, P = 0.019)
cards.people: Three sequential randomised double-blind trials of homeopathic Arnica montana D30 vs placebo around knee surgery: arthroscopy (n = 227), artificial knee joint implantation (n = 35) and cruciate ligament reconstruction (n = 57); primary outcome the change in knee circumference (swelling)
cards.result: Swelling change was similar between groups after arthroscopy (difference −0.25%, 95% CI −0.85 to 0.41; P = 0.204) and joint implantation (−1.68%, −4.24 to 0.77; P = 0.184), and significantly favoured arnica only after cruciate reconstruction (−1.80%, −3.30 to −0.30; P = 0.019). All three trials showed a non-significant trend toward less swelling on arnica.
cards.watchOut: One significant result among three trials (and the smallest-but-one sample) is the pattern chance produces; the authors present the programme as a trend, which is generous. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Arnica gel vs ibuprofen gel for hand osteoarthritis: no differences in pain or function (n = 204) — and no placebo arm
cards.summary: Arnica gel vs ibuprofen gel for hand osteoarthritis: no differences in pain or function (n = 204) — and no placebo arm
cards.people: 204 patients with radiologically confirmed, symptomatically active osteoarthritis of the finger joints randomised to arnica gel (50 g tincture per 100 g) or ibuprofen 5% gel for 21 days, double-blind
cards.result: There were no differences between groups in pain intensity, hand function or any secondary endpoint; adverse events were reported by 5 patients (4.8%) on arnica and 6 (6.1%) on ibuprofen. The authors conclude this arnica preparation is not inferior to ibuprofen gel.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the bruising remedy has not beaten placebo anywhere it has been tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: the bruising remedy has not beaten placebo anywhere it has been tested
cards.people: 64 hand-surgery and 319 knee-surgery patients in the homeopathic trials; 204 hand-osteoarthritis patients in the gel trial

shelves.title: Ginger for postoperative nausea: nausea eased modestly across 14 trials; vomiting not demonstrably reduced — and no tested product is named
shelves.question: In adults having surgery, does ginger reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antiemetics*/therapeutic use · Zingiber officinale* · Humans · Incidence · Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting/chemically induced, drug therapy, prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a consistent, modest effect on nausea, none demonstrated on vomiting. The meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (1,417 participants) found ginger, versus placebo, lowered nausea severity (mean difference −0.71), cut nausea incidence in the first 6 hours (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.85 — a 32% relative reduction) and reduced rescue antiemetic use (RR 0.71, 0.62 to 0.82), while vomiting was not significantly reduced (RR 0.78, 0.42 to 1.44) (Zhu 2021, PMID: 34312974). The classic trial found combined nausea-and-vomiting in 21% on powdered ginger root versus 41% on placebo in 120 women (Phillips 1993, PMID: 8214465), and a 150-woman trial of 500 mg ginger capsules found lower nausea severity but no difference in vomiting (Bameshki 2018, PMID: 29629059). Product naming, per the supplement rule: none of the carded publications names a specific product, brand or manufacturer — the trials used powdered root or locally prepared capsules — so no purchasable product can be identified from this record, and today's ginger products may differ in safety and effectiveness; that statement is carried on the cards. Not Tier C: the claim rests on a 14-trial synthesis and is symptom-only.

cards.headline: Zhu 2021: ginger for postoperative nausea and vomiting — nausea severity and rescue-antiemetic use lower than placebo across 14 trials; vomiting itself not significantly reduced
cards.summary: Zhu 2021: ginger for postoperative nausea and vomiting — nausea severity and rescue-antiemetic use lower than placebo across 14 trials; vomiting itself not significantly reduced
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 14 RCTs (Zhu 2021, Journal of Nursing Scholarship)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of ginger for prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV): 14 studies, 1,417 participants, comparing ginger with placebo or with prophylactic antiemetics. Preparations and doses varied across trials (powdered ginger root or extracts, typically around 1 g).
cards.result: Versus placebo, ginger lowered nausea severity (mean difference −0.71, 95% CI −1.37 to −0.06) and reduced rescue antiemetic use (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.82 — a 29% relative reduction). Nausea incidence in the first 6 hours was lower (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.85); vomiting incidence was not significantly reduced (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.44). Versus prophylactic antiemetics, ginger had lower nausea incidence (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.99) with no significant difference in vomiting or rescue use.
cards.watchOut: Small, short, heterogeneous trials of a food product with variable preparations — the pooled nausea effects are consistent but modest, and the vomiting outcome, the one patients count, is null. None of the included publications names a commercial product or brand in the record; see the synthesis card for the product statement.

cards.headline: Phillips 1993: powdered ginger root versus metoclopramide versus placebo — postoperative nausea and vomiting 21% vs 27% vs 41%
cards.summary: Phillips 1993: powdered ginger root versus metoclopramide versus placebo — postoperative nausea and vomiting 21% vs 27% vs 41%
cards.people: Prospective randomised double-blind trial in 120 women having elective day-case laparoscopic gynaecological surgery, comparing powdered ginger root, metoclopramide, and placebo, with postoperative nausea and vomiting incidence as the outcome.
cards.result: The incidence of nausea and vomiting was 21% with ginger, 27% with metoclopramide and 41% with placebo; the requirement for postoperative antiemetics was lower in the ginger group, while analgesia requirements, recovery time, time to discharge and side effects (sedation, abnormal movement, itch, visual disturbance) did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: The publication does not name a specific product, brand or manufacturer — it tested powdered ginger root — so no purchasable product can be identified from this record, and today's ginger products may differ in composition, safety and effectiveness. A single 120-patient trial from 1993 in one operation type; its role here is as the classic direct test behind the pooled estimate.

cards.headline: Bameshki 2018: ginger 500 mg before laparoscopic cholecystectomy — nausea severity lower at 2 and 12 hours; vomiting episodes not significantly different
cards.summary: Bameshki 2018: ginger 500 mg before laparoscopic cholecystectomy — nausea severity lower at 2 and 12 hours; vomiting episodes not significantly different
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Bameshki 2018, Electronic Physician)
cards.people: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial in 150 women undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy (Imam Raza Hospital, Mashhad, Iran, 2016): 75 received two capsules containing 250 mg ginger each (500 mg total) one hour before surgery and 75 received placebo capsules. Nausea severity and vomiting frequency were assessed at 2, 4, 6 and 12 hours after surgery.
cards.result: Nausea severity was lower in the ginger group at every time point, significantly so at 2 hours (p = 0.034) and 12 hours (p = 0.043) but not at 4 or 6 hours. Vomiting episodes did not differ significantly between groups at any time point (p > 0.05). The authors conclude 500 mg oral ginger one hour before surgery decreased the severity of postoperative nausea in this population.
cards.watchOut: The record carries no MeSH terms. A single-centre trial in women having one operation, testing a locally prepared capsule: the publication names no commercial product, brand or manufacturer, so no purchasable product can be identified from this record, and today's ginger products may differ in composition, safety and effectiveness. Its nausea-severity result agrees with the pooled estimate; its vomiting result agrees with the pooled null.

shelves.title: Rhodiola SHR-5 for burnout fatigue: better than placebo on burnout and concentration scores in 60 people — in a literature reviewers call contradictory
shelves.question: In adults with stress-related fatigue, does the standardised Rhodiola rosea extract SHR-5 (Swedish Herbal Institute) reduce fatigue and improve concentration compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analysis of Variance · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/metabolism · Attention/drug effects · Burnout, Professional/drug therapy · Depression · Double-Blind Method · Fatigue/drug therapy, etiology, metabolism · Female · Humans · Hydrocortisone/metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Phytotherapy* · Plant Extracts/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Plant Roots · Rhodiola* · Stress, Psychological/complications
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one small trial of one named extract, positive on some measures, inside a literature a systematic review calls contradictory. The trial (Olsson EM et al., PMID: 19016404) randomised 60 adults with stress-related fatigue to the standardised Rhodiola rosea root extract SHR-5 (Swedish Herbal Institute; 576 mg/day) or placebo for 28 days: both groups improved, but SHR-5 was superior on the Pines burnout scale and on several attention indices (omissions, Hit RT SE, variability on the Conners test), with a blunted cortisol response to awakening and no serious attributable side-effects. The systematic review (Ishaque S et al., PMID: 22643043) found 11 trials, judged all at high or unclear risk of bias, and concluded efficacy cannot be accurately assessed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): SHR-5 may reduce stress-related fatigue over four weeks; the claim belongs to that named extract and dose, and current Rhodiola products — which vary widely in extract and dose — cannot be assumed to share its safety or effectiveness.

cards.headline: Olsson 2009: SHR-5 extract (576 mg/day, 28 days) beat placebo on burnout scores and attention-test indices in 60 people with stress-related fatigue — with placebo improving too
cards.summary: Olsson 2009: SHR-5 extract (576 mg/day, 28 days) beat placebo on burnout scores and attention-test indices in 60 people with stress-related fatigue — with placebo improving too
cards.people: 60 men and women aged 20–55 years meeting Swedish National Board of Health and Welfare criteria for fatigue syndrome, randomised double-blind to four tablets daily of the standardised Rhodiola rosea root extract SHR-5 (576 mg extract/day, n=30) or matching placebo (n=30) for 28 days; outcomes included quality of life (SF-36), Pines burnout scale, depression (MADRS), attention (Conners CPT II), and salivary cortisol response to awakening.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly on the Pines burnout scale, SF-36 mental health, MADRS, and several attention indices (a substantial placebo effect). Between groups, SHR-5 was significantly better on the Pines burnout scale and on the Conners indices omissions, Hit RT SE, and variability, and the pre- versus post-treatment cortisol response to awakening differed significantly between groups. No serious side-effects attributable to the extract were reported. The authors conclude repeated SHR-5 administration exerts an anti-fatigue effect increasing mental performance, particularly concentration.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, 28 days, and many outcome measures with significance on a subset is the classic small-herbal-trial profile; the strong placebo response shows how much of the experience is context. The tested product is the named SHR-5 extract (the Swedish Herbal Institute standardised preparation identified in the miner's source check; the PubMed record itself names the extract SHR-5 but does not print the company name) — results do not transfer to generic 'Rhodiola' capsules of unknown extract, dose, or rosavin content, which may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Olsson EM et al. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study of the standardised extract SHR-5 of the roots of Rhodiola rosea in the treatment of subjects with stress-related fatigue. cards.headline: Ishaque 2012 (systematic review): 11 Rhodiola trials for physical and mental fatigue — every one at high or unclear risk of bias, results contradictory
cards.summary: Ishaque 2012 (systematic review): 11 Rhodiola trials for physical and mental fatigue — every one at high or unclear risk of bias, results contradictory
cards.people: Systematic review of 11 controlled trials (10 described as randomised) of Rhodiola rosea for physical or mental fatigue, in healthy populations and clinical populations, searched across six databases.
cards.result: Two of six trials of physical fatigue in healthy people reported Rhodiola effective, as did three of five trials of mental fatigue. All included studies exhibited either a high risk of bias or reporting flaws that hinder assessment of validity (unclear risk of bias). The reviewers conclude the research is contradictory: some evidence suggests benefit for physical performance and mental fatigue, but methodological flaws limit accurate assessment of efficacy, and a rigorously designed trial is needed.
cards.watchOut: The review pools different extracts, doses, and populations — precisely the heterogeneity the herb-naming rule exists to expose — so its 'contradictory' verdict is about the Rhodiola literature as a whole, not about SHR-5 specifically. It predates no decisive later trial: the field still lacks the rigorous study the reviewers asked for.
cards.source: Ishaque S et al. Rhodiola rosea for physical and mental fatigue: a systematic review. BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22643043. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a named extract with a positive small trial, inside a genus-wide literature nobody can grade — the weakest form of 'promising'
cards.summary: Synthesis: a named extract with a positive small trial, inside a genus-wide literature nobody can grade — the weakest form of 'promising'
cards.people: One RCT of the SHR-5 extract (60 patients, 28 days) plus an 11-trial systematic review of Rhodiola rosea for fatigue.
cards.result: Fatigue/burnout: SHR-5 significantly better than placebo on the Pines burnout scale. Attention: significant advantages on three Conners CPT II indices; several other indices improved in both arms. Cortisol awakening response: significantly different between groups. Harms: no serious attributable side-effects in the trial. Literature-wide: 5 of 11 trials positive, all at high or unclear risk of bias. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Stress-related fatigue over four weeks in Swedish working-age adults is the whole claim — not chronic fatigue syndrome, not athletic performance, not depression treatment. Because the tested product is a specific standardised extract (SHR-5), and the record does not support extending results to other preparations, current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single 60-patient trial.

shelves.title: Bacopa for the ageing memory: the tested extract was BacoMind, and it improved word-list learning and delayed recall — not the memory people complain about
shelves.question: In healthy older adults, does Bacopa monnieri extract (standardised extract CDRI 08, the KeenMind preparation) improve memory performance compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bacopa* · Dementia/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Male · Memory/drug effects · Middle Aged · Phytotherapy* · Plant Extracts/adverse effects, pharmacology, therapeutic use · Reference Values
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small trials, consistent direction, narrow outcome. The direct trial (Morgan A & Stevens J, PMID: 20590480) randomised 98 healthy adults over 55 to the Bacopa monnieri extract BacoMind (Natural Remedies Pvt. Ltd.), 300 mg/day, or placebo for 12 weeks: the Bacopa group improved significantly on verbal learning, memory acquisition, and delayed recall on the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (delayed recall p=0.001; total learning p=0.011), while visual memory, trail-making, and subjective memory scores did not differ significantly; gastrointestinal side-effects (increased stool frequency, abdominal cramps, nausea) were more frequent on Bacopa. A meta-analysis of nine trials (Kongkeaw C et al., PMID: 24252493) found improved attention speed (Trail B −17.9 ms; choice reaction time −10.6 ms). Note: the tested preparation in the record is BacoMind, not the CDRI 08/KeenMind preparation named in the mining note — the card follows the publication. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): standardised Bacopa extract probably improves some memory-test performance in healthy older adults over 12 weeks; whether that is a difference anyone notices in daily life, or any protection against dementia, is untested.

cards.headline: Morgan & Stevens 2010: BacoMind 300 mg/day for 12 weeks improved verbal learning and delayed recall (p=0.001) in healthy over-55s — visual and subjective memory did not significantly differ; gut side-effects did
cards.summary: Morgan & Stevens 2010: BacoMind 300 mg/day for 12 weeks improved verbal learning and delayed recall (p=0.001) in healthy over-55s — visual and subjective memory did not significantly differ; gut side-effects did
cards.people: 98 healthy participants over 55 years of age from the general population in Lismore, Australia (81 completed), randomised double-blind to Bacopa monnieri extract BacoMind (Natural Remedies Pvt. Ltd.), 300 mg/day, or identical placebo for 12 weeks; memory was assessed with the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (AVLT), Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test, Reitan Trail Making Test, and the Memory Complaint Questionnaire.
cards.result: Bacopa significantly improved verbal learning, memory acquisition, and delayed recall on the AVLT: trial A4 (p=0.000), A5 (p=0.016), A6 (p=0.000), A7 delayed recall (p=0.001), total learning (p=0.011), and retroactive interference (p=0.048). Complex Figure, Memory Complaint Questionnaire, and Trail Making scores improved but group differences were not significant. Bacopa caused gastrointestinal side-effects of increased stool frequency, abdominal cramps, and nausea.
cards.watchOut: The publication names the tested preparation as BacoMind (Natural Remedies Pvt. Ltd.) — the mining note for this topic named a different preparation (CDRI 08/KeenMind), and this card follows the publication, per the naming rule; results should not be transferred between preparations, and other current Bacopa products may differ in safety and effectiveness. Seventeen of 98 starters did not complete, many p-values were generated across subtests without a single prespecified primary endpoint visible in the record, and 12 weeks in healthy volunteers says nothing about dementia prevention.
cards.source: Morgan A et al. Does Bacopa monnieri improve memory performance in older persons? Results of a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20590480. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kongkeaw 2014 (meta-analysis): nine trials — Bacopa improved speed of attention (Trail B −17.9 ms; choice reaction time −10.6 ms) across 437 analysed subjects
cards.summary: Kongkeaw 2014 (meta-analysis): nine trials — Bacopa improved speed of attention (Trail B −17.9 ms; choice reaction time −10.6 ms) across 437 analysed subjects
cards.people: Meta-analysis of nine randomised placebo-controlled trials of chronic (≥12 weeks) standardised Bacopa monnieri extract without co-medication, 518 subjects in total, 437 eligible for the pooled analysis; included trials were assessed as low risk of bias with high reporting quality by the reviewers.
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed improved cognition by shortened Trail B test time (−17.9 ms, 95% CI −24.6 to −11.2, p<0.001) and decreased choice reaction time (reported as 10.6 ms, 95% CI −12.1 to −9.2, p<0.001). The authors conclude Bacopa has potential to improve cognition, particularly speed of attention, while noting only a large well-designed head-to-head trial would provide definitive data.
cards.watchOut: Millisecond differences on reaction-time tests are statistically tidy and clinically opaque — no included trial shows better daily functioning, and the pooled preparations are not all the same extract, which sits uneasily with the naming discipline this shelf applies to its anchor trial. The reviewers' 'low risk of bias' grading is more generous than most assessments of this literature.
cards.source: Kongkeaw C et al. Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on cognitive effects of Bacopa monnieri extract. Journal of Ethnopharmacology. 2014. PMID: 24252493. shelves.title: Hawthorn WS 1442 in heart failure: more watts on the bike and less breathlessness across 14 trials — and not one usable number on staying alive
shelves.question: In adults with chronic heart failure (NYHA class II–III) on standard therapy, does hawthorn extract WS 1442 (Dr. Willmar Schwabe) improve exercise capacity and symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Flavonoids/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Heart Failure/drug therapy, physiopathology · Heart Function Tests · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phytotherapy* · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — symptom and exercise benefits, consistently shown, with the outcomes that matter most never measured. In the largest single trial (Tauchert M, PMID: 12040357), 209 patients with NYHA class III heart failure on diuretics received the hawthorn extract WS 1442 (Dr. Willmar Schwabe) at 1,800 mg or 900 mg daily or placebo for 16 weeks: maximal tolerated workload rose significantly more on 1,800 mg than on either comparator, typical heart-failure symptoms improved significantly at both doses, and adverse events — particularly dizziness and vertigo — were fewest in the high-dose group. The Cochrane review (Pittler MH et al., PMID: 18254076) pooled 10 trials (855 patients): maximal workload +5.35 watts (95% CI 0.71–10.00), exercise tolerance up, pressure–heart-rate product down, and breathlessness and fatigue significantly improved — but no mortality or cardiac-event data apart from one trial's unexplained death counts (three on hawthorn, one on control). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): as an add-on to standard therapy, WS 1442 probably improves exercise capacity and symptoms in chronic heart failure; it is not a substitute for prognostic heart-failure drugs, whose benefit it has never been shown to share.

cards.headline: Tauchert 2002: WS 1442 1,800 mg/day significantly increased maximal workload versus placebo and versus 900 mg in 209 NYHA III patients — symptoms improved at both doses, adverse events fewest at the high dose
cards.summary: Tauchert 2002: WS 1442 1,800 mg/day significantly increased maximal workload versus placebo and versus 900 mg in 209 NYHA III patients — symptoms improved at both doses, adverse events fewest at the high dose
cards.people: 209 patients with chronic stable New York Heart Association class III heart failure on pre-existing diuretic treatment, randomised (single-blind) to hawthorn extract WS 1442 (Dr. Willmar Schwabe) 1,800 mg/day, WS 1442 900 mg/day, or placebo for 16 weeks; exercise capacity was measured by seated bicycle ergometry with incremental workloads, alongside patient-rated symptom scores and safety laboratory monitoring.
cards.result: After 16 weeks, maximal tolerated workload increased significantly more with 1,800 mg WS 1442 than with both placebo and 900 mg WS 1442 — a dose-dependent effect. Typical heart-failure symptoms as rated by patients were reduced more by WS 1442 than placebo, significantly for both doses. Efficacy and tolerability were rated best for the 1,800 mg group by patients and investigators. The incidence of adverse events was lowest in the 1,800 mg group, particularly dizziness and vertigo.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports significance without the workload numbers themselves, so this card claims direction and dose-dependence, not magnitude — the pooled magnitude is in the Cochrane card. The trial was single-blind, 16 weeks, on a diuretic-only background that predates modern heart-failure therapy; the record names the extract WS 1442 but does not print the manufacturer's name (the WS 1442 designation is Dr. Willmar Schwabe's standardised extract, as identified in the miner's source check) — other hawthorn products are not this extract and may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Tauchert M et al. Efficacy and safety of crataegus extract WS 1442 in comparison with placebo in patients with chronic stable New York Heart Association class-III heart failure. American Heart Journal. 2002. PMID: 12040357. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pittler 2008 (Cochrane): 14 trials — hawthorn raised maximal workload by 5.35 watts and eased breathlessness and fatigue as add-on therapy; mortality and cardiac events essentially unreported
cards.summary: Pittler 2008 (Cochrane): 14 trials — hawthorn raised maximal workload by 5.35 watts and eased breathlessness and fatigue as add-on therapy; mortality and cardiac events essentially unreported
cards.people: Cochrane review of 14 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trials of hawthorn leaf-and-flower extract monopreparations in chronic heart failure (mostly NYHA classes I–III, mostly as adjunct to conventional treatment); 10 trials with 855 patients provided meta-analysable data.
cards.result: Maximal workload favoured hawthorn (weighted mean difference 5.35 watts, 95% CI 0.71–10.00, p<0.02, n=380). Exercise tolerance increased (weighted mean difference 122.76 watt×min, 32.74–212.78, n=98). The pressure–heart-rate product fell (−19.22 mmHg/min, −30.46 to −7.98, n=264). Symptoms such as shortness of breath and fatigue improved significantly (weighted mean difference −5.47, −8.68 to −2.26, n=239). No data on mortality or morbidity such as cardiac events were reported, apart from one trial reporting deaths (three in the hawthorn group, one in control) without further details. Adverse events were infrequent, mild, and transient (nausea, dizziness, cardiac and gastrointestinal complaints).
cards.watchOut: The review's search closed in 2006 and its trials are small, short, and largely industry-linked to extract manufacturers; a 5-watt workload gain is a modest physiological effect, and the complete absence of mortality or hospitalisation data — in a condition where modern drugs are judged on exactly those — is the shelf's central limitation. The unexplained 3-versus-1 death split in one trial cannot be interpreted either way.

shelves.title: Ivy leaf extract EA 575 (Prospan) for acute cough: two placebo-controlled trials and their pooled analysis show faster recovery — BSS down 8.6 versus 6.2 points at a week, and twice as many cough-free
shelves.question: In adults with acute bronchitis or acute cough, does ivy leaf dry extract EA 575 (Prospan, Engelhard Arzneimittel) reduce cough severity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Area Under Curve · Bronchitis/drug therapy · Cough/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hedera/chemistry · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Plant Extracts/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Plant Leaves · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the tested product matters here: every positive trial used the same named preparation, ivy leaf dry extract EA 575 (Prospan, Engelhard Arzneimittel), not generic ivy products. In the Schaefer 2016 trial (PMID: 29441845), 181 adults with acute cough treated three times daily for one week showed statistically significant and clinically relevant reductions in cough severity on visual analogue scale, Bronchitis Severity Score and verbal category scores versus placebo, with a significant advantage detectable within 48 hours and persisting 7 days after treatment ended; all adverse events were non-serious, mild or moderate, and none was judged drug-related. The individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of EA 575 (Völp A et al., PMID: 36414647; 228 on EA 575, 162 on placebo) found Bronchitis Severity Score reductions of 8.6 versus 6.2 points at 7 days (p < 0.001), with the placebo group's 7-day score reduction matching what EA 575 achieved by day 4, and cough-free proportions of 18.1% versus 9.3% at treatment end and 56.2% versus 25.6% after a further untreated week; adverse event rates were comparable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for this specific extract, two placebo-controlled trials and their pooled analysis point the same way — faster, greater cough relief than placebo with no safety signal — but the evidence base is two industry-era trials of one proprietary extract, the outcomes are symptom scores in a self-limiting illness, and the result cannot be extended to other ivy preparations, which may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Schaefer 2016: 181 adults with acute cough — EA 575 ivy liquid beat placebo on cough severity within 48 hours, with the advantage still present a week after treatment stopped
cards.summary: Schaefer 2016: 181 adults with acute cough — EA 575 ivy liquid beat placebo on cough severity within 48 hours, with the advantage still present a week after treatment stopped
cards.people: 181 adult patients with acute cough, randomised double-blind to ivy leaves cough liquid containing EA 575 or matched placebo, three times daily for one week, with follow-up to 7 days after the end of treatment (visits 1–6).
cards.result: The primary outcome was cough severity on a visual analogue scale over the treatment period (area under the curve over 7 days). The evaluation of the VAS, Bronchitis Severity Score and Verbal Category Descriptive score showed statistically significant and clinically relevant reductions in cough severity and bronchitis symptoms in the EA 575 group compared with placebo; significant reductions were detected within 48 hours of the first dose and the treatment advantage was present at all following visits and 7 days after treatment ended. All adverse events were non-serious, mild or of moderate severity, and not drug-related. (The abstract reports the direction and significance of the score differences rather than their point values.)
cards.watchOut: Acute cough is self-limiting, so both arms improve; the claim is faster and greater relief, not cure. The trial tests one proprietary extract (EA 575, Prospan, Engelhard Arzneimittel) at one dose — other ivy products are not the tested product and may differ in safety and effectiveness. The abstract gives no numeric score differences, so the size of the advantage has to be taken from the pooled analysis carded next.

cards.headline: Völp 2022 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 390 patients): Bronchitis Severity Score fell 8.6 points on EA 575 versus 6.2 on placebo at 7 days, and 56.2% versus 25.6% were cough-free a week later
cards.summary: Völp 2022 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 390 patients): Bronchitis Severity Score fell 8.6 points on EA 575 versus 6.2 on placebo at 7 days, and 56.2% versus 25.6% were cough-free a week later
cards.type: Meta-analysis of 2 RCTs, individual patient data (Völp 2022)
cards.people: Individual patient data from two double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials in patients with acute respiratory tract infection: 228 received ivy leaves dry extract EA 575 and 162 placebo for 7 days, followed by a 7-day period without treatment. Main outcome: Bronchitis Severity Score (BSS).
cards.result: Significant BSS differences between EA 575 and placebo occurred already after 2 days and increased until treatment end, with BSS reductions of 8.6 ± 0.2 versus 6.2 ± 0.2 (marginal means ± SEM; p < 0.001). The score reduction for placebo after 7 days was comparable to that for EA 575 after 4 days. The proportion of cough-free patients in the EA 575 group was 18.1% at treatment end and 56.2% at end of follow-up, compared with 9.3% and 25.6% for placebo. Adverse event rates for EA 575 and placebo were comparable, and no safety signals were observed.
cards.watchOut: A two-trial pool of a single manufacturer's extract, analysed with industry involvement — the consistency is reassuring but the independence is limited, and two trials cannot exclude small-study or reporting effects. Absolute cough-free rates at treatment end were still low in both arms (18.1% versus 9.3%); the benefit is an acceleration of recovery in a self-limiting illness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one named extract, two placebo-controlled trials, one pooled analysis — faster cough recovery than placebo, no safety signal, and no licence to generalise to other ivy products
cards.summary: Synthesis: one named extract, two placebo-controlled trials, one pooled analysis — faster cough recovery than placebo, no safety signal, and no licence to generalise to other ivy products
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of ivy leaf dry extract EA 575 (Prospan, Engelhard Arzneimittel) in adults with acute cough / acute respiratory tract infection (181 patients in Schaefer 2016; 390 patients pooled in Völp 2022).
cards.result: Cough and bronchitis severity: significantly greater reductions on EA 575 in both the single trial and the pooled analysis (BSS −8.6 versus −6.2 at 7 days, p < 0.001). Speed: significant separation by 48 hours; placebo at day 7 matched EA 575 at day 4. Cough-free: 18.1% versus 9.3% at treatment end, 56.2% versus 25.6% one week later. Safety: adverse event rates comparable, all events non-serious in the single trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Everything here is about EA 575 as tested; the publication names the product and company (Prospan, Engelhard Arzneimittel), and current or alternative ivy products may differ in safety and effectiveness. No trial compared EA 575 with another active cough treatment, and none measured antibiotic use, complications, or return to work. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials plus an individual-patient meta-analysis agree, but the base is narrow and single-product.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schaefer A et al. Die Pharmazie. 2016 (PMID: 29441845); Völp A et al. Scientific reports. 2022 (PMID: 36414647).

shelves.title: Cineole (Soledum) for acute nonpurulent sinusitis: symptom score 3.0 versus 9.2 on placebo at 7 days in the one direct trial — a big gap resting on 152 patients
shelves.question: In adults with acute non-purulent rhinosinusitis, does cineole (1,8-cineole, the Soledum preparation) improve symptoms and sinus findings compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · C-Reactive Protein/metabolism · Cyclohexanols/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Eucalyptol · Female · Humans · Male · Monoterpenes/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Sinusitis/drug therapy/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted double-blind trial carries this shelf. In Kehrl 2004 (PMID: 15064633), 152 patients with acute nonpurulent rhinosinusitis took cineole (the Soledum preparation; two 100-mg capsules three times daily) or placebo for 7 days: the symptom-sum-score, 15.6 in both groups at baseline, fell to 6.9 versus 12.2 at day 4 and 3.0 versus 9.2 at day 7 — differences the authors describe as clinically relevant and statistically significant — with parallel improvements in headache on bending, frontal headache, trigeminal pressure-point sensitivity, general condition, nasal obstruction and secretion, and only two mild possibly-related side effects (heartburn and exanthema). A 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis of herbal medicines for rhinosinusitis (Hoang MP et al., PMID: 36609950; 47 randomised trials, 18 herbal medicines) independently placed cineole among the most effective treatments for symptom control in acute post-viral rhinosinusitis, at moderate certainty of evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the effect size in the single trial is large and the network synthesis concurs, but the direct evidence remains one 152-patient, 7-day trial of one named preparation in nonpurulent (largely viral/post-viral) disease — it says nothing about bacterial sinusitis, where the antibiotic question is separate, and other cineole products may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Kehrl 2004: 152 patients — symptom-sum-score fell to 3.0 on cineole versus 9.2 on placebo after 7 days, from 15.6 in both groups at baseline
cards.summary: Kehrl 2004: 152 patients — symptom-sum-score fell to 3.0 on cineole versus 9.2 on placebo after 7 days, from 15.6 in both groups at baseline
cards.people: 152 patients with acute nonpurulent rhinosinusitis (76 per group), randomised double-blind to cineole capsules (two 100-mg capsules three times daily — the Soledum preparation) or placebo capsules for 7 days; all patients analysed intention-to-treat. Primary endpoint: change in a defined symptoms-sum-score of symptoms and signs.
cards.result: Baseline mean symptoms-sum-score was 15.6 in both groups. After 4 days the score was 6.9 ± 2.9 on cineole versus 12.2 ± 2.5 on placebo, and after 7 days 3.0 ± 2.8 versus 9.2 ± 3.0; the differences were clinically relevant and statistically significant at both time points. Secondary endpoints moved the same way: headache on bending, frontal headache, sensitivity of pressure points of the trigeminal nerve, impairment of general condition, nasal obstruction, and rhinological secretion. Mild side effects possibly associated with medication occurred in two cineole patients (heartburn and exanthema).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, one week long, in nonpurulent disease — the population in which symptoms settle spontaneously and placebo responses are large; the between-group gap is nonetheless wide. The tested preparation is the named Soledum cineole product; the publication names the preparation, and other cineole/eucalyptus products may differ in safety and effectiveness. This trial does not address acute bacterial rhinosinusitis or antibiotic-sparing.
cards.source: Kehrl W et al. Therapy for acute nonpurulent rhinosinusitis with cineole: results of a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. The Laryngoscope. 2004. PMID: 15064633. cards.headline: Hoang 2023 (network meta-analysis, 47 RCTs): cineole ranked among the most effective herbal treatments for symptom control in acute post-viral rhinosinusitis, at moderate certainty
cards.summary: Hoang 2023 (network meta-analysis, 47 RCTs): cineole ranked among the most effective herbal treatments for symptom control in acute post-viral rhinosinusitis, at moderate certainty
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 47 RCTs (Hoang 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 47 randomised controlled trials evaluating 18 herbal medicines across six rhinosinusitis populations, with certainty assessed by GRADE.
cards.result: For acute post-viral rhinosinusitis, cineole and Pelargonium sidoides were the most effective treatments for controlling symptoms (moderate certainty of evidence). For the common cold, Pelargonium sidoides offered the most beneficial effect on symptom improvement (moderate certainty). Evidence for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis and chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps was restricted to a limited number of studies, and the authors note adverse events should be of concern for some herbal medicines and that further studies with adequate sample sizes and long-term follow-up are warranted.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings lean heavily on indirect comparisons and on the same small direct trials — for cineole the direct base is essentially the Kehrl trial carded here, so the review corroborates rather than multiplies the evidence. 'Most effective among herbal medicines' is a ranking within this class, not a comparison with intranasal steroids, saline, or watchful waiting.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a large symptom-score gap in one 7-day trial, backed by a moderate-certainty network ranking — promising for nonpurulent sinusitis symptoms, untested beyond it
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large symptom-score gap in one 7-day trial, backed by a moderate-certainty network ranking — promising for nonpurulent sinusitis symptoms, untested beyond it
cards.people: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial of cineole (Soledum preparation), 152 patients with acute nonpurulent rhinosinusitis, plus a 47-trial network meta-analysis of herbal medicines for rhinosinusitis.
cards.result: Symptom-sum-score at 7 days: 3.0 on cineole versus 9.2 on placebo (baseline 15.6 both groups); at 4 days 6.9 versus 12.2. Secondary symptom and sign endpoints concordant. Harms: two mild possibly-related events (heartburn, exanthema). Network meta-analysis: cineole among the most effective for acute post-viral rhinosinusitis symptoms, moderate certainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not extrapolate to bacterial sinusitis, chronic sinusitis, or children — none was studied here. shelves.title: Bronchipret (thyme–ivy, Bionorica) for acute bronchitis: coughing fits down 68.7% versus 47.6% on placebo and 96% responders by day 10 — in a single 361-patient trial
shelves.question: In adults with acute bronchitis with productive cough, does the thyme–ivy fluid extract combination Bronchipret (Bionorica) shorten cough compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bronchitis/drug therapy · Cough/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hedera/adverse effects/chemistry · Humans · Male · Patient Compliance · Plant Extracts/adverse effects/pharmacology · Plant Leaves/chemistry · Prospective Studies · Sample Size · Thymus Plant/adverse effects/chemistry
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-reported double-blind trial of the named combination product. In Kemmerich 2006 (PMID: 17063641), 361 outpatients with acute bronchitis and productive cough took the thyme–ivy fluid extract combination Bronchipret (Bionorica), 5.4 mL three times daily, or matched placebo for 11 days: the mean reduction in daytime coughing fits on days 7–9 was 68.7% relative to baseline on Bronchipret versus 47.6% on placebo (p < 0.0001), a 50% relative reduction in coughing fits was reached 2 days earlier on the combination, and Bronchitis Severity Score responder rates were 83.0% versus 53.9% at day 4 and 96.2% versus 74.7% at day 10 (p < 0.0001), with no difference in the frequency or severity of adverse events and no severe or serious events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the trial is big for this field and internally consistent across counted coughing fits, severity scores and responder rates — but it is a single trial of one proprietary combination (Bronchipret, Bionorica), in a self-limiting illness, with symptom-count outcomes; it cannot be read across to ivy alone (shelf #3039, a different product), to thyme alone, or to other thyme–ivy products, which may differ in safety and effectiveness. No qualifying systematic review or meta-analysis of this combination was found, so no synthesis card is added.

cards.headline: Kemmerich 2006: 361 outpatients — coughing fits fell 68.7% on Bronchipret versus 47.6% on placebo by days 7–9 (p < 0.0001), and responders were 96.2% versus 74.7% at day 10
cards.summary: Kemmerich 2006: 361 outpatients — coughing fits fell 68.7% on Bronchipret versus 47.6% on placebo by days 7–9 (p < 0.0001), and responders were 96.2% versus 74.7% at day 10
cards.people: 361 outpatients with acute bronchitis, at least 10 coughing fits during the day, onset of bronchial mucus production with impaired ability to cough up at most 2 days before recruitment, and a Bronchitis Severity Score of at least 5, randomised double-blind in a multicentre phase IV study to thyme–ivy fluid extract combination syrup (Bronchipret; n = 182) or matched placebo syrup (n = 179), 5.4 mL three times daily for 11 days.
cards.result: Primary outcome (change in daytime coughing-fit frequency on days 7–9, counted by patients with a manual counter): mean reduction relative to baseline was 68.7% on the thyme–ivy combination versus 47.6% on placebo (p < 0.0001). A 50% relative reduction in coughing fits from baseline was reached 2 days earlier in the combination group. Bronchitis Severity Score responder rates favoured the combination at visit 2, day 4 (83.0% versus 53.9%) and visit 3, day 10 (96.2% versus 74.7%), both p < 0.0001, with faster symptom regression overall. Tolerability: no difference in frequency or severity of adverse events between groups; no severe or serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Percentages here are relative reductions in coughing-fit counts within each arm, printed with the placebo arm's own 47.6% relative reduction beside them — acute bronchitis improves on its own, and the drug's added value is the roughly 21-point gap and the 2-day head start, not the headline 68.7%. Single trial, single proprietary product (Bronchipret, Bionorica); a phase IV design run in the product's home market. No antibiotic-use, complication, or work-loss outcomes.

shelves.title: Devil's claw for chronic low back pain: two small placebo trials (315 people) favoured extracts standardised to 50–100 mg harpagoside — low-quality evidence, short-term only
shelves.question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does devil's claw (Harpagophytum procumbens, e.g. the Doloteffin preparation) reduce pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/drug therapy · Adult · Benzyl Alcohols/therapeutic use · Capsicum · Chronic Pain/drug therapy · Cyclooxygenase 2 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Glucosides/therapeutic use · Harpagophytum · Humans · Lactones/therapeutic use · Low Back Pain/drug therapy · Phytotherapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Salix · Sulfones/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term, on low-quality evidence. The Cochrane review of herbal medicine for low back pain (Oltean et al., PMID: 25536022) concluded that daily doses of Harpagophytum procumbens standardised to 50 mg or 100 mg harpagoside may be better than placebo for short-term improvements in pain and may reduce use of rescue medication (two trials, 315 participants, low-quality evidence), with a further trial showing relative equivalence to rofecoxib 12.5 mg/day on very-low-quality evidence. The largest placebo trial (Chrubasik et al., PMID: 10101629; 197 patients with exacerbations of chronic back pain) counted patients pain-free without rescue tramadol in the last treatment week: 3 on placebo, 6 on extract providing 50 mg harpagoside/day, and 10 on 100 mg/day (P = 0.027 for the dose trend) — real, but absolute responder numbers are small. Neither record names the Doloteffin preparation or its maker: the trial extract is identified as WS 1531, and the review by standardised harpagoside dose; current commercial products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest short-term pain benefit is the most the evidence supports.

cards.headline: Oltean 2014 (Cochrane): devil's claw at 50 or 100 mg harpagoside/day 'may be better than placebo' — two trials, 315 participants, low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Oltean 2014 (Cochrane): devil's claw at 50 or 100 mg harpagoside/day 'may be better than placebo' — two trials, 315 participants, low-quality evidence
cards.people: 14 randomised trials (2,050 participants) of herbal medicines for acute, sub-acute or chronic non-specific low back pain; the devil's claw (Harpagophytum procumbens) placebo comparison rests on two trials totalling 315 participants, with a third trial (88 participants) comparing devil's claw with rofecoxib.
cards.result: Daily doses of Harpagophytum procumbens, standardised to 50 mg or 100 mg harpagoside, may be better than placebo for short-term improvements in pain and may reduce use of rescue medication (two trials, 315 participants, low-quality evidence). Another Harpagophytum trial demonstrated relative equivalence to 12.5 mg/day rofecoxib but was graded very low quality (one trial, 88 participants). No significant adverse events were noted within the included trials. The review's wider verdict: for devil's claw and the other herbs that beat placebo, evidence was of moderate quality at best, and reporting completeness in the trials was poor.
cards.watchOut: This is a multi-herb review — the devil's claw slice is two small trials graded low quality. The candidate question names the Doloteffin preparation; neither this review nor the trial carded below names Doloteffin or a manufacturer, so this shelf cannot vouch for that specific product.
cards.source: Oltean H et al. Herbal medicine for low-back pain. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 25536022. cards.headline: Chrubasik 1999: pain-free without rescue tramadol in 10 patients on 100 mg harpagoside, 6 on 50 mg, 3 on placebo (P = 0.027 dose trend)
cards.summary: Chrubasik 1999: pain-free without rescue tramadol in 10 patients on 100 mg harpagoside, 6 on 50 mg, 3 on placebo (P = 0.027 dose trend)
cards.people: 197 patients with chronic susceptibility to back pain and a current exacerbation producing pain worse than 5 on a 0–10 scale (183 completed), randomised for 4 weeks to Harpagophytum extract WS 1531 at 600 or 1,200 mg/day (providing 50 or 100 mg of the marker harpagoside) or placebo, with tramadol permitted as rescue medication. The record names the extract as WS 1531 and names no manufacturer.
cards.result: The principal outcome — patients pain-free without permitted rescue medication for 5 days of the last week — occurred in 3 patients on placebo, 6 on the 50 mg harpagoside dose, and 10 on the 100 mg dose (P = 0.027, one-tailed Cochrane–Armitage trend test). Subgroup analyses suggested the effect was confined to patients with more severe, radiating pain with neurological deficit, though subsidiary analyses of the Arhus index pain component pointed somewhat differently. There was no evidence of Harpagophytum-related side effects except possibly mild, infrequent gastrointestinal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The headline is a trend across three small responder counts (3, 6, 10) tested one-tailed; most patients in every group were not pain-free, follow-up is 4 weeks in an exacerbation population (not steady chronic pain), and the internal subgroup signals contradict each other.
cards.source: Chrubasik S et al. Effectiveness of Harpagophytum extract WS 1531 in the treatment of exacerbation of low back pain: a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study. cards.result: Pain: both sources favour devil's claw over placebo short-term, with a dose trend (50 mg versus 100 mg harpagoside/day; pain-free responders 3 versus 6 versus 10 in the largest trial). shelves.title: Flaxseed and blood pressure: one PAD trial found a striking −10/−7 mmHg — the pooled effect across 15 trials is a tenth of that (−2.85/−2.39 mmHg)
shelves.question: In hypertensive patients with peripheral arterial disease, does milled flaxseed (30 g/day in food) lower blood pressure versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Diet · Double-Blind Method · Female · Flax · Humans · Hypertension/blood/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Phytotherapy · Plant Preparations/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Seeds · Treatment Outcome · alpha-Linolenic Acid/blood
shelves.balance: SPLIT — one remarkable trial, one modest pool. In FLAX-PAD (Rodriguez-Leyva et al., PMID: 24126178), 110 patients with peripheral artery disease ate foods containing 30 g/day of milled flaxseed or placebo for 6 months: systolic pressure was ≈10 mmHg lower and diastolic ≈7 mmHg lower on flaxseed, and patients entering with systolic ≥140 mmHg fell 15 mmHg systolic and 7 mmHg diastolic — described by its authors as one of the most potent antihypertensive effects achieved by a dietary intervention. But the meta-analysis of flaxseed trials (Ursoniu et al., PMID: 26071633; 15 trials, 1,302 participants) found much smaller average effects: systolic −2.85 mmHg (95% CI −5.37 to −0.33) and diastolic −2.39 mmHg (95% CI −3.78 to −0.99), with significant systolic reduction for flaxseed powder specifically (−1.81 mmHg) but not for oil or lignan extract. PROPOSED SPLIT: in the PAD population asked about, the single dedicated trial is strongly positive; across hypertensive populations generally, expect a small average effect — the FLAX-PAD number should not be quoted as the typical result.

cards.headline: Rodriguez-Leyva 2013 (FLAX-PAD): systolic ≈10 and diastolic ≈7 mmHg lower on 30 g/day milled flaxseed at 6 months — −15/−7 in those starting ≥140 systolic
cards.summary: Rodriguez-Leyva 2013 (FLAX-PAD): systolic ≈10 and diastolic ≈7 mmHg lower on 30 g/day milled flaxseed at 6 months — −15/−7 in those starting ≥140 systolic
cards.people: 110 patients with peripheral artery disease, in a prospective double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, ingesting a variety of foods containing 30 g of milled flaxseed or placebo daily over 6 months; body weights did not differ between groups at any time.
cards.result: After 6 months, systolic blood pressure was ≈10 mmHg lower and diastolic ≈7 mmHg lower in the flaxseed group compared with placebo. Patients who entered with systolic ≥140 mmHg obtained a significant reduction of 15 mmHg systolic and 7 mmHg diastolic from flaxseed ingestion; the effect was achieved selectively in hypertensive patients. Plasma α-linolenic acid and enterolignans increased 2- to 50-fold on flaxseed but not placebo, and circulating α-linolenic acid levels correlated with systolic and diastolic pressure.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 110 patients from one research group, with effect sizes larger than most antihypertensive drugs achieve — the record itself invites scepticism by its superlative framing, and the hypertensive-subgroup figure (−15 mmHg) is a within-trial split, not the primary whole-group result.
cards.source: Rodriguez-Leyva D et al. Potent antihypertensive action of dietary flaxseed in hypertensive patients. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2013. PMID: 24126178. cards.summary: Ursoniu 2016 (meta-analysis): pooled flaxseed effect is systolic −2.85 and diastolic −2.39 mmHg across 15 trials and 1,302 participants
cards.people: 15 randomised controlled trials (19 treatment arms, 1,302 participants) of flaxseed supplements (powder, oil, or lignan extract) versus control, searching to February 2015.
cards.result: Flaxseed supplementation significantly reduced systolic pressure (weighted mean difference −2.85 mmHg, 95% CI −5.37 to −0.33, p = 0.027) and diastolic pressure (−2.39 mmHg, 95% CI −3.78 to −0.99, p = 0.001). By preparation, systolic reduction was significant for flaxseed powder (−1.81 mmHg, 95% CI −2.03 to −1.59) but not oil (−4.62, CI crossing zero) or lignan extract (+0.28); diastolic reduction was significant for powder (−1.28) and oil (−4.10) but not lignan extract. Effects were larger in trials of at least 12 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate mixes preparations, doses, and populations — almost none of them the PAD population of FLAX-PAD — so it answers 'flaxseed in general' rather than this shelf's exact question; heterogeneity between the big single trial and the pool is the finding, not a nuisance.
cards.source: Ursoniu S et al. Effects of flaxseed supplements on blood pressure: A systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled clinical trial. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2016. PMID: 26071633. cards.headline: Synthesis: believe the direction, not the FLAX-PAD magnitude — flaxseed lowers pressure a little on average, perhaps more in PAD, unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: believe the direction, not the FLAX-PAD magnitude — flaxseed lowers pressure a little on average, perhaps more in PAD, unproven
cards.people: One double-blind trial in 110 peripheral-artery-disease patients eating 30 g/day milled flaxseed in foods for 6 months, set against a 15-trial meta-analysis of 1,302 participants across flaxseed preparations.
cards.result: FLAX-PAD: ≈−10/−7 mmHg versus placebo (≈−15/−7 in the hypertensive subgroup). Pooled: −2.85/−2.39 mmHg. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the question's exact population rests on a single trial whose effect size is an outlier against the wider literature — a pattern that usually resolves toward the pooled estimate on replication, which has not yet happened in PAD.
cards.watchOut: Neither source reports clinical events (stroke, myocardial infarction, death); blood pressure is the whole story here, and flaxseed in food is an adjunct to — never a substitute for — prescribed antihypertensive treatment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rodriguez-Leyva D et al. Hypertension (Dallas, Tex. : 1979). 2013 (PMID: 24126178); Ursoniu S et al. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2016 (PMID: 26071633).

shelves.title: Olive leaf extract (EFLA 943) for blood pressure: it matched captopril in one trial (−11.5 versus −13.7 mmHg systolic) — but no placebo-controlled trial exists, and the only other human study was open-label in 40 twins
shelves.question: In adults with mild hypertension, does the olive leaf extract EFLA 943 (Benolea) lower blood pressure versus placebo — and how did it compare with captopril in a head-to-head trial?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Antihypertensive Agents/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Captopril/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypertension/drug therapy/physiopathology · Lipids/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Olea/chemistry · Plant Extracts/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Plant Leaves/chemistry
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the placebo question has never been tested. The head-to-head trial (Susalit et al., PMID: 21036583) randomised patients with stage-1 hypertension to olive leaf extract EFLA 943, 500 mg twice daily, or captopril 12.5 mg twice daily titrated to 25 mg, for 8 weeks: systolic pressure fell −11.5 ± 8.5 mmHg on the extract and −13.7 ± 7.6 mmHg on captopril, diastolic −4.8 ± 5.5 versus −6.4 ± 5.2, with no significant difference between groups — but with no placebo arm, the trial cannot show the extract beats doing nothing, since stage-1 pressures commonly fall on trial entry alone. The earlier human study (Perrinjaquet-Moccetti et al., PMID: 18729245) was an open study in 40 borderline-hypertensive monozygotic twins: blood pressure was unchanged in the lifestyle-advice controls and the 500 mg/day group, and fell significantly only at 1,000 mg/day (137 ± 10/80 ± 10 to 126 ± 9/76 ± 6 mmHg). Neither record names a manufacturer; both test the extract identified as EFLA 943. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a real pharmacological signal is plausible, but 'similar to captopril in an unblinded-by-design comparison without placebo' is not evidence of efficacy.

cards.headline: Susalit 2011: EFLA 943 lowered systolic by 11.5 mmHg versus captopril's 13.7 over 8 weeks — not significantly different, and no placebo group to beat
cards.summary: Susalit 2011: EFLA 943 lowered systolic by 11.5 mmHg versus captopril's 13.7 over 8 weeks — not significantly different, and no placebo group to beat
cards.people: Patients with stage-1 hypertension (baseline systolic 149.3 ± 5.58 mmHg on olive leaf extract, 148.4 ± 5.56 on captopril; diastolic ≈93.9 in both) in a double-blind randomised parallel study: olive (Olea europaea) leaf extract EFLA 943, 500 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, versus captopril 12.5 mg twice daily, titrated to 25 mg twice daily after 2 weeks if needed. The record names the extract EFLA 943 and no manufacturer; the enrolled number is not stated in the record.
cards.result: Both groups reduced systolic and diastolic pressure significantly from baseline, with no significant difference between groups: mean systolic reduction −11.5 ± 8.5 mmHg (olive) versus −13.7 ± 7.6 mmHg (captopril); diastolic −4.8 ± 5.5 versus −6.4 ± 5.2 mmHg. A significant reduction in triglycerides was observed in the olive group but not the captopril group.
cards.watchOut: Active-comparator equivalence without a placebo arm cannot distinguish 'both work' from 'neither works and pressures regressed to the mean after a 4-week run-in' — the classic assay-sensitivity problem; 8 weeks is also too short to judge a chronic therapy, and the record does not state how many patients were randomised.
cards.source: Susalit E et al. Olive (Olea europaea) leaf extract effective in patients with stage-1 hypertension: comparison with Captopril. Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology. 2011. PMID: 21036583. cards.headline: Perrinjaquet-Moccetti 2008: in 40 monozygotic twins, only the 1,000 mg/day dose lowered pressure (137/80 to 126/76) — open study, no placebo, no blinding
cards.summary: Perrinjaquet-Moccetti 2008: in 40 monozygotic twins, only the 1,000 mg/day dose lowered pressure (137/80 to 126/76) — open study, no placebo, no blinding
cards.type: Open controlled study in monozygotic twins (Perrinjaquet-Moccetti 2008)
cards.people: 40 borderline-hypertensive monozygotic twins; within each pair, twins were assigned to EFLA 943 at 500 or 1,000 mg/day for 8 weeks, or to advice on a favourable lifestyle, with blood pressure, weight, glucose and lipids measured fortnightly.
cards.result: Mean blood pressure remained unchanged from baseline in controls (133 ± 5/77 ± 6 versus 135 ± 11/80 ± 7 mmHg) and in the low-dose group (136 ± 7/77 ± 7 versus 133 ± 10/76 ± 7), but decreased significantly in the high-dose group (137 ± 10/80 ± 10 versus 126 ± 9/76 ± 6). Within-pair systolic differences were ≤6 mmHg (500 mg versus control) and ≤13 mmHg (1,000 versus 500 mg), with diastolic differences ≤5 mmHg; LDL cholesterol fell with significant dose-dependent within-pair differences.
cards.watchOut: Open and unblinded with a lifestyle-advice comparator — expectation and co-intervention effects are uncontrolled; the twin design is elegant for genetics but the study is a food-supplement pilot of 40 people, and the 500 mg dose (the dose later used against captopril) did not lower pressure here.
cards.source: Perrinjaquet-Moccetti T et al. Food supplementation with an olive (Olea europaea L.) leaf extract reduces blood pressure in borderline hypertensive monozygotic twins. Phytotherapy research : PTR. 2008. PMID: 18729245. cards.headline: Synthesis: an extract with a plausible dose–response that has never faced a placebo — MAYBE is the honest grade
cards.summary: Synthesis: an extract with a plausible dose–response that has never faced a placebo — MAYBE is the honest grade
cards.people: One double-blind active-comparator trial in stage-1 hypertension (EFLA 943 1,000 mg/day versus captopril, 8 weeks) and one open twin study (40 participants; 500 versus 1,000 mg/day versus lifestyle advice).
cards.result: Versus captopril: systolic −11.5 versus −13.7 mmHg, diastolic −4.8 versus −6.4, no significant difference. Versus lifestyle advice (open): only 1,000 mg/day lowered pressure. Versus placebo: never tested in any record carded here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: until a placebo-controlled trial exists, EFLA 943's blood-pressure effect is unproven however suggestive the captopril comparison looks — and no carded record names the extract's manufacturer, so other olive leaf products cannot borrow even this evidence.
cards.watchOut: Stage-1 hypertension is precisely where regression to the mean and white-coat effects are largest; both carded studies are short (8 weeks) and small, and neither reports clinical events.
cards.source: Synthesis of Susalit E et al. Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology. 2011 (PMID: 21036583); Perrinjaquet-Moccetti T et al. Phytotherapy research : PTR. 2008 (PMID: 18729245).

shelves.title: Skipping the antibiotic in uncomplicated UTI: uva-ursi did nothing for symptoms or antibiotic use — ibuprofen advice cut antibiotic use in one trial, but as a replacement treatment it cured fewer women and caused 7 cases of pyelonephritis
shelves.question: In women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, does uva-ursi extract combined with ibuprofen reduce antibiotic use without worsening symptoms versus usual antibiotic-first care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease/therapy · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Arctostaphylos/chemistry · Complementary Therapies/methods · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Ibuprofen/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Primary Health Care · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Urinary Tract Infections/drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the herb failed; the painkiller strategy trades antibiotics for a small, real risk. In the ATAFUTI factorial trial (Moore et al., PMID: 30685500; 382 women with suspected uncomplicated UTI, all given a back-up antibiotic prescription), uva-ursi extract did not improve frequency symptoms versus placebo (−0.06, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.21, p = 0.661) and did not significantly reduce antibiotic consumption (39.9% versus 47.4%; OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.58, p = 0.293); ibuprofen advice likewise did not improve symptoms (−0.01, p = 0.951) but did reduce antibiotic use (34.9% versus 51.0%; OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.72, p = 0.009 — one less antibiotic user for every seven women advised), with no upper-tract infections recorded. The companion evidence is colder: when ibuprofen was tested as a replacement for an antibiotic (Vik et al., PMID: 29763434; 383 women), only 38.7% felt cured by day 4 versus 73.6% on pivmecillinam, and 7 cases of pyelonephritis occurred, all on ibuprofen (number needed to harm 26), though 53% of the ibuprofen group recovered without antibiotics. PROPOSED SPLIT: uva-ursi — no effect; ibuprofen with a safety-net prescription — fewer antibiotics, slower relief, and a pyelonephritis risk that the back-up prescription exists to catch.

cards.headline: Moore 2019 (ATAFUTI): uva-ursi no better than placebo on symptoms (−0.06, p = 0.661) or antibiotic use (39.9% versus 47.4%, NS) — ibuprofen advice cut antibiotic use (OR 0.27)
cards.summary: Moore 2019 (ATAFUTI): uva-ursi no better than placebo on symptoms (−0.06, p = 0.661) or antibiotic use (39.9% versus 47.4%, NS) — ibuprofen advice cut antibiotic use (OR 0.27)
cards.people: 382 women aged 18–70 in UK primary care with dysuria, urgency or frequency and suspected lower UTI, in a 2 × 2 factorial placebo-controlled trial of uva-ursi extract and/or ibuprofen advice; every participant also received a delayed ('back-up') antibiotic prescription. The record does not name the extract's manufacturer.
cards.result: Mean frequency-symptom score on days 2–4: no evidence of difference for uva-ursi versus placebo (−0.06, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.21, p = 0.661) or ibuprofen advice versus none (−0.01, 95% CI −0.27 to 0.26, p = 0.951). Antibiotic consumption: no significant reduction with uva-ursi (39.9% versus 47.4%; OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.58, p = 0.293), but a significant reduction with ibuprofen advice (34.9% versus 51.0%; OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.72, p = 0.009) — for every seven women given this advice, one less used antibiotics. There were no safety concerns and no episodes of upper tract infection were recorded.
cards.watchOut: Everyone had a back-up prescription in hand, so 'antibiotic use' here means use despite safety-netting — a different question from withholding antibiotics outright; the uva-ursi confidence interval for antibiotic use (0.22 to 1.58) is wide, but the symptom result is a clean null at the point estimate, and the trial was not powered to detect rare pyelonephritis.
cards.source: Moore M et al. Uva-ursi extract and ibuprofen as alternative treatments for uncomplicated urinary tract infection in women (ATAFUTI): a factorial randomized trial. Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases. 2019. PMID: 30685500. Registry ID: ISRCTN43397016. cards.headline: Vik 2018: ibuprofen as antibiotic replacement — cured by day 4 in 38.7% versus 73.6% on pivmecillinam, with 7 pyelonephritis cases, all on ibuprofen (NNH 26)
cards.summary: Vik 2018: ibuprofen as antibiotic replacement — cured by day 4 in 38.7% versus 73.6% on pivmecillinam, with 7 pyelonephritis cases, all on ibuprofen (NNH 26)
cards.people: 383 non-pregnant women aged 18–60 with uncomplicated UTI in Scandinavian general practice, randomised double-blind to ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily (n = 194; 181 analysed) or pivmecillinam 200 mg three times daily (n = 189; 178 analysed) for 3 days, with a 10% non-inferiority margin for feeling cured by day 4.
cards.result: By day 4, 38.7% of the ibuprofen group felt cured versus 73.6% on pivmecillinam — an adjusted risk difference of 35% (90% CI 27% to 43%) in favour of the antibiotic, crossing the non-inferiority margin. After 4 weeks, 53% of the ibuprofen group had recovered without antibiotic treatment. Seven cases of pyelonephritis occurred, all in the ibuprofen group (number needed to harm 26, 95% CI 13 to 103); five were hospitalised as serious adverse events. The authors conclude ibuprofen alone cannot be recommended as initial treatment until patients at risk of complications can be identified.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers a harder question than ATAFUTI — ibuprofen instead of an antibiotic, with no back-up prescription strategy — and its extensive exclusion criteria removed almost half of screened patients, so its pyelonephritis rate may not transfer to lower-risk women; it is carded here because it is the safety evidence any antibiotic-sparing advice must reckon with.
cards.source: Vik I et al. Ibuprofen versus pivmecillinam for uncomplicated urinary tract infection in women-A double-blind, randomized non-inferiority trial. PLoS medicine. 2018. PMID: 29763434. randomised non-inferiority trial (vik 2018) 383 non-pregnant women aged 18–60 with uncomplicated uti in scandinavian general practice, randomised double-blind to ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily (n = 194; 181 analysed) or pivmecillinam 200 mg three times daily (n = 189; 178 analysed) for 3 days, with a 10% non-inferiority margin for feeling cured by day 4. by day 4, 38.7% of the ibuprofen group felt cured versus 73.6% on pivmecillinam — an adjusted risk difference of 35% (90% ci 27% to 43%) in favour of the antibiotic, crossing the non-inferiority margin. after 4 weeks, 53% of the ibuprofen group had recovered without antibiotic treatment. seven cases of pyelonephritis occurred, all in the ibuprofen group (number needed to harm 26, 95% ci 13 to 103); five were hospitalised as serious adverse events. the authors conclude ibuprofen alone cannot be recommended as initial treatment until patients at risk of complications can be identified. this trial answers a harder question than atafuti — ibuprofen instead of an antibiotic, with no back-up prescription strategy — and its extensive exclusion criteria removed almost half of screened patients, so its pyelonephritis rate may not transfer to lower-risk women; it is carded here because it is the safety evidence any antibiotic-sparing advice must reckon with. vik i et al. ibuprofen versus pivmecillinam for uncomplicated urinary tract infection in women-a double-blind, randomized non-inferiority trial. plos medicine. 2018. pmid: 29763434. registry id: nct01849926. mesh: adult · amdinocillin pivoxil/therapeutic use · anti-infective agents, urinary/therapeutic use · anti-inflammatory agents, non-steroidal/therapeutic use · double-blind method · female · humans · ibuprofen/therapeutic use · urinary tract infections/drug therapy

cards.headline: Synthesis: the herbal half of the strategy is dead; the ibuprofen half is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch
cards.summary: Synthesis: the herbal half of the strategy is dead; the ibuprofen half is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch
cards.people: Two randomised trials in women with uncomplicated UTI (382 in a factorial symptom-relief/antibiotic-sparing trial with universal back-up prescriptions; 383 in a head-to-head ibuprofen-versus-antibiotic trial).
cards.result: Uva-ursi: no symptom benefit, no significant antibiotic saving — the treatment made no difference. Ibuprofen advice with safety-netting: antibiotic use 34.9% versus 51.0% (OR 0.27), no upper-tract infections in 382 women. Ibuprofen as outright replacement: cure by day 4, 38.7% versus 73.6%; pyelonephritis 7 cases versus 0 (NNH 26); 53% recovered without any antibiotic. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the harm claim (pyelonephritis) and the single-trial herb null both warrant the developer's personal review.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial supports uva-ursi in any role. The ibuprofen findings are not contradictory once the designs are separated: advice-plus-back-up-prescription in ATAFUTI is a safety-netted strategy; Vik's unsupervised substitution is where the harm appeared.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moore M et al. Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases. 2019 (PMID: 30685500); Vik I et al. PLoS medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29763434).

shelves.title: Curcumin to keep ulcerative colitis quiet: relapse 4.65% versus 20.51% over 6 months in one 89-patient trial — never replicated, and the benefit faded after stopping
shelves.question: In adults with ulcerative colitis in remission, does curcumin maintenance therapy reduce relapse versus placebo on top of standard aminosalicylates?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Colitis, Ulcerative/drug therapy/pathology · Colonoscopy · Curcumin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Mesalamine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Sulfasalazine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single small trial, unreplicated in this role. Hanai and colleagues (PMID: 17101300) randomised 89 patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis to curcumin 1 g twice daily or placebo, each on top of sulfasalazine or mesalamine, for 6 months: among completers, 2 of 43 patients (4.65%) relapsed on curcumin versus 8 of 39 (20.51%) on placebo (P = .040), with the intention-to-treat comparison also significant (P = .049), and curcumin improved both the clinical activity index (P = .038) and the endoscopic index (P = .0001). In the 6 months after treatment stopped — both groups on aminosalicylates alone — 8 more curcumin-group patients and 6 more placebo-group patients relapsed, eroding the separation. The record names no curcumin product or manufacturer, so no branded preparation can claim this result. (Curcumin for inducing remission in active colitis is a different question, answered on its own shelf from a different trial; it is not carded here.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a promising maintenance signal that one 89-patient trial cannot carry further than POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Hanai 2006: relapse during 6 months of therapy in 2/43 (4.65%) on curcumin versus 8/39 (20.51%) on placebo (P = .040) — then 8 versus 6 more relapses after stopping
cards.summary: Hanai 2006: relapse during 6 months of therapy in 2/43 (4.65%) on curcumin versus 8/39 (20.51%) on placebo (P = .040) — then 8 versus 6 more relapses after stopping
cards.people: 89 patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis in a multicentre double-blind trial: 45 received curcumin 1 g after breakfast and 1 g after the evening meal plus sulfasalazine or mesalamine, and 44 received placebo plus sulfasalazine or mesalamine, for 6 months, followed by 6 months of follow-up on aminosalicylates alone. Seven patients were protocol violators; 43 and 39 patients form the completer denominators. The record names no curcumin product or manufacturer.
cards.result: Relapse during the 6 treatment months: 2 of 43 (4.65%) on curcumin versus 8 of 39 (20.51%) on placebo (P = .040); recurrence rates on intention-to-treat also differed significantly (P = .049). Curcumin improved the clinical activity index (P = .038) and the endoscopic index (P = .0001). During the 6-month post-treatment follow-up, 8 additional patients in the curcumin group and 6 in the placebo group relapsed. The authors describe curcumin as a promising and safe medication for maintaining remission in quiescent ulcerative colitis.
cards.watchOut: Eighty-nine patients and ten on-treatment relapses in total: moving two relapses between arms would erase significance, the completer analysis (4.65% versus 20.51%) flatters the result relative to intention-to-treat, and the post-treatment relapse pattern suggests suppression while taking it rather than any durable change in the disease.
cards.source: Hanai H et al. Curcumin maintenance therapy for ulcerative colitis: randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2006. PMID: 17101300.
