cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, ten events, a fourfold relative difference — POSSIBLE (benefit) with Tier C is as far as this goes
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, ten events, a fourfold relative difference — POSSIBLE (benefit) with Tier C is as far as this goes
cards.people: One randomised double-blind multicentre maintenance trial (89 patients with quiescent ulcerative colitis on background aminosalicylates, 6 months of treatment plus 6 months of follow-up).
cards.result: Relapse on treatment: 4.65% versus 20.51% (completers), significant also by intention-to-treat. Clinical and endoscopic indices both improved. After stopping: relapses accumulated in both groups (8 versus 6 further relapses), narrowing the gap. Safety: described as safe in the record, with no comparative adverse-event table in the abstract. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial benefit claim is exactly what the developer reviews personally, and no second maintenance trial was found to card alongside it.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is maintenance of remission only. Evidence for curcumin inducing remission in active ulcerative colitis rests on different trials and lives on its own shelf; pooling the two roles would overstate both.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hanai H et al. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2006 (PMID: 17101300).

shelves.title: Liquorice raises blood pressure and lowers potassium, dose-dependently: pooled systolic +5.45 mmHg, diastolic +3.19 mmHg, potassium −0.33 mmol/L at ≥100 mg glycyrrhizic acid a day
shelves.question: Does regular liquorice (glycyrrhizin) consumption raise blood pressure and lower potassium in a dose-dependent way?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aldosterone/blood · Biomarkers/blood · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Female · Glycyrrhiza/adverse effects/chemistry · Glycyrrhizic Acid/adverse effects/isolation & purification · Humans · Hypertension/chemically induced/diagnosis/physiopathology · Hypokalemia/blood/chemically induced/diagnosis · Male · Middle Aged · Plant Extracts/adverse effects/isolation & purification · Potassium/blood · Renin/blood · Renin-Angiotensin System/drug effects · Risk Factors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a consistent, dose-related physiological effect in feeding studies, sitting on top of a case-report literature of severe events. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Penninkilampi et al., PMID: 28660884) pooled 18 studies (337 participants) of products providing at least 100 mg of glycyrrhizic acid daily: chronic ingestion raised mean systolic blood pressure by 5.45 mmHg (95% CI 3.51 to 7.39) and diastolic by 3.19 mmHg (95% CI 0.10 to 6.29), and lowered plasma potassium by 0.33 mmol/L, plasma renin activity by 0.82 ng/mL per hour, and plasma aldosterone by 173.24 pmol/L — the hormonal signature of apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Daily glycyrrhizic acid dose correlated with the systolic (r² = 0.55) and diastolic (r² = 0.65) rises, supporting the dose-dependence this question asks about. The authors note the effect appears even at modest doses and matters most for people with existing cardiovascular disease; the review's background records case reports of severe adverse events including deaths after chronic liquorice ingestion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): regular liquorice at these doses measurably raises pressure and lowers potassium — a food with a drug-like effect, not a benign sweet.

cards.headline: Penninkilampi 2017: systolic +5.45 mmHg, diastolic +3.19 mmHg, potassium −0.33 mmol/L — and dose explained over half the variance in the pressure rise
cards.summary: Penninkilampi 2017: systolic +5.45 mmHg, diastolic +3.19 mmHg, potassium −0.33 mmol/L — and dose explained over half the variance in the pressure rise
cards.people: 18 studies totalling 337 participants ingesting a product containing at least 100 mg of glycyrrhizic acid daily, pooled for mean change from baseline in blood pressure, plasma potassium, renin activity and aldosterone (random-effects model); the review's background also surveys case reports of severe adverse events, including deaths, following chronic liquorice ingestion.
cards.result: Chronic glycyrrhizic acid ingestion significantly increased mean systolic blood pressure (5.45 mmHg, 95% CI 3.51 to 7.39) and diastolic blood pressure (3.19 mmHg, 95% CI 0.10 to 6.29). Plasma potassium fell (−0.33 mmol/L), as did plasma renin activity (−0.82 ng/mL per hour, 95% CI −1.27 to −0.37) and plasma aldosterone (−173.24 pmol/L, 95% CI −231.65 to −114.83). A significant correlation was found between daily glycyrrhizic acid dose and systolic (r² = 0.55) and diastolic (r² = 0.65) blood pressure, but not for the other outcomes. The authors conclude chronic liquorice ingestion is associated with raised blood pressure and lower potassium even at modest doses, of particular relevance in existing cardiovascular disease.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are small, short feeding experiments (337 people across 18 studies) in mostly healthy volunteers, analysed as change-from-baseline rather than against parallel placebo arms in most cases; individual susceptibility varies widely, and the severe outcomes (arrhythmia, paralysis, death) come from the case-report literature the review cites, not from these pooled data.
cards.source: Penninkilampi R et al. The association between consistent licorice ingestion, hypertension and hypokalaemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of human hypertension. 2017. PMID: 28660884. cards.headline: Synthesis: mechanism, dose–response and effect all point the same way — POSSIBLE (harm) for regular liquorice at real-world doses
cards.summary: Synthesis: mechanism, dose–response and effect all point the same way — POSSIBLE (harm) for regular liquorice at real-world doses
cards.people: One systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 glycyrrhizic-acid feeding studies (337 participants) at doses of at least 100 mg/day, read alongside the case-report literature its authors cite.
cards.result: Systolic +5.45 mmHg (3.51 to 7.39), diastolic +3.19 mmHg (0.10 to 6.29), potassium −0.33 mmol/L, with renin and aldosterone suppressed and a dose–response correlation (r² 0.55–0.65) for pressure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: harm claims come to the developer personally, and the pooled base is small short-term studies rather than large randomised trials — but the direction is unanimous and mechanistically coherent (glycyrrhizin blocks 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, letting cortisol activate the mineralocorticoid receptor).
cards.watchOut: Most liquorice-flavoured confectionery outside northern-European salted liquorice contains little or no glycyrrhizin; this shelf is about products that actually contain it — liquorice root, extracts, teas and traditional medicines — at sustained daily doses.
cards.source: Synthesis of Penninkilampi R et al. Journal of human hypertension. 2017 (PMID: 28660884).

shelves.title: Black seed oil in asthma: control scores improved modestly in one 4-week trial (ACT 21.1 versus 19.6) and eosinophils fell — lung function did not significantly change
shelves.question: In adults with asthma, does Nigella sativa (black seed) supplementation improve asthma control and lung function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage · Asthma/blood/drug therapy/physiopathology · Biomarkers/analysis/blood · Combined Modality Therapy · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Lung/drug effects/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Nigella sativa/chemistry · Phytotherapy/methods · Placebos · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage · Respiratory Function Tests · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptom control scores, from one small short trial. Koshak and colleagues (PMID: 28093815) randomised 80 asthmatic patients to Nigella sativa oil capsules 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 4 weeks as supplementary treatment (60 patients completed; ten withdrew from each group): the Asthma Control Test score was significantly higher on the oil (21.1 ± 2.6 versus 19.6 ± 3.7, p = 0.044), blood eosinophils fell significantly (median change −50 versus +15 cells/µL, p = 0.013), and FEV₁ as percent predicted improved by a median of 4 versus 1 points without reaching significance (p = 0.170). Total serum IgE is listed among the secondary outcomes but no comparative result for it appears in the record. The record names no brand or manufacturer for the oil capsules. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a borderline-significant 1.5-point control-score gain over 4 weeks in 60 completers is a signal worth a larger trial — it is not yet a treatment.

cards.headline: Koshak 2017: Asthma Control Test 21.1 versus 19.6 (p = 0.044) and eosinophils down — FEV₁ difference not significant (p = 0.170), a quarter of patients withdrew
cards.summary: Koshak 2017: Asthma Control Test 21.1 versus 19.6 (p = 0.044) and eosinophils down — FEV₁ difference not significant (p = 0.170), a quarter of patients withdrew
cards.people: 80 asthmatic patients randomised to Nigella sativa oil capsules 500 mg twice daily (n = 40) or placebo (n = 40) for 4 weeks as supplementary treatment alongside conventional therapy; after 4 weeks, ten patients had withdrawn from each group, leaving 60 in the reported comparisons. The record names no brand or manufacturer for the oil.
cards.result: Mean Asthma Control Test score improved significantly more on Nigella sativa oil: 21.1 (SD 2.6) versus 19.6 (SD 3.7) (p = 0.044). Blood eosinophils fell by a median of −50 cells/µL (IQR −155 to −1) versus a rise of 15 (−60 to 87) on placebo (p = 0.013). FEV₁ as percent of predicted improved by a median of 4 (−1.25 to 8.75) versus 1 (−2 to 5), which was not significant (p = 0.170). The authors conclude the oil improves asthma control with a trend in pulmonary function, alongside normalisation of blood eosinophilia, and call for longer multicentre studies.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks, 60 completers from 80 randomised (25% attrition, equal across arms), a primary-outcome p-value of 0.044, and a 1.5-point ACT difference at the edge of what patients can feel; the trial is single-centre and the preparation is an unnamed oil, so other black seed products cannot borrow this result. Safety of Nigella sativa is covered on its own shelf and is not re-litigated here.

cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial, one borderline p-value, biomarkers agree with symptoms — POSSIBLE, and no more
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of Nigella sativa oil 500 mg twice daily for 4 weeks in asthma (80 randomised, 60 completing).
cards.result: Asthma Control Test: 21.1 versus 19.6 (p = 0.044). Eosinophils: median −50 versus +15 cells/µL (p = 0.013). FEV₁ % predicted: median +4 versus +1 (p = 0.170, not significant). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single small short trial is the whole evidence base for this question, and its lung-function endpoint — half of what the question asks — was null.
cards.watchOut: Asthma control scores are patient-reported and this trial's margin is thin; nothing here supports replacing or reducing inhaled controller therapy, which all participants continued.
cards.source: Synthesis of Koshak A et al. Phytotherapy research : PTR. 2017 (PMID: 28093815).

shelves.title: Ginkgo (EGb 761) as dementia treatment: pooled cognition favoured ginkgo (SMD −0.58) across 9 trials — daily functioning did not reach significance overall, and the trials are heterogeneous
shelves.question: In adults with dementia, does the standardised ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 improve cognition and daily functioning versus placebo as a treatment (as distinct from prevention)?
shelves.mesh: Alzheimer Disease/drug therapy/epidemiology/psychology · Controlled Clinical Trials as Topic/methods · Dementia/drug therapy/epidemiology/psychology · Ginkgo biloba · Humans · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · United States/epidemiology · Ginkgo Extract
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, heterogeneous, and confined to the standardised extract. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Weinmann et al., PMID: 20236541) pooled nine trials of the standardised extract EGb 761 in Alzheimer's, vascular or mixed dementia (2,372 patients, 12–52 weeks): change scores for cognition favoured ginkgo (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −1.14 to −0.01, p = 0.04), while activities of daily living did not differ significantly overall (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.66 to 0.03, p = 0.08); in the Alzheimer subgroup both cognition and daily-living effects were larger and the ADL effect was significant (SMD −0.44, 95% CI −0.77 to −0.12, p = 0.008), with high heterogeneity throughout and no difference in drop-outs or side effects. The largest single trial carded here (Ihl et al., PMID: 22086747; 404 outpatients, 240 mg once daily for 24 weeks) found EGb 761 superior on the SKT cognitive battery (drug–placebo difference 1.7 points in Alzheimer's disease, p < 0.001; 1.4 in vascular dementia, p < 0.05) and on neuropsychiatric symptoms. Neither record names the extract's manufacturer. This shelf is treatment of established dementia only: ginkgo to prevent dementia is a separate question with two large null trials, answered on its own shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effect sizes are moderate on paper and, as the reviewers note, of difficult-to-determine clinical relevance.

cards.headline: Weinmann 2010 (meta-analysis): cognition SMD −0.58 (p = 0.04) favours EGb 761 — ADL SMD −0.32 not significant overall, significant in Alzheimer's disease (−0.44, p = 0.008)
cards.summary: Weinmann 2010 (meta-analysis): cognition SMD −0.58 (p = 0.04) favours EGb 761 — ADL SMD −0.32 not significant overall, significant in Alzheimer's disease (−0.44, p = 0.008)
cards.people: Nine controlled trials of the standardised extract EGb 761 in Alzheimer's disease, vascular or mixed dementia, totalling 2,372 patients, with treatment durations of 12 to 52 weeks and at least ten participants per group. Neither this record nor the trial below names the extract's manufacturer.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of change scores: cognition favoured ginkgo over placebo (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −1.14 to −0.01, p = 0.04). Activities of daily living did not differ significantly overall (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.66 to 0.03, p = 0.08). In the Alzheimer subgroup, standardised mean differences for both ADL and cognition were larger, with statistical superiority for ginkgo also on ADL (SMD −0.44, 95% CI −0.77 to −0.12, p = 0.008). Heterogeneity among studies was high. Drop-out rates and side effects did not differ between ginkgo and placebo; no consistent results were available for quality of life or neuropsychiatric symptoms.
cards.watchOut: High heterogeneity means the pooled −0.58 averages trials that disagree with each other; the overall cognition confidence interval nearly touches zero (−0.01), the ADL headline depends on a subgroup, and the authors themselves state that clinical relevance is, as with other dementia drugs, difficult to determine.
cards.source: Weinmann S et al. Effects of Ginkgo biloba in dementia: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC geriatrics. 2010. PMID: 20236541. cards.headline: Ihl 2012: EGb 761 240 mg once daily beat placebo on cognition (SKT difference 1.7 in Alzheimer's, 1.4 in vascular dementia) and neuropsychiatric symptoms over 24 weeks
cards.summary: Ihl 2012: EGb 761 240 mg once daily beat placebo on cognition (SKT difference 1.7 in Alzheimer's, 1.4 in vascular dementia) and neuropsychiatric symptoms over 24 weeks
cards.people: 404 outpatients aged 50 or over with mild to moderate dementia (SKT score 9–23) with neuropsychiatric features (NPI total ≥5) — 333 with Alzheimer's disease and 71 with vascular dementia — randomised to a once-daily 240 mg formulation of Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 or placebo for 24 weeks.
cards.result: EGb 761 was superior to placebo on the SKT total score (drug–placebo differences: 1.7 for Alzheimer's disease, p < 0.001; 1.4 for vascular dementia, p < 0.05) and on the NPI total score (differences: 3.1 for Alzheimer's, p < 0.001; 3.2 for vascular dementia, p < 0.05). Significant drug–placebo differences were found for most secondary outcomes, with no major differences between diagnostic subgroups; adverse-event rates were essentially similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A single 24-week trial using the manufacturer's standardised extract, with several of this literature's trials industry-associated — the record does not state funding, so the point is flagged as a general caution for the EGb 761 trial base rather than a documented fact about this study; SKT point differences of 1.4–1.7 are statistically firm but clinically modest.
cards.source: Ihl R et al. Efficacy and tolerability of a once daily formulation of Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761® in Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia: results from a randomised controlled trial. Pharmacopsychiatry. 2012. PMID: 22086747. cards.headline: Synthesis: treatment evidence is genuinely positive but soft — and it does not rescue ginkgo for prevention, which failed separately
cards.summary: Synthesis: treatment evidence is genuinely positive but soft — and it does not rescue ginkgo for prevention, which failed separately
cards.people: A 9-trial meta-analysis of EGb 761 in established dementia (2,372 patients) plus a 404-patient 24-week randomised trial of the same extract at 240 mg/day.
cards.result: Cognition: pooled SMD −0.58 (p = 0.04); single-trial SKT advantage 1.4–1.7 points (p < 0.05 to < 0.001). Daily functioning: null overall (p = 0.08), positive in the Alzheimer subgroup (SMD −0.44, p = 0.008). Harms: no excess drop-outs or adverse events in either source. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant sources carry the stamp; the heterogeneity and near-zero confidence bound keep it below LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Every positive number here concerns the standardised extract EGb 761 at studied doses. Generic ginkgo supplements are not interchangeable with it, and the prevention question — where two large long trials found no protection — must not borrow this shelf's stamp.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weinmann S et al. BMC geriatrics. 2010 (PMID: 20236541); Ihl R et al. Pharmacopsychiatry. 2012 (PMID: 22086747).

shelves.title: American ginseng blunts warfarin: peak INR fell significantly after 2 weeks of ginseng in a placebo-controlled trial — in 20 healthy volunteers, not patients
shelves.question: In patients taking warfarin, does American ginseng reduce warfarin's anticoagulant effect (INR) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anticoagulants/pharmacokinetics/pharmacology · Area Under Curve · Drug Interactions · Female · Humans · International Normalized Ratio · Male · Panax/adverse effects · Phytotherapy/adverse effects · Plant Preparations/adverse effects · Warfarin/pharmacokinetics/pharmacology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a pharmacokinetic interaction demonstrated under controlled conditions, in the wrong population to size the clinical risk. Yuan and colleagues (PMID: 15238367) randomised 20 healthy volunteers who received warfarin for 3 days in weeks 1 and 4, with American ginseng or placebo given from week 2: after 2 weeks of ginseng, peak INR fell significantly compared with placebo (between-group difference −0.19, 95% CI −0.36 to −0.07, P = 0.0012), and INR area under the curve, peak plasma warfarin level, and warfarin AUC were all significantly reduced, with peak INR correlating positively with peak warfarin level — a coherent exposure-and-effect reduction. The record names no ginseng product or manufacturer. The authors themselves flag the limitation that decides how far this travels: the volunteers were young and healthy and received brief low-intensity warfarin, not therapeutic anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation or a mechanical valve. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): the interaction is real in the laboratory sense; its size in a patient whose INR must stay between 2 and 3 is unmeasured — which is precisely why the safe advice is to ask about ginseng, as the authors conclude, rather than to assume the effect is trivial.

cards.headline: Yuan 2004: peak INR difference −0.19 (95% CI −0.36 to −0.07, P = 0.0012) after 2 weeks of American ginseng — warfarin levels fell in parallel
cards.summary: Yuan 2004: peak INR difference −0.19 (95% CI −0.36 to −0.07, P = 0.0012) after 2 weeks of American ginseng — warfarin levels fell in parallel
cards.people: 20 healthy volunteers at a US General Clinical Research Center, in a 4-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial: all received warfarin for 3 days during weeks 1 and 4, and from week 2 were assigned to American ginseng or placebo. The record names no ginseng product or manufacturer.
cards.result: Peak INR decreased statistically significantly after 2 weeks of ginseng administration compared with placebo (difference between ginseng and placebo −0.19, 95% CI −0.36 to −0.07, P = 0.0012). INR area under the curve, peak plasma warfarin level, and warfarin AUC were also statistically significantly reduced in the ginseng group, and peak INR and peak plasma warfarin level were positively correlated. The authors conclude that American ginseng reduces warfarin's anticoagulant effect and that physicians prescribing warfarin should ask patients about ginseng use.
cards.watchOut: Twenty young, healthy volunteers given 3-day warfarin courses — not patients on therapeutic anticoagulation. A −0.19 INR shift in a volunteer starting near 1.0 cannot be mapped directly onto a patient targeted to 2.0–3.0, in whom the same proportional exposure loss could mean subtherapeutic anticoagulation and clot risk; the trial proves the interaction exists, not how big it is where it matters.
cards.source: Yuan CS et al. Brief communication: American ginseng reduces warfarin's effect in healthy patients: a randomized, controlled Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2004. PMID: 15238367. cards.headline: Synthesis: interaction proven, clinical magnitude unknown — POSSIBLE (harm) with the volunteer caveat on the face of the shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: interaction proven, clinical magnitude unknown — POSSIBLE (harm) with the volunteer caveat on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled interaction trial (20 healthy volunteers, 4 weeks) of American ginseng against warfarin pharmacokinetics and INR.
cards.result: Peak INR: −0.19 versus placebo (P = 0.0012). Warfarin exposure (peak level and AUC) and INR AUC: all significantly reduced. Clinical events (thrombosis, bleeding): not studied — no patient in this record was anticoagulated for a clinical indication. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: a single small trial and a harm claim both route this shelf to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: This is American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) specifically, in an unnamed preparation. It should not be generalised to Asian ginseng products — nor assumed away for them; each ginseng product is its own interaction question, and none has been shown safe with warfarin.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yuan CS et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15238367).

shelves.title: St John's wort switches on drug-clearing enzymes: it cut indinavir exposure by 57% in volunteers, and the interaction literature runs from transplant rejection to contraceptive failure
shelves.question: Can St John's wort preparations cause clinically serious interactions — transplant rejection, contraceptive failure, loss of drug effect — by inducing drug-metabolising enzymes?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Trials as Topic · Cytochrome P-450 Enzyme System/drug effects/metabolism · Herb-Drug Interactions/physiology · Humans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the enzyme induction is trial-proven; the catastrophic outcomes rest on case reports, and both halves belong on the shelf. The updated systematic review (Izzo & Ernst, PMID: 19719333) assembled 128 case reports or case series and 80 clinical trials across seven herbs: clinical trials show St John's wort, via cytochrome P450 and/or P-glycoprotein induction, reduces plasma concentrations (or increases clearance) of a long list including ciclosporin, tacrolimus, oral contraceptives, indinavir, irinotecan, imatinib, digoxin, warfarin, simvastatin, atorvastatin, omeprazole and methadone, while case reports link it to transplant-relevant ciclosporin and tacrolimus failures, contraceptive failure, and serotonin-toxicity combinations. The cleanest single demonstration (Piscitelli et al., PMID: 10683007): in healthy volunteers, St John's wort reduced the area under the curve of the HIV protease inhibitor indinavir by a mean of 57% (SD 19) and the extrapolated 8-hour trough by 81% (SD 16) — a loss of exposure the authors warn could produce drug resistance and treatment failure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): no other common herbal product has this breadth of documented, mechanism-backed interaction — treat it as an interacting drug, not a benign supplement.

cards.headline: Izzo & Ernst 2009: 80 clinical trials show St John's wort lowers levels of ciclosporin, tacrolimus, contraceptives, indinavir, warfarin and dozens more — 128 case reports supply the clinical disasters
cards.summary: Izzo & Ernst 2009: 80 clinical trials show St John's wort lowers levels of ciclosporin, tacrolimus, contraceptives, indinavir, warfarin and dozens more — 128 case reports supply the clinical disasters
cards.people: A literature review of interactions between seven popular herbal medicines (ginkgo, St John's wort, ginseng, garlic, echinacea, saw palmetto, kava) and conventional drugs, identifying 128 case reports or case series and 80 clinical trials; the St John's wort findings are the shelf's subject.
cards.result: Clinical trials indicate St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), via cytochrome P450 (CYP) and/or P-glycoprotein induction, reduces the plasma concentrations (and/or increases the clearance) of alprazolam, amitriptyline, atorvastatin, chlorzoxazone, ciclosporin, debrisoquine, digoxin, erythromycin, fexofenadine, gliclazide, imatinib, indinavir, irinotecan, ivabradine, mephenytoin, methadone, midazolam, nifedipine, omeprazole, oral contraceptives, quazepam, simvastatin, tacrolimus, talinolol, verapamil, voriconazole and warfarin. Case reports or case series additionally suggest interactions with ciclosporin, tacrolimus, oral contraceptives, sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine, nefazodone, buspirone, bupropion, anaesthetics, adrenergic vasopressors and others. The authors conclude that while the significance of many interactions is uncertain, several — particularly those with St John's wort — may have serious clinical consequences.
cards.watchOut: The review gives the direction of interactions without pooled magnitudes — effect sizes live in the individual trials (one is carded below) — and the gravest outcomes (rejection episodes, unintended pregnancy) come from case reports, which establish possibility and mechanism, not incidence. St John's wort's efficacy for depression is a separate question on its own shelf.
cards.source: Izzo AA et al. Interactions between herbal medicines and prescribed drugs: an updated systematic review. Drugs. 2009. PMID: 19719333. MeSH: Clinical Trials as Topic · Cytochrome P-450 Enzyme System/drug effects/metabolism · Herb-Drug Interactions/physiology · Humans

cards.headline: Piscitelli 2000: St John's wort cut indinavir AUC by a mean of 57% and the 8-hour trough by 81% in healthy volunteers
cards.summary: Piscitelli 2000: St John's wort cut indinavir AUC by a mean of 57% and the 8-hour trough by 81% in healthy volunteers
cards.people: Healthy volunteers given the HIV-1 protease inhibitor indinavir with and without St John's wort, with indinavir exposure measured by high-performance liquid chromatography; the record is a brief Lancet report and does not state the volunteer number in its abstract.
cards.result: St John's wort reduced the area under the curve of indinavir by a mean of 57% (SD 19) and decreased the extrapolated 8-hour indinavir trough concentration by 81% (SD 16). The authors warn that a reduction in indinavir exposure of this magnitude could lead to the development of drug resistance and treatment failure.
cards.watchOut: A small volunteer pharmacokinetic study from the era when indinavir was standard HIV therapy — the drug is now little used, but the measurement stands as the quantified proof-of-mechanism for the whole interaction class: trough levels, the number that protects against resistance and rejection alike, fell furthest.
cards.source: Piscitelli SC et al. Indinavir concentrations and St John's wort. Lancet (London, England). 2000. PMID: 10683007. cards.summary: Synthesis: the best-documented interaction profile of any herbal product — POSSIBLE (harm), and practically a prescribing rule
cards.people: A systematic review of herb–drug interactions (128 case reports/series, 80 clinical trials) plus a controlled pharmacokinetic study of St John's wort with indinavir in healthy volunteers.
cards.result: Mechanism: CYP and P-glycoprotein induction, shown across dozens of substrates in clinical trials. Magnitude, exemplar: indinavir AUC −57%, trough −81%. Clinical consequences documented at case-report level: ciclosporin/tacrolimus failure (transplant rejection risk), oral contraceptive failure, loss of effect of antiretrovirals, irinotecan, imatinib, warfarin and others. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: harm claims route to the developer personally, and the catastrophic outcomes are case-report-grade even though the pharmacology is trial-grade.
cards.watchOut: Induction varies by product and hyperforin content, and it persists after stopping while enzymes recover — 'I stopped it last week' does not end the interaction. Anyone taking a narrow-therapeutic-index drug should treat St John's wort as contraindicated unless their prescriber says otherwise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Izzo AA et al. Drugs. 2009 (PMID: 19719333); Piscitelli SC et al. Lancet (London, England). 2000 (PMID: 10683007).

shelves.title: Passionflower for anxiety: it matched oxazepam over 4 weeks in one 36-patient trial with less job impairment — and cut pre-operative anxiety versus placebo in another; no placebo trial in generalised anxiety exists
shelves.question: In adults with generalised anxiety disorder, does passionflower (Passiflora incarnata) extract reduce anxiety versus placebo — and how did it compare with oxazepam in the head-to-head trial?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Anxiety Agents/therapeutic use · Anxiety Disorders/drug therapy · Ataxia/chemically induced · Dizziness/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypersensitivity/etiology · Male · Oxazepam/therapeutic use · Passiflora · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Task Performance and Analysis
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — two small trials, neither of which is the trial the question really needs. The head-to-head study (Akhondzadeh et al., PMID: 11679026) randomised 36 outpatients with generalised anxiety disorder to Passiflora incarnata extract 45 drops/day or oxazepam 30 mg/day for 4 weeks: both treatments were effective, no significant difference was observed between the protocols at trial end, oxazepam acted faster, and significantly more problems with impairment of job performance occurred on oxazepam. There was no placebo arm, so the trial cannot exclude that both arms simply rode the natural course and expectation effects. The only placebo-controlled anxiety trial carded (Movafegh et al., PMID: 18499602) is a different setting — a single 500 mg oral dose of Passiflora incarnata (the record names the product Passipy, from IranDarouk) before ambulatory surgery in 60 patients — where anxiety scores were significantly lower than placebo (P < 0.001) without sedation or psychomotor impairment. The Akhondzadeh record names no product or manufacturer. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): passionflower is plausibly anxiolytic; for generalised anxiety disorder the evidence is one small active-comparator pilot, exactly as its authors said in calling for a large-scale trial.

cards.headline: Akhondzadeh 2001: passionflower and oxazepam both improved GAD over 4 weeks with no significant difference between them — oxazepam faster, but with more job-performance impairment
cards.summary: Akhondzadeh 2001: passionflower and oxazepam both improved GAD over 4 weeks with no significant difference between them — oxazepam faster, but with more job-performance impairment
cards.people: 36 outpatients diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder by DSM-IV criteria, allocated to Passiflora incarnata extract 45 drops/day plus placebo tablet (n = 18) or oxazepam 30 mg/day plus placebo drops (n = 18) for a 4-week double-blind trial. The record names no extract product or manufacturer.
cards.result: Passiflora extract and oxazepam were both effective in the treatment of generalised anxiety disorder, with no significant difference observed between the two protocols at the end of the trial. Oxazepam showed a rapid onset of action. Significantly more problems relating to impairment of job performance were encountered in subjects on oxazepam. The authors conclude the extract is effective for the management of generalised anxiety disorder, that the low incidence of job-performance impairment is an advantage, and that a large-scale trial is justified.
cards.watchOut: A pilot of 36 patients with no placebo group: 'no difference from oxazepam' in an underpowered trial is not equivalence, and without placebo neither arm's improvement can be separated from natural course and expectation. The record reports outcomes qualitatively — no anxiety-scale scores appear in the abstract — so effect sizes cannot be stated.

cards.headline: Movafegh 2008: a single 500 mg dose of Passiflora (Passipy, IranDarouk) cut pre-operative anxiety versus placebo (P < 0.001) without sedation
cards.summary: Movafegh 2008: a single 500 mg dose of Passiflora (Passipy, IranDarouk) cut pre-operative anxiety versus placebo (P < 0.001) without sedation
cards.people: 60 ambulatory-surgery patients randomised to oral Passiflora incarnata 500 mg (Passipy, IranDarouk — product and company as named in the record) (n = 30) or placebo (n = 30) as premedication 90 minutes before surgery, with anxiety and sedation rated on a numerical scale and psychomotor function tested after surgery.
cards.result: Numerical rating scale anxiety scores were significantly lower in the passiflora group than in the control group (P < 0.001). Sedation scores, psychomotor recovery (Trieger Dot Test and Digit-Symbol Substitution Test), and discharge time did not differ significantly between groups. The authors conclude oral Passiflora incarnata as premedication reduces anxiety without inducing sedation.
cards.watchOut: Situational pre-operative anxiety after a single dose is not generalised anxiety disorder — this card proves the plant can do something measurable against placebo, in a different condition and timeframe from the shelf's question; the record gives the p-value without the actual anxiety scores.
cards.source: Movafegh A et al. Preoperative oral Passiflora incarnata reduces anxiety in ambulatory surgery patients: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2008. shelves.title: Fenugreek for type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis reports HbA1c −1.16% — but the named placebo-controlled trial found fasting and 2-hour glucose no different between groups
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does fenugreek seed powder lower fasting glucose and HbA1c versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus/blood/therapy · Humans · Hyperglycemia/therapy · Hyperlipidemias/therapy · Prediabetic State/blood/therapy · Trigonella
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pooled answer and the checkable trial disagree. The meta-analysis (Gong et al., PMID: 27496582; 10 articles, 12 studies in diabetes and prediabetes) pooled significant reductions with fenugreek: fasting blood glucose −0.84 mmol/L (≈-15 mg/dL) (95% CI −1.38 to −0.31, p = 0.002), 2-hour glucose −1.30 mmol/L (≈-23 mg/dL) (95% CI −1.78 to −0.83, p < 0.0001), HbA1c −1.16 (95% CI −1.23 to −1.09, p < 0.00001) and total cholesterol −0.30 mmol/L (≈-12 mg/dL), while triglycerides, LDL and HDL effects were not significant — with the authors' own caveat that some included studies were of low quality, and the main side effects gastrointestinal discomfort. Yet the double-blind placebo-controlled trial carded here (Gupta et al., PMID: 11868855; 25 newly diagnosed patients, fenugreek seed extract 1 g/day for 2 months) found fasting glucose and 2-hour glucose not different between groups at the end, with benefit confined to glucose and insulin areas under the curve, HOMA insulin-resistance indices, triglycerides and HDL. Neither record names a fenugreek product or manufacturer. PROPOSED SPLIT: small, low-quality pooled trials say fenugreek lowers glucose and HbA1c by amounts that would matter; the individual placebo-controlled evidence is far weaker — do not dose diabetes treatment around it.

cards.headline: Gong 2016 (meta-analysis): fasting glucose −0.84 mmol/L (≈-15 mg/dL), 2-hour glucose −1.30 mmol/L (≈-23 mg/dL), HbA1c −1.16 across 12 studies — with low-quality studies inside the pool
cards.summary: Gong 2016 (meta-analysis): fasting glucose −0.84 mmol/L (≈-15 mg/dL), 2-hour glucose −1.30 mmol/L (≈-23 mg/dL), HbA1c −1.16 across 12 studies — with low-quality studies inside the pool
cards.people: 10 articles reporting 12 randomised studies of fenugreek in diabetes or prediabetes, drawn from international and Chinese databases (PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and several Chinese databases); preparations and doses varied across studies and no product or manufacturer is named in the record.
cards.result: Fenugreek significantly decreased fasting blood glucose (mean difference −0.84 mmol/L (≈-15 mg/dL), 95% CI −1.38 to −0.31, p = 0.002), 2-hour postprandial glucose (−1.30 mmol/L (≈-23 mg/dL), 95% CI −1.78 to −0.83, p < 0.0001), HbA1c (−1.16, 95% CI −1.23 to −1.09, p < 0.00001) and total cholesterol (−0.30 mmol/L (≈-12 mg/dL), 95% CI −0.56 to −0.03, p = 0.03). Reductive trends in triglycerides and LDL and an incremental trend in HDL were not statistically significant. No liver or kidney toxicity was found in the included studies; the main side effects were gastrointestinal discomfort. The authors note some studies were of low quality.
cards.watchOut: The HbA1c confidence interval (−1.23 to −1.09) is implausibly narrow for a pool of small heterogeneous trials and is reproduced here exactly as the record prints it — treat the pooled precision with suspicion; much of the underlying literature is small, short, and published in regional journals, the classic profile for publication bias inflating an herbal effect.
cards.source: Gong J et al. Effect of fenugreek on hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidemia in diabetes and prediabetes: A meta-analysis. Journal of ethnopharmacology. 2016. PMID: 27496582. cards.headline: Gupta 2001: fasting glucose and 2-hour glucose NOT different between fenugreek and placebo groups at 2 months — only curve areas and insulin-resistance indices moved
cards.summary: Gupta 2001: fasting glucose and 2-hour glucose NOT different between fenugreek and placebo groups at 2 months — only curve areas and insulin-resistance indices moved
cards.people: 25 newly diagnosed patients with mild to moderate type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose <200 mg/dL), randomised to a hydroalcoholic extract of fenugreek seeds 1 g/day (n = 12) or usual care (dietary control and exercise) plus placebo capsules (n = 13) for two months. No product or manufacturer is named in the record.
cards.result: At the end of two months, fasting blood glucose (119.9 ± 25 versus 113.0 ± 36.0 mg/dL in the fenugreek and control groups' end values as reported) and two-hour post-glucose blood glucose were not different between groups. Areas under the curve for blood glucose and for insulin were significantly lower with fenugreek (p < 0.001), HOMA-derived insulin sensitivity increased and beta-cell secretion percentage decreased (p < 0.05), and serum triglycerides decreased while HDL cholesterol increased significantly in the fenugreek group compared with control (p < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five patients for two months, with the headline glucose measures null between groups — the positive findings are secondary curve and surrogate indices; the record's printed glucose AUC figures contain an apparent typographical error and are therefore not quoted numerically on this card.
cards.source: Gupta A et al. Effect of Trigonella foenum-graecum (fenugreek) seeds on glycaemic control and insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes mellitus: a double blind placebo controlled study. The Journal of the Association of Physicians of India. 2001. PMID: 11868855. cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled promise, individual-trial null — fenugreek's glucose effect is unproven where it can be checked cleanly
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled promise, individual-trial null — fenugreek's glucose effect is unproven where it can be checked cleanly
cards.people: A 12-study meta-analysis in diabetes and prediabetes and a 25-patient double-blind placebo-controlled trial of fenugreek seed extract in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: Pooled: fasting glucose −0.84 mmol/L (≈-15 mg/dL), HbA1c −1.16 (as printed), total cholesterol −0.30 mmol/L (≈-12 mg/dL). Single checkable trial: fasting and 2-hour glucose not different between groups; insulin-resistance indices and lipids favoured fenugreek. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the meta-analytic HbA1c figure (−1.16%) rivals metformin's effect and is not credible at face value from this trial base; the shelf records both numbers because both are what the literature says.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here tests fenugreek against, or added to, standard glucose-lowering therapy at meaningful scale or duration, and no outcome beyond glucose and lipids (complications, events) has been studied. Fenugreek for breast-milk production is a different question on its own shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gong J et al. Journal of ethnopharmacology. 2016 (PMID: 27496582); Gupta A et al. The Journal of the Association of Physicians of India. 2001 (PMID: 11868855).

shelves.question: In adults with functional dyspepsia, does artichoke leaf extract improve dyspeptic symptoms and quality of life versus placebo?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-sized trial, never independently replicated in this record set. Holtmann and colleagues (PMID: 14653829) randomised 247 patients with functional dyspepsia to a commercial artichoke leaf extract preparation (two 320 mg capsules three times daily) or placebo for 6 weeks (244 in the intention-to-treat analysis): the primary outcome — overall change in dyspeptic symptoms on the patient's weekly four-point rating — improved significantly more on the extract (8.3 ± 4.6 versus 6.7 ± 4.8, P < 0.01), as did disease-specific quality of life on the Nepean Dyspepsia Index (−41.1 ± 47.6 versus −24.8 ± 35.6, P < 0.01). The record describes the preparation only as a commercial artichoke leaf extract and names no brand or manufacturer, so no product on sale today can claim this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a statistically solid 1.6-point advantage on the trial's symptom scale over 6 weeks — real, modest, short-term, and resting on a single trial.

cards.headline: Holtmann 2003: overall symptom improvement 8.3 versus 6.7 points (P < 0.01) and Nepean quality-of-life change −41.1 versus −24.8 (P < 0.01) at 6 weeks
cards.summary: Holtmann 2003: overall symptom improvement 8.3 versus 6.7 points (P < 0.01) and Nepean quality-of-life change −41.1 versus −24.8 (P < 0.01) at 6 weeks
cards.people: 247 patients with functional dyspepsia in a double-blind multicentre trial, treated with a commercial artichoke leaf extract preparation (2 × 320 mg plant extract three times daily) or placebo for 6 weeks; data from 244 patients (129 active, 115 placebo) entered the intention-to-treat analysis. The record names no brand or manufacturer for the preparation.
cards.result: The primary efficacy variable — the sum score of the patient's weekly rating of overall change in dyspeptic symptoms (four-point scale) — improved significantly more with artichoke leaf extract than placebo over 6 weeks (8.3 ± 4.6 versus 6.7 ± 4.8, P < 0.01). Individual dyspeptic symptom scores also favoured the extract, and global quality-of-life scores on the Nepean Dyspepsia Index improved significantly more (−41.1 ± 47.6 versus −24.8 ± 35.6, P < 0.01).
cards.watchOut: A single trial with a patient-rated global-change scale as its primary outcome — a soft, expectation-sensitive measure in a condition with a large placebo response (the placebo group itself improved 6.7 points); six weeks says nothing about the relapsing long-term course of functional dyspepsia, and the unnamed preparation blocks any product-specific conclusion.
cards.source: Holtmann G et al. Efficacy of artichoke leaf extract in the treatment of patients with functional dyspepsia: a six-week placebo-controlled, double-blind, multicentre trial. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2003. PMID: 14653829. cards.headline: Synthesis: one good trial is a beginning, not a verdict — POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C, product unnamed
cards.summary: Synthesis: one good trial is a beginning, not a verdict — POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C, product unnamed
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (247 patients with functional dyspepsia, 6 weeks) of a commercial artichoke leaf extract, 1,920 mg/day.
cards.result: Symptoms: +1.6 points over placebo on the trial's global-change sum score (P < 0.01). Quality of life: −16.3 points further improvement on the Nepean Dyspepsia Index (P < 0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-trial benefit claims go to the developer personally, and no second trial in functional dyspepsia was found to card beside this one. Artichoke leaf extract for cholesterol is a different question, answered on its own shelf.
cards.watchOut: Effect durability, dose–response, and comparative performance against standard dyspepsia care (acid suppression, prokinetics, H. pylori treatment where relevant) are all untested in this record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Holtmann G et al. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2003 (PMID: 14653829).

shelves.title: Pycnogenol for knee osteoarthritis: WOMAC scores fell 56% versus 9.6% in one small trial and symptoms improved in a second — 3 months, small numbers, a branded extract
shelves.question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does Pycnogenol (French maritime pine bark extract, Horphag Research) reduce pain and improve function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Adult · Age Distribution · Ankle/pathology · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Edema/drug therapy/pathology · Female · Flavonoids/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Foot/pathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis/drug therapy/pathology/physiopathology · Pain/drug therapy/pathology · Plant Extracts · Sex Distribution · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small 3-month placebo trials of the same branded extract point the same way. In the SVOS study (Belcaro G et al., PMID: 18386255), 100 mg/day Pycnogenol in 156 patients with osteoarthritis cut the global WOMAC score by 56% versus 9.6% on placebo, and treadmill walking distance rose from 68 m to 198 m versus 65 m to 88 m. In the second trial (Cisár P et al., PMID: 18570266), 150 mg/day in 100 patients with stage I–II knee osteoarthritis significantly improved the WOMAC index (p<0.05) and visual-analogue pain (p<0.04) while placebo had no effect, and analgesic use fell on Pycnogenol but rose on placebo. Both trials tested Pycnogenol, the French maritime pine bark extract of Horphag Research — the specific tested product named in the question — so the shelf vouches for that extract, not for generic pine bark products, which may differ in safety and effectiveness. Neither trial runs beyond 3 months or reports structural joint outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): short-term symptom relief in two small concordant trials of one branded extract; durability and any effect on the joint itself are unproven.

cards.headline: Belcaro 2008 (SVOS): WOMAC down 56% versus 9.6%, walking distance 68→198 m versus 65→88 m on placebo
cards.summary: Belcaro 2008 (SVOS): WOMAC down 56% versus 9.6%, walking distance 68→198 m versus 65→88 m on placebo
cards.people: 156 patients with osteoarthritis (77 treatment, 79 placebo; groups comparable for age, sex, WOMAC scores, walking distance and anti-inflammatory drug use) given Pycnogenol 100 mg daily or placebo for 3 months; symptoms by WOMAC, mobility by treadmill walking performance.
cards.result: The global WOMAC score decreased by 56% (p<0.05) on Pycnogenol versus 9.6% on placebo. Walking distance rose from 68 m at baseline to 198 m after 3 months (p<0.05) versus 65 m to 88 m on placebo (not significant). Use of anti-inflammatory drugs decreased by 58% on Pycnogenol (p<0.05) versus 1% on placebo; gastrointestinal complications decreased by 63% versus 3%; foot oedema, present in about three-quarters at entry, decreased in 79% of Pycnogenol patients versus 1% of controls.
cards.watchOut: Very large percentage improvements on modest absolute numbers, from a single research group with a long line of positive Pycnogenol studies; the record reports percentage changes rather than absolute WOMAC scores, follow-up is 3 months, and the population is described as osteoarthritis without the knee-specific staging of the companion trial.
cards.source: Belcaro G et al. Treatment of osteoarthritis with Pycnogenol. The SVOS (San Valentino Osteo-arthrosis Study). Evaluation of signs, symptoms, physical performance and vascular aspects. Phytotherapy Research. 2008. PMID: 18386255. cards.headline: Cisár 2008: WOMAC index and pain scores significantly improved on 150 mg/day — placebo had no effect
cards.summary: Cisár 2008: WOMAC index and pain scores significantly improved on 150 mg/day — placebo had no effect
cards.people: 100 patients with knee osteoarthritis stages I–II treated for 3 months with Pycnogenol 150 mg/day taken at meals or placebo; WOMAC questionnaire every 2 weeks and weekly visual-analogue pain ratings; changes in previously prescribed anti-inflammatory medication recorded.
cards.result: Patients on Pycnogenol reported an improvement in the WOMAC index (p<0.05) and a significant alleviation of pain by visual analogue scale (p<0.04); the placebo had no effect. The use of analgesics diminished in the Pycnogenol group but increased under placebo. Treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The record gives p-values without the absolute WOMAC or pain scores, so the size of the benefit cannot be judged from the record; 100 patients, 3 months, mild-to-moderate disease only.
cards.source: Cisár P et al. Effect of pine bark extract (Pycnogenol) on symptoms of knee osteoarthritis. Phytotherapy Research. 2008. PMID: 18570266. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small, short, concordant trials of one branded extract — a symptom signal, nothing more
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small, short, concordant trials of one branded extract — a symptom signal, nothing more
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo trials totalling 256 patients with osteoarthritis (knee disease specified in one), testing Pycnogenol 100–150 mg/day for 3 months.
cards.result: Symptoms: WOMAC improved in both trials (global score −56% versus −9.6% in SVOS; significant index improvement in Cisár). Function: treadmill distance nearly tripled in SVOS (68→198 m versus 65→88 m). Analgesic sparing in both trials. Harms: well tolerated in both records; gastrointestinal complications fell in SVOS. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: small single-product trials, short horizon, one trial reporting percentages without absolute scores.
cards.watchOut: Pycnogenol is a specific branded extract (Horphag Research); these results do not transfer automatically to other pine bark products, and no trial here exceeds 3 months or examines joint structure.
cards.source: Synthesis of Belcaro G et al. Phytotherapy Research. 2008 (PMID: 18386255); Cisár P et al. Phytotherapy Research. 2008 (PMID: 18570266).

shelves.title: Micronised purified flavonoid fraction for chronic venous disease: a meta-analysis of 7 trials favours it on most leg symptoms — but the two largest individual trials were null or inconclusive on their main measures
shelves.question: In chronic venous insufficiency, does micronised purified flavonoid fraction (diosmin/hesperidin) reduce leg oedema and symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Chi-Square Distribution · Chronic Disease · Diosmin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Edema/drug therapy/physiopathology/psychology · Humans · Odds Ratio · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recovery of Function · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Varicose Veins/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology/psychology · Venous Insufficiency/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology/psychology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pooled evidence and the biggest single trials tell different stories. The meta-analysis of 7 randomised double-blind placebo trials (1,692 patients; Kakkos SK et al., PMID: 29385792) found MPFF (Daflon, Laboratoires Servier) significantly improved nine defined leg symptoms, with categorical risk ratios of 0.53 for leg pain (NNT 4.2), 0.35 for heaviness (NNT 2.0) and 0.39 for feeling of swelling (NNT 3.1), and reduced ankle circumference (standardised mean difference −0.59). But the largest prospective trial (Rabe E et al., PMID: 25972136; 1,137 patients) was inconclusive on its primary oedema measure (water-displacement volumetry, for methodological reasons) and found only a −0.5 cm pain/heaviness difference in a post-hoc symptomatic subgroup, and an earlier 101-patient trial (Danielsson G et al., PMID: 11748952) found no significant symptom benefit at all except night cramps. PROPOSED SPLIT: symptom relief is supported by pooling many small trials; objective oedema reduction rests on much thinner ice, and no trial here addresses ulcers, thrombosis, or long-term disease course.

cards.headline: Kakkos 2018 meta-analysis: 7 trials, 1,692 patients — pain RR 0.53, heaviness RR 0.35, swelling sensation RR 0.39 versus placebo
cards.summary: Kakkos 2018 meta-analysis: 7 trials, 1,692 patients — pain RR 0.53, heaviness RR 0.35, swelling sensation RR 0.39 versus placebo
cards.people: 7 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (1,692 patients with chronic venous disease) of micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF, Daflon) versus placebo, identified to September 2017; outcomes were individual leg symptoms and signs, leg oedema, quality of life and physician global assessment; most trials at low risk of bias, evidence graded with GRADE.
cards.result: On categorical analysis MPFF reduced leg pain (RR 0.53, P=0.0001, NNT 4.2), heaviness (RR 0.35, P<0.00001, NNT 2.0), feeling of swelling (RR 0.39, P<0.00001, NNT 3.1), cramps (RR 0.51, P=0.02, NNT 4.8), paraesthesia (RR 0.45, P=0.03, NNT 3.5) and functional discomfort (RR 0.41, P=0.0004, NNT 3.0) versus placebo. On continuous measures it reduced pain (SMD −0.25), heaviness (SMD −0.80) and swelling sensation (SMD −0.99), reduced ankle circumference (SMD −0.59, 95% CI −1.15 to −0.02) and leg redness (RR 0.50, NNT 3.6), and improved skin changes (RR 0.18, P=0.0003) and quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Pooling many small, short trials can manufacture consistency the individual trials do not show — the two largest trials carded below were null or inconclusive on their primary measures. Symptom outcomes are subjective and the pooled ankle-circumference effect has a confidence interval that nearly reaches zero.
cards.source: Kakkos SK et al. Efficacy of micronized purified flavonoid fraction (Daflon®) on improving individual symptoms, signs and quality of life in patients with chronic venous disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials. International Angiology. 2018. PMID: 29385792. cards.headline: Danielsson 2002: no significant symptom improvement on MPFF versus placebo in 101 patients — night cramps the only exception
cards.summary: Danielsson 2002: no significant symptom improvement on MPFF versus placebo in 101 patients — night cramps the only exception
cards.people: 101 patients with symptomatic chronic venous disease (51 MPFF, 50 placebo; mean age 48 years) treated with MPFF 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 60 days; symptoms by a global score, with foot-volumetry plethysmography and duplex ultrasonography before and after treatment.
cards.result: Improvement in the global symptom score was reported by 21 patients on MPFF and 16 on placebo (not significant). No significant differences were recorded before and after treatment in foot-volumetric or ultrasonographic parameters for the whole groups. In the subgroup with oedema (20 MPFF, 23 placebo), ultrasonographic reflux time fell significantly on MPFF (p=0.03) without correlating with symptoms. The authors conclude MPFF did not change the symptoms of chronic venous disease except night cramps.
cards.watchOut: A small, 60-day trial — underpowered for modest symptom effects, and its null does not erase the pooled signal; but it is a properly blinded placebo trial that found essentially nothing, and it sits inside the meta-analysis above.
cards.source: Danielsson G et al. A randomised controlled trial of micronised purified flavonoid fraction vs placebo in patients with chronic venous disease. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2002. PMID: 11748952. cards.headline: Rabe 2015: main trial inconclusive on oedema volume; in the symptomatic subgroup pain/heaviness fell by an extra 0.5 cm and quality of life by 3.1%
cards.summary: Rabe 2015: main trial inconclusive on oedema volume; in the symptomatic subgroup pain/heaviness fell by an extra 0.5 cm and quality of life by 3.1%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial, post-hoc subgroup analysis (Rabe 2015)
cards.people: 1,137 patients with CEAP class C3–C4 chronic venous disease randomised to MPFF (Daflon 500 mg, Laboratoires Servier, France) once daily or placebo for 4 months; primary measure vesperal oedema by water-displacement volumetry, with leg pain/heaviness by visual analogue scale and quality of life by CIVIQ-20. The carded analysis covers the 592 symptomatic patients (296 per group) with baseline VAS >4 cm.
cards.result: The main study was inconclusive on water-displacement volumetry for methodological reasons. In the symptomatic subgroup, MPFF was associated with a greater reduction in VAS score than placebo (between-group difference −0.5 cm; P=0.031) and greater improvement in CIVIQ score (between-group difference 3.1%; P=0.040). Treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The positive findings come from a post-hoc subgroup after the primary oedema endpoint failed on methodology — hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory; a 0.5 cm difference on a 10 cm pain scale is small, and the trial says nothing about ulcer healing or thrombosis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled symptom benefit, fragile objective benefit — the split is the story
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled symptom benefit, fragile objective benefit — the split is the story
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 7 randomised placebo trials (1,692 patients) plus the two largest individual trials carded separately (101 and 1,137 patients), all of MPFF 500 mg (Daflon, Laboratoires Servier) in chronic venous disease.
cards.result: Symptoms: pooled risk ratios favour MPFF across pain (0.53), heaviness (0.35), swelling sensation (0.39), cramps (0.51) and paraesthesia (0.45). Individual trials: Danielsson 2002 null on symptoms (21 versus 16 improvers); Rabe 2015 positive only in a post-hoc symptomatic subgroup (−0.5 cm VAS). Oedema: pooled ankle circumference SMD −0.59, but the largest trial's volumetric primary measure was inconclusive. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the symptom claim and the oedema claim rest on different strengths of evidence.
cards.watchOut: MPFF is a defined manufactured product (Daflon, Laboratoires Servier); results should not be read across to generic diosmin or citrus flavonoid supplements, which may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Ashwagandha root extract in novice resistance trainees: bench press up 46.0 kg versus 26.4 kg and testosterone up 96 ng/dL in one 57-man, 8-week trial
shelves.question: In resistance-training men, does the ashwagandha root extract KSM-66 increase muscle strength, size, and testosterone versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Composition · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Exercise · Humans · Male · Muscle Strength/drug effects/physiology · Muscle, Skeletal/drug effects/physiology · Physical Endurance/drug effects/physiology · Plant Preparations/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Resistance Training · Sports Nutritional Physiological Phenomena · Treatment Outcome · Withania
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single small, short trial. In 57 young men (18–50 years) with little resistance-training experience, ashwagandha root extract 300 mg twice daily for 8 weeks (Wankhede S et al., PMID: 26609282) produced greater strength gains than placebo — bench press 46.0 kg versus 26.4 kg (p=0.001), leg extension 14.5 kg versus 9.8 kg (p=0.04) — greater arm and chest muscle-size gains, a larger testosterone rise (96.2 versus 18.0 ng/dL, p=0.004) and a larger fall in body-fat percentage (3.5% versus 1.5%, p=0.03). The question names the KSM-66 extract; the PubMed record itself identifies the intervention only as ashwagandha root extract 300 mg twice daily and names no brand or manufacturer, so this shelf cannot vouch for any specific commercial product — products on sale may differ in safety and effectiveness. Eight weeks in novices, whose strength rises fast on any programme, is the easiest possible test-bed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real signal in one small trial; replication in trained men over longer periods does not exist in this record.

cards.headline: Wankhede 2015: bench press +46.0 kg versus +26.4 kg, testosterone +96.2 versus +18.0 ng/dL over 8 weeks
cards.summary: Wankhede 2015: bench press +46.0 kg versus +26.4 kg, testosterone +96.2 versus +18.0 ng/dL over 8 weeks
cards.people: 57 healthy young men (18–50 years) with little experience in resistance training, randomised to ashwagandha root extract 300 mg twice daily (29 subjects) or starch placebo (28 subjects) for 8 weeks, both groups resistance training; primary measure muscle strength (1-RM bench press and leg extension), with muscle size, body composition, serum testosterone and creatine kinase as secondary measures. The record names no branded extract or manufacturer.
cards.result: Strength gains were significantly greater on ashwagandha: bench press 46.0 kg (95% CI 36.6 to 55.5) versus 26.4 kg (19.5 to 33.3) (p=0.001); leg extension 14.5 kg (10.8 to 18.2) versus 9.8 kg (7.2 to 12.3) (p=0.04). Muscle size increased more at the arms (8.6 versus 5.3 cm², p=0.01) and chest (3.3 versus 1.4 cm, p<0.001). Testosterone rose by 96.2 ng/dL (54.7 to 137.5) versus 18.0 ng/dL (−15.8 to 51.8) (p=0.004), and body-fat percentage fell by 3.5% versus 1.5% (p=0.03).
cards.watchOut: One trial, 57 novices, 8 weeks: beginners gain strength rapidly regardless, the trial is the sole evidence for the named KSM-66 question while its own record names no brand, and the creatine-kinase 'muscle damage' result is reported as stabilisation despite a higher absolute value in the ashwagandha group (1,462.6 versus 1,307.5 U/L) — that secondary claim is not carried into this shelf's balance.
cards.source: Wankhede S et al. Examining the effect of Withania somnifera supplementation on muscle strength and recovery: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. 2015. PMID: 26609282. shelves.title: Curcumin extract in prediabetes: 0 of the curcumin group developed diabetes in 9 months versus 16.4% on placebo — one 240-person trial, so a delay signal awaiting replication
shelves.question: In adults with prediabetes, does a standardised curcumin extract delay progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Curcumin/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Prediabetic State/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking result from exactly one trial. In 240 people with prediabetes randomised to curcumin extract capsules or placebo for 9 months (Chuengsamarn S et al., PMID: 22773702), 16.4% of the placebo group were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and none of the curcumin group were; beta-cell function was better on curcumin (HOMA-β 61.58 versus 48.72, P<0.01), insulin resistance lower (HOMA-IR 3.22 versus 4.04, P<0.001) and adiponectin higher (22.46 versus 18.45, P<0.05), with very minor adverse effects. In this library's language that is, at most, a delay in the formal diagnosis over 9 months — whether the effect persists, or merely postpones crossing the diagnostic threshold while treatment continues, is untested, and a zero-event arm in a single-centre trial is exactly the kind of result that shrinks on replication. The record identifies the intervention only as curcumin extract capsules and names no brand or manufacturer, so no commercial curcumin product can claim this result; current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one small trial with a zero-event treatment arm — promising, fragile, and unreplicated.

cards.headline: Chuengsamarn 2012: diabetes developed in 0% on curcumin versus 16.4% on placebo at 9 months
cards.summary: Chuengsamarn 2012: diabetes developed in 0% on curcumin versus 16.4% on placebo at 9 months
cards.people: 240 subjects meeting criteria for prediabetes, randomly assigned to curcumin extract capsules or placebo capsules for 9 months, with assessments at baseline and 3, 6 and 9 months of diabetes progression, beta-cell function (HOMA-β, C-peptide, proinsulin/insulin), insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and adiponectin. The record names no branded product or manufacturer.
cards.result: After 9 months, 16.4% of subjects in the placebo group were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, whereas none were diagnosed in the curcumin-treated group. The curcumin group showed better beta-cell function (HOMA-β 61.58 versus 48.72; P<0.01; C-peptide 1.7 versus 2.17; P<0.05), lower insulin resistance (HOMA-IR 3.22 versus 4.04; P<0.001) and higher adiponectin (22.46 versus 18.45; P<0.05). Adverse effects were very minor.
cards.watchOut: A zero-event arm is the most fragile result a trial can produce — a handful of cases either way would change the headline; single centre, 9 months, no follow-up after stopping, and no named standardised product in the record, so neither durability nor product identity is established. Nine months of non-progression is delay within the trial window only — nothing beyond that window is shown.
cards.source: Chuengsamarn S et al. Curcumin extract for prevention of type 2 diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2012. PMID: 22773702. Registry ID: NCT01052025. shelves.title: White willow bark for low back pain: pain-free in the last week in 39% on the high salicin dose, 21% on the low dose, 6% on placebo — one 210-patient exacerbation trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does white willow bark extract reduce pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid/therapeutic use · Benzyl Alcohols/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucosides · Humans · Low Back Pain/drug therapy/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Tramadol/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a dose-ordered result in one good-sized trial, graded moderate at best by the Cochrane reviewers. In 210 patients with an exacerbation of chronic low back pain (Chrubasik S et al., PMID: 10936472), the proportion pain-free without rescue tramadol for at least 5 days of the final week was 39% on willow bark extract providing 240 mg salicin/day, 21% on 120 mg/day, and 6% on placebo (P<0.001), with significantly more placebo patients needing tramadol in every week; one patient had a severe allergic reaction, perhaps to the extract. The Cochrane review update (Gagnier JJ et al., PMID: 26630428) concluded that Salix alba (white willow bark), like several other herbs, seems to reduce pain more than placebo, but that the evidence was of moderate quality at best and trial reporting was poor. The tested preparation is a standardised extract dosed by salicin content; the records name no brand or manufacturer, so shop products — whose salicin content varies — cannot be assumed equivalent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): short-term relief of back-pain exacerbations at the 240 mg salicin dose; steady chronic pain, function, and longer use are untested here.

cards.headline: Chrubasik 2000: pain-free without tramadol in 39% on 240 mg salicin, 21% on 120 mg, 6% on placebo (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Chrubasik 2000: pain-free without tramadol in 39% on 240 mg salicin, 21% on 120 mg, 6% on placebo (P<0.001)
cards.people: 210 patients with an exacerbation of chronic low back pain and current pain of at least 5 out of 10, randomly assigned to oral willow bark extract providing 120 mg or 240 mg of salicin daily, or placebo, for 4 weeks, with tramadol as the sole rescue medication; 191 patients completed the study. The record names no brand or manufacturer.
cards.result: The numbers of patients pain-free without tramadol for at least 5 days during the final week were 27 (39%) of 65 in the high-dose group, 15 (21%) of 67 in the low-dose group, and 4 (6%) of 59 in the placebo group (P<0.001). The high-dose response was evident after only 1 week. Significantly more placebo patients required tramadol during each week (P<0.001). One patient suffered a severe allergic reaction, perhaps to the extract.
cards.watchOut: An exacerbation trial, not a steady chronic-pain trial: spontaneous improvement is common in flares, follow-up is 4 weeks, and the endpoint bundles pain relief with rescue-medication use. Salicin is a salicylate prodrug — the aspirin-family cautions (allergy, bleeding, interacting anticoagulants) apply in principle even though harms in this trial were few.
cards.source: Chrubasik S et al. Treatment of low back pain exacerbations with willow bark extract: a randomized double-blind study. American Journal of Medicine. 2000. PMID: 10936472. cards.headline: Gagnier 2016 (Cochrane update): Salix alba 'seems to reduce pain more than placebo' — evidence of moderate quality at best
cards.summary: Gagnier 2016 (Cochrane update): Salix alba 'seems to reduce pain more than placebo' — evidence of moderate quality at best
cards.people: 14 randomised trials (2,050 participants) of herbal medicines for acute, sub-acute or chronic non-specific low back pain in adults, searching to September 2014, with risk-of-bias and GRADE assessment; the willow (Salix alba) conclusion rests on the placebo-controlled willow trials within that set, including the trial carded above.
cards.result: The reviewers concluded that Capsicum frutescens (cayenne) reduces pain more than placebo, and that Harpagophytum procumbens (devil's claw), Salix alba (white willow bark), Symphytum officinale (comfrey), Solidago chilensis (Brazilian arnica) and lavender essential oil also seem to reduce pain more than placebo — but the evidence for these substances was of moderate quality at best. No significant adverse events were noted within the included trials, reporting completeness was poor, and the reviewers call for additional well-designed large trials against standard treatments.
cards.watchOut: A multi-herb review whose willow slice is small; 'moderate quality at best' is the ceiling for the whole group, not a willow-specific grade, and the review adds no new willow trial beyond the primary evidence carded here.
cards.source: Gagnier JJ et al. Herbal Medicine for Low Back Pain: A Cochrane Review. Spine. 2016. PMID: 26630428. cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial (210 patients, 4 weeks, back-pain exacerbations) and the Cochrane herbal-medicine review update that pools the willow evidence.
cards.result: Pain-free without rescue tramadol in the final week: 39% on 240 mg salicin/day, 21% on 120 mg/day, 6% on placebo. Review verdict: Salix alba seems to reduce pain more than placebo, evidence of moderate quality at best. Harms: one severe allergic reaction, perhaps extract-related, in the trial; no significant adverse events across the review's included trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: essentially one trial, in exacerbations, short-term.
cards.watchOut: The earlier Cochrane version (Oltean 2014) is already carded on the devil's-claw shelf (#3461) and is deliberately not re-carded here; this shelf rests on the primary trial plus the 2016 Cochrane update (Gagnier) as a distinct record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chrubasik S et al. American Journal of Medicine. 2000 (PMID: 10936472); Gagnier JJ et al. Spine. 2016 (PMID: 26630428).

shelves.title: Avocado-soybean unsaponifiables for knee and hip arthritis: pain down 20.8 mm versus 10.4 mm on placebo at 6 months in one trial — but the 3-year structure trial found no difference in joint-space loss
shelves.question: In adults with symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee or hip, do avocado/soybean unsaponifiables (ASU) reduce pain, disability and NSAID use compared with placebo — and do they slow joint-space narrowing?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hip Joint · Humans · Kinetics · Knee Joint · Lauraceae · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Hip/drug therapy · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Plant Oils/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Prospective Studies · Glycine max · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms over months, from two 1990s French trials of one preparation family; the structure claim failed its main test. In Maheu E et al. (PMID: 9433873; 164 patients, 6 months), pain fell from 56.1 mm to 35.3 mm on ASU versus 56.1 to 45.7 mm on placebo (p=0.003), the Lequesne functional index improved significantly more (to 6.8 versus 8.9; p<0.001), success rate was 39% versus 18%, and fewer ASU patients required NSAIDs (48% versus 63%; p=0.054). In Blotman F et al. (PMID: 9476272; 163 evaluable patients, 3 months), 43.4% of the ASU group resumed NSAID therapy after a protocol stop versus 69.7% on placebo (p<0.001), with a better functional index (-2.3 versus -1.0; p<0.01) but similar pain scores. The 3-year ERADIAS trial (Maheu E et al., PMID: 23345601; 399 patients with hip osteoarthritis, testing the named product Piascledine — avocado-soybean unsaponifiable-Expanscience, ASU-E) found no significant difference in mean joint-space-width loss (-0.638 mm versus -0.672 mm; p=0.72) and no difference in clinical outcomes, though progressors (loss of at least 0.5 mm) were fewer on ASU-E (40% versus 50%; p=0.040); safety was excellent. The two symptom trials' records do not name the tested product or its maker; ERADIAS names Piascledine (Expanscience) — current ASU products may differ in composition, safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest symptomatic effect over 2-6 months is supported; a joint-saving effect is not.

cards.headline: Maheu 1998: pain 56.1→35.3 mm on ASU versus 56.1→45.7 mm on placebo at 6 months (p=0.003); success 39% versus 18%
cards.summary: Maheu 1998: pain 56.1→35.3 mm on ASU versus 56.1→45.7 mm on placebo at 6 months (p=0.003); success 39% versus 18%
cards.people: 164 patients with regular painful primary osteoarthritis of the knee (114) or hip (50), in a multicentre trial with a 15-day NSAID washout, 6 months of ASU (85 patients) or placebo (79) and a 2-month post-treatment follow-up; 144 patients were evaluable at month 6. The record does not name the tested product or its manufacturer.
cards.result: Lequesne functional index fell from 9.7 to 6.8 on ASU versus 9.4 to 8.9 on placebo (p<0.001 for the intergroup difference at month 6). Pain (100 mm VAS) fell from 56.1 to 35.3 mm on ASU versus 56.1 to 45.7 mm on placebo (p=0.003). Fewer ASU patients required NSAIDs (48% versus 63%; p=0.054). Success rate was 39% versus 18%. Improvement appeared more marked in hip osteoarthritis, a residual effect was observed at month 8, and tolerance was good to excellent for most patients.
cards.watchOut: A 1998 trial of an unnamed preparation, with a borderline NSAID-sparing result (p=0.054) and subgroup flavour (hip better than knee) that was not the primary question. Because the record names no product or company, this result cannot be assumed to transfer to any ASU supplement sold today.
cards.source: Maheu E et al. Symptomatic efficacy of avocado/soybean unsaponifiables in the treatment of osteoarthritis of the knee and hip: a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter clinical trial with a six-month treatment period and a two-month followup demonstrating a persistent effect. Arthritis and rheumatism. 1998. PMID: 9433873. cards.headline: Blotman 1997: after stopping NSAIDs, 43.4% on ASU had resumed them by day 45 versus 69.7% on placebo (p<0.001) — pain scores themselves were similar
cards.summary: Blotman 1997: after stopping NSAIDs, 43.4% on ASU had resumed them by day 45 versus 69.7% on placebo (p<0.001) — pain scores themselves were similar
cards.people: 164 patients (163 evaluable; 80 ASU, 83 placebo; mean age 62.9 years) with femorotibial (101) or hip (62) osteoarthritis of at least 6 months requiring NSAID therapy, given one capsule daily of ASU or placebo for 3 months, with a predefined NSAID supplied to both groups for the first 45 days and resumption tracked thereafter. The record does not name the tested product or its manufacturer.
cards.result: Patients resuming NSAID therapy: 43.4% (33 patients) on ASU versus 69.7% (53) on placebo (p<0.001), and beyond day 54 the time spent off NSAID therapy was shorter in the placebo group. The functional index improved more on ASU (-2.3 versus -1.0; p<0.01) and overall patient ratings were significantly better (p<0.01), but pain scores over time were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a behaviour (reaching back for an NSAID) rather than pain itself — and pain, measured directly, did not differ. NSAID-sparing is worth having, but a shelf that quoted only the resumption figures would overstate what patients felt.
cards.source: Blotman F et al. Efficacy and safety of avocado/soybean unsaponifiables in the treatment of symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee and hip. A prospective, multicenter, three-month, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Revue du rhumatisme (English ed.). 1997. PMID: 9476272.
