cards.headline: Maheu 2014 (ERADIAS): 3 years of Piascledine (ASU-Expanscience) — joint-space loss -0.638 versus -0.672 mm (p=0.72), symptoms unchanged; progressors 40% versus 50% (p=0.040)
cards.summary: Maheu 2014 (ERADIAS): 3 years of Piascledine (ASU-Expanscience) — joint-space loss -0.638 versus -0.672 mm (p=0.72), symptoms unchanged; progressors 40% versus 50% (p=0.040)
cards.people: 399 patients with symptomatic hip osteoarthritis (pain for at least 1 year, Lequesne index 3-10, joint space width 1-4 mm; mean age 62, 54% women) randomised to the named product Piascledine — avocado-soybean unsaponifiable-Expanscience (ASU-E) 300 mg/day — or placebo for 3 years; 345 patients had at least two successive radiographs and formed the full analysis set. Registry ID: NCT01062737.
cards.result: Primary outcome: no significant difference in mean joint-space-width loss at 3 years (-0.638 mm on ASU-E versus -0.672 mm on placebo; p=0.72). Progressors (joint-space loss of at least 0.5 mm) were 20% fewer in relative terms on ASU-E — 40% versus 50% in absolute terms (p=0.040). No difference was observed on clinical outcomes. Safety was excellent.
cards.watchOut: The one positive structural signal is a dichotomised secondary reading of a null primary outcome — exactly the pattern that should be labelled 'to be confirmed', as the authors themselves put it. And its symptom results, in the largest ASU trial ever run, were null, which tempers the two smaller 1990s symptom trials.

cards.headline: Synthesis: symptoms probably improve a little over months; joints are not saved — and only the null trial names the product it tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: symptoms probably improve a little over months; joints are not saved — and only the null trial names the product it tested
cards.people: Three double-blind placebo-controlled trials: two 1990s symptom trials (164 and 163 patients, knee and hip osteoarthritis, product unnamed in the records) and the 3-year ERADIAS structure trial (399 patients, hip osteoarthritis, Piascledine/ASU-Expanscience 300 mg/day).
cards.result: Symptoms: pain fell 20.8 mm versus 10.4 mm at 6 months (Maheu 1998); NSAID resumption 43.4% versus 69.7% at 3 months (Blotman 1997) with pain scores similar. Structure: joint-space loss -0.638 versus -0.672 mm over 3 years (p=0.72), progressors 40% versus 50% (p=0.040), symptoms null in ERADIAS. Safety good to excellent across trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for symptoms only.
cards.watchOut: The symptom evidence is old, French, and from unnamed preparations, while the named-product trial is the null one — the naming discipline cuts against the marketing here, and the shelf says so. Current ASU products may differ in safety and effectiveness from anything tested. Tier C is not set: two concordant double-blind trials support the symptom claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Maheu E et al. Arthritis and rheumatism. 1998 (PMID: 9433873); Blotman F et al. Revue du rhumatisme (English ed.). 1997 (PMID: 9476272); Maheu E et al. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2014 (PMID: 23345601).

shelves.title: Ginkgo biloba does not help tinnitus: 34 of 360 versus 35 of 360 called it less troublesome in the largest trial, and the Cochrane pool of 1,543 patients found no evidence of effect
shelves.question: In adults with subjective tinnitus, does Ginkgo biloba extract improve tinnitus severity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Ginkgo biloba · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Plants, Medicinal · Tinnitus/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large trial, a small trial with its own meta-analysis, and a Cochrane review agree. Drew & Davies 2001 (PMID: 11154618) randomised matched participants with stable tinnitus to Ginkgo biloba extract LI 1370, 50 mg three times daily, or placebo for 12 weeks: 34 of 360 on ginkgo and 35 of 360 on placebo reported their tinnitus less troublesome, with no significant differences on primary or secondary outcomes; the record names the extract (LI 1370) but names no company. Rejali 2004 (PMID: 15142066) found no significant difference on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory in its own 66-patient trial, and its meta-analysis of six trials found benefit in 21.6% on ginkgo versus 18.4% on placebo (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI 0.89–1.71). Hilton 2013 (PMID: 23543524, Cochrane) pooled four trials with 1,543 participants and found no evidence that Ginkgo biloba was effective in patients whose primary complaint was tinnitus. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): ginkgo extract did not improve tinnitus severity over placebo in any adequate comparison.

cards.headline: Drew & Davies 2001 (BMJ): tinnitus 'less troublesome' in 34 of 360 on ginkgo extract LI 1370 versus 35 of 360 on placebo after 12 weeks
cards.summary: Drew & Davies 2001 (BMJ): tinnitus 'less troublesome' in 34 of 360 on ginkgo extract LI 1370 versus 35 of 360 on placebo after 12 weeks
cards.people: 1,121 healthy people aged 18–70 years with comparatively stable tinnitus enrolled by postal questionnaire; 978 participants were matched (489 pairs). Treatment was 50 mg Ginkgo biloba extract LI 1370 three times daily or placebo for 12 weeks. The record names the extract (LI 1370); it names no company.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in primary or secondary outcome measures between the groups. 34 of 360 participants receiving active treatment reported their tinnitus was less troublesome after 12 weeks, compared with 35 of 360 who took placebo. The authors concluded 50 mg Ginkgo biloba extract LI 1370 three times daily for 12 weeks is no more effective than placebo in treating tinnitus.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes were self-rated by postal questionnaire in a community sample rather than clinic patients with severe tinnitus — but that is the population that buys ginkgo for tinnitus, and the near-identical responder counts leave little room for a missed large effect.
cards.source: Drew S et al. Effectiveness of Ginkgo biloba in treating tinnitus: double blind, placebo controlled trial. BMJ. 2001. PMID: 11154618. cards.headline: Rejali 2004: own 66-patient trial null on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory; six-trial meta-analysis 21.6% versus 18.4% benefited (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.89–1.71)
cards.summary: Rejali 2004: own 66-patient trial null on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory; six-trial meta-analysis 21.6% versus 18.4% benefited (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.89–1.71)
cards.people: 66 adult patients with tinnitus randomised to Ginkgo biloba or placebo, plus a meta-analysis of six randomised placebo-controlled double-blind trials (552 ginkgo, 504 placebo patients). The record names no specific extract product or company.
cards.result: In the trial, the mean difference in change between ginkgo (n = 31) and placebo (n = 29) was 2.51 for the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (CI −10.1 to 5.1, P = 0.51), 0.58 for the Glasgow Health Status Inventory (P = 0.38), and 0.68 dB for average hearing threshold (P = 0.69) — none significant. In the meta-analysis, 21.6% of ginkgo-treated patients (107/552) gained benefit versus 18.4% on placebo (87/504), odds ratio 1.24 (CI 0.89–1.71).
cards.watchOut: The trial itself is small; its weight is the embedded meta-analysis, whose confidence interval (0.89–1.71) excludes a large benefit but not a small one — the larger Drew trial and the Cochrane review close that gap.
cards.source: Rejali D et al. Ginkgo biloba does not benefit patients with tinnitus: a randomized placebo-controlled double-blind trial and meta-analysis of randomized trials. Clinical Otolaryngology and Allied Sciences. 2004. PMID: 15142066. cards.headline: Hilton 2013 (Cochrane): four trials, 1,543 participants, all low risk of bias — no evidence ginkgo is effective when tinnitus is the primary complaint
cards.summary: Hilton 2013 (Cochrane): four trials, 1,543 participants, all low risk of bias — no evidence ginkgo is effective when tinnitus is the primary complaint
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of Ginkgo biloba in adults complaining of tinnitus (or cerebral insufficiency with tinnitus); four trials with 1,543 participants, three (1,143 participants) in patients with a primary complaint of tinnitus and one (400 participants) in mild-to-moderate dementia.
cards.result: There was no evidence that Ginkgo biloba was effective in patients with a primary complaint of tinnitus. In the dementia study, baseline tinnitus levels were low (1.7 to 2.5 on a 10-point scale) and small statistically significant reductions (1.5 and 0.7 points in vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease) were of unclear clinical significance. The incidence of side effects was low.
cards.watchOut: The dementia-trial signal is sometimes quoted for tinnitus; the reviewers themselves flag the low baseline severity and unclear clinical significance, and it does not concern patients whose primary complaint is tinnitus.
cards.source: Hilton MP et al. Ginkgo biloba for tinnitus. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 23543524. cards.headline: Synthesis: three independent evidence layers, one answer — ginkgo performs like placebo for tinnitus
cards.summary: Synthesis: three independent evidence layers, one answer — ginkgo performs like placebo for tinnitus
cards.people: One large community trial (978 matched participants), one clinic trial with a six-trial meta-analysis (1,056 patients pooled), and a Cochrane review of four trials (1,543 participants).
cards.result: Less-troublesome tinnitus: 34/360 versus 35/360 (Drew & Davies 2001). Pooled benefit: 21.6% versus 18.4%, OR 1.24 (95% CI 0.89–1.71) (Rejali 2004). Cochrane conclusion: no evidence of effectiveness for primary tinnitus (Hilton 2013). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Extracts differed across trials (LI 1370 in the largest; others unnamed in their records), so the null is a class-level statement about tested ginkgo extracts, not a proof that no conceivable preparation could differ. Tier C per this band's rule.
cards.source: Synthesis of Drew S et al. BMJ. 2001 (PMID: 11154618); Rejali D et al. Clinical Otolaryngology and Allied Sciences. 2004 (PMID: 15142066); Hilton MP et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23543524).

shelves.title: MCT oil: swapping it for other fats lost an extra 0.51 kg across 13 small trials — and the Alzheimer's cognition claim failed its 413-patient confirmatory trial (ADAS-Cog difference 0.76 points, P=0.2458, not significant)
shelves.question: Should I take MCT oil? In adults, does medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil — swapped for other dietary fats, or taken as a ketogenic medical food — reduce weight and body fat, or improve memory and thinking in Alzheimer's disease?
shelves.mesh: Body Composition/drug effects · Databases, Factual · Energy Intake · Energy Metabolism · Humans · Lipid Metabolism/drug effects · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Triglycerides/administration & dosage · Waist Circumference · Weight Loss/drug effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). For weight: the meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (Mumme & Stonehouse 2015; 749 adults) found that replacing long-chain triglycerides with MCTs reduced body weight by 0.51 kg (95% CI −0.80 to −0.23), waist circumference by 1.46 cm and total body fat (SMD −0.39), with no difference in blood lipids — but many trials lacked information for full quality assessment, commercial bias was detected, and the design was substitution: adding MCT oil (extra calories) on top of an unchanged diet was not what was tested. For cognition, the tested products were specific caprylic-triglyceride medical foods, named here per library rule: AC-1202 and AC-1204, developed by the sponsoring company (Accera, Inc. — the first author's affiliation on the 2009 record; Cerecin, Inc. on the 2020 record). AC-1202 (Henderson 2009; 152 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's) differed from placebo on ADAS-Cog at day 45 (1.9 points, P=0.0235) and at day 90 only within the APOE4-non-carrier subgroup (3.36 points, P=0.0148); the larger confirmatory trial of AC-1204 (Henderson 2020; 413 patients, 26 weeks) found no benefit in that same pre-specified subgroup (difference 0.76 points, P=0.2458) and no drug effect on secondary outcomes. Generic MCT oil and coconut oil sold as supplements were not the tested products in the cognition trials.

cards.headline: Mumme & Stonehouse 2015 (meta-analysis, 13 trials, 749 adults): replacing other fats with MCTs — weight −0.51 kg, waist −1.46 cm, visceral fat SMD −0.55, no change in blood lipids; commercial bias detected
cards.summary: Mumme & Stonehouse 2015 (meta-analysis, 13 trials, 749 adults): replacing other fats with MCTs — weight −0.51 kg, waist −1.46 cm, visceral fat SMD −0.55, no change in blood lipids; commercial bias detected
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Mumme & Stonehouse 2015)
cards.people: 749 adults in 13 randomised trials longer than 3 weeks comparing medium-chain triglycerides (specifically C8:0 and C10:0) with long-chain triglycerides, in healthy adults.
cards.result: Compared with long-chain triglycerides, MCTs decreased body weight (−0.51 kg, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.23; P<0.001; I²=35%), waist circumference (−1.46 cm, −2.04 to −0.87; I²=0%), hip circumference (−0.79 cm, −1.27 to −0.30; P=0.002), total body fat (standardised mean difference −0.39, −0.57 to −0.22), total subcutaneous fat (SMD −0.46, −0.64 to −0.27) and visceral fat (SMD −0.55, −0.75 to −0.34). No differences were seen in blood lipid levels. The authors conclude replacement of long-chain fats with MCTs could potentially induce modest reductions in body weight and composition, and call for independent, large, well-designed trials to confirm efficacy and determine dose.
cards.watchOut: Substitution, not addition: the trials replaced other fats with MCTs, so they say nothing about spooning MCT oil on top of an unchanged diet. Many trials lacked sufficient information for a complete quality assessment, commercial bias was detected, and study designs varied in duration, dose and control of energy intake.
cards.source: Mumme K, Stonehouse W. Effects of medium-chain triglycerides on weight loss and body composition: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. 2015. PMID: 25636220. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Henderson 2009 (152 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's, maker-run): the caprylic-triglyceride product AC-1202 beat placebo on ADAS-Cog at day 45 (1.9 points, P=0.0235); at day 90, significance appears only in the APOE4-non-carrier subgroup (3.36 points, P=0.0148)
cards.summary: Henderson 2009 (152 patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's, maker-run): the caprylic-triglyceride product AC-1202 beat placebo on ADAS-Cog at day 45 (1.9 points, P=0.0235); at day 90, significance appears only in the APOE4-non-carrier subgroup (3.36 points, P=0.0148)
cards.people: 152 subjects with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease in a US-based 90-day trial of daily AC-1202 (a caprylic triglyceride ketogenic compound) versus placebo, on a normal diet and continuing approved Alzheimer's medications; the first author's affiliation on the record is Accera, Inc., the product's developer. Results were stratified by APOE4 carriage, a pre-defined analysis.
cards.result: AC-1202 significantly elevated the serum ketone body beta-hydroxybutyrate 2 hours after administration versus placebo. ADAS-Cog differences at day 45: 1.9 points in the intention-to-treat population (P=0.0235), 2.53 per protocol (P=0.0324) and 2.6 in the dosage-compliant group (P=0.0215). Among APOE4 non-carriers (E4−), intention-to-treat (N=55): 4.77 points at day 45 (P=0.0005) and 3.36 points at day 90 (P=0.0148); per protocol (N=37): 5.73 (P=0.0027) and 4.39 (P=0.0143); dosage compliant (N=38 at day 45, N=35 at day 90): 6.26 (P=0.0011) and 5.33 (P=0.0063). Adverse events occurred more frequently on AC-1202, were mainly gastrointestinal, and were mainly mild to moderate and transient.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports a significant overall (intention-to-treat) difference at day 45 only; at day 90 significance is reported only inside the APOE4-non-carrier subgroup — a pattern (multiple populations × multiple time points) that inflates false-positive risk. The trial was run by the company selling the product, and the confirmatory trial carded next, five times larger in the target subgroup, did not reproduce the finding.
cards.source: Henderson ST, Vogel JL, Barr LJ, Garvin F, Jones JJ, Costantini LC. Study of the ketogenic agent AC-1202 in mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial. Nutrition & Metabolism. 2009. PMID: 19664276. Registry ID: NCT00142805. MeSH: none listed in the record

cards.headline: Henderson 2020 — the NOURISH AD confirmatory trial (413 patients, 26 weeks): AC-1204 failed — ADAS-Cog change 0.6 on drug versus 0.0 on placebo in APOE4 non-carriers (difference 0.76 points, P=0.2458); no drug effect on any secondary outcome
cards.summary: Henderson 2020 — the NOURISH AD confirmatory trial (413 patients, 26 weeks): AC-1204 failed — ADAS-Cog change 0.6 on drug versus 0.0 on placebo in APOE4 non-carriers (difference 0.76 points, P=0.2458); no drug effect on any secondary outcome
cards.people: 413 patients with mild-to-moderate probable Alzheimer's disease, stratified by APOE genotype and randomised 1:1 to AC-1204 (a caprylic triglyceride formulation, 40 g daily providing 20 g caprylic triglyceride) or placebo for 26 weeks; the primary outcome was pre-specified in APOE4 non-carriers (placebo n=138, AC-1204 n=137 in that analysis).
cards.result: Mean change from baseline in ADAS-Cog11 at 26 weeks in APOE4 non-carriers: 0.0 on placebo and 0.6 on AC-1204 (least-squares difference of means −0.761, P=0.2458) — not significant. Secondary outcome measures failed to detect any drug effects. Administration of AC-1204 was safe and well-tolerated. The authors conclude the AC-1204 formulation of caprylic triglyceride failed to improve cognition or functional ability in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, noting lower-than-expected ketone formation and a lack of decline in the placebo group as possible contributors.
cards.watchOut: A null confirmatory trial does not prove the earlier subgroup signal was false — the authors point to weaker ketosis from AC-1204 than from AC-1202 and an unusually stable placebo group — but for a person deciding whether to buy MCT products for memory, the largest and longest test of the actual claim found nothing. This was a specific medical-food formulation, not shop-bought MCT oil or coconut oil.
cards.source: Henderson ST, Morimoto BH, Cummings JL, Farlow MR, Walker J. A Placebo-Controlled, Parallel-Group, Randomized Clinical Trial of AC-1204 in Mild-to-Moderate Alzheimer's Disease. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2020. PMID: 32310169. Registry ID: NCT01741194. cards.headline: Synthesis: half a kilogram for fat-swapping in small trials; the memory claim failed confirmation — MAYBE at best
cards.summary: Synthesis: half a kilogram for fat-swapping in small trials; the memory claim failed confirmation — MAYBE at best
cards.people: Adults considering MCT oil for weight control, and people with Alzheimer's disease or their families considering ketogenic MCT products for cognition.
cards.result: Weight: across 13 small trials, swapping dietary long-chain fats for MCTs produced about half a kilogram more weight loss (−0.51 kg) and about 1.5 cm off the waist, with no lipid penalty — a real but small substitution effect, from trials with detected commercial bias. Cognition: one 152-patient, maker-run trial of the medical food AC-1202 was positive at day 45 and in a genetic subgroup at day 90; the 413-patient, 26-week confirmatory trial of its successor formulation in exactly that subgroup was null (P=0.2458). On the present record the cognition claim should be treated as unproven, and neither cognition trial tested the MCT oil sold in shops.
cards.watchOut: Doses, formulations and products differ across all of this evidence, follow-up is short (the weight trials were only required to exceed 3 weeks), and the field is commercially interested — independent replication is the authors' own stated need for the weight claim, and the cognition claim has already failed its largest test.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mumme K, Stonehouse W. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. 2015 (PMID: 25636220); Henderson ST et al. Nutrition & Metabolism. 2009 (PMID: 19664276); Henderson ST et al. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2020 (PMID: 32310169).

shelves.title: Ginkgo biloba (EGb 761) for cognition in Alzheimer's disease (partial completion of #3470, dementia broadly): small but consistent cognitive gains in the Alzheimer's trials — POSSIBLE benefit, confined to the tested standardised extract
shelves.question: Does ginkgo biloba extract improve cognition in Alzheimer's disease?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alzheimer Disease · Dementia, Multi-Infarct · Double-Blind Method · Electroencephalography · Free Radical Scavengers · Ginkgo biloba · Humans · Middle Aged · Plant Extracts · Psychomotor Performance · Ginkgo Extract
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3470, which covers the standardised ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 in dementia broadly (its Weinmann 2010 meta-analysis and Ihl 2012 trial are carded there and are not re-carded here). This shelf narrows to the Alzheimer's disease slice and to cognition. The tested product in every carded trial is the standardised extract EGb 761, named as such in each record; the fetched trial records do not name the manufacturing company, so no company is printed here, and ginkgo products other than EGb 761 — which are not standardised to the same specification — may differ in safety and effectiveness. In the Alzheimer's-type populations of the older trials, EGb 761 beat placebo on cognitive scores by small margins: a 1.4-point ADAS-Cog advantage over 52 weeks (Le Bars 1997, PMID: 9343463), a significant responder advantage at 240 mg/day (Kanowski 1996, PMID: 8741021), and a roughly 1.9-point SKT advantage in dementia with neuropsychiatric symptoms (Herrschaft 2012, PMID: 22459264). An Alzheimer's-only meta-analysis of seven studies (Liao 2020, PMID: 32658034) found a relative response advantage for cognition (risk ratio 1.98). The effects are consistent but modest, the older trials mixed Alzheimer's with multi-infarct/vascular dementia, and no carded trial enrolled a purely Alzheimer's population with modern biomarker confirmation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — EGb 761 probably improves cognition slightly in Alzheimer's disease; the size of the gain is small and product-specific.

cards.headline: Kanowski 1996: EGb 761 240 mg/day beat placebo on a responder analysis in mild to moderate dementia of the Alzheimer type or multi-infarct dementia (p < 0.005)
cards.summary: Kanowski 1996: EGb 761 240 mg/day beat placebo on a responder analysis in mild to moderate dementia of the Alzheimer type or multi-infarct dementia (p < 0.005)
cards.people: 216 outpatients with presenile or senile primary degenerative dementia of the Alzheimer type or multi-infarct dementia (DSM-III-R), randomised after a 4-week run-in to a daily oral dose of 240 mg of the ginkgo biloba special extract EGb 761 or placebo for 24 weeks; the confirmatory valid-case analysis covered 156 patients who completed the study per protocol, and the intent-to-treat analysis 205 patients.
cards.result: Therapy response was defined as response in at least two of three primary variables (Clinical Global Impressions item 2, the SKT attention and memory test, and the Nürnberger Alters-Beobachtungsskala for activities of daily life). The frequency of therapy responders differed significantly in favour of EGb 761 (p < 0.005, Fisher's exact test), and the intent-to-treat analysis led to similar efficacy results. The record reports the responder comparison as a significance test and does not print the responder rates for each group. The investigational drug was found to be well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The population mixed Alzheimer's-type with multi-infarct dementia and the headline result is a composite responder definition, not a cognitive score difference; the record does not print the group responder rates, so no effect size is claimed here.
cards.source: Kanowski S et al. Proof of efficacy of the ginkgo biloba special extract EGb 761 in outpatients suffering from mild to moderate primary degenerative dementia of the Alzheimer type or multi-infarct dementia. Pharmacopsychiatry. 1996. PMID: 8741021. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised controlled trial (kanowski 1996) 216 outpatients with presenile or senile primary degenerative dementia of the alzheimer type or multi-infarct dementia (dsm-iii-r), randomised after a 4-week run-in to a daily oral dose of 240 mg of the ginkgo biloba special extract egb 761 or placebo for 24 weeks; the confirmatory valid-case analysis covered 156 patients who completed the study per protocol, and the intent-to-treat analysis 205 patients. therapy response was defined as response in at least two of three primary variables (clinical global impressions item 2, the skt attention and memory test, and the nürnberger alters-beobachtungsskala for activities of daily life). the frequency of therapy responders differed significantly in favour of egb 761 (p < 0.005, fisher's exact test), and the intent-to-treat analysis led to similar efficacy results. the record reports the responder comparison as a significance test and does not print the responder rates for each group. the investigational drug was found to be well tolerated. the population mixed alzheimer's-type with multi-infarct dementia and the headline result is a composite responder definition, not a cognitive score difference; the record does not print the group responder rates, so no effect size is claimed here. kanowski s et al. proof of efficacy of the ginkgo biloba special extract egb 761 in outpatients suffering from mild to moderate primary degenerative dementia of the alzheimer type or multi-infarct dementia. pharmacopsychiatry. 1996. pmid: 8741021. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · alzheimer disease · dementia, multi-infarct · double-blind method · electroencephalography · free radical scavengers · ginkgo biloba · humans · middle aged · plant extracts · psychomotor performance · ginkgo extract

cards.headline: Le Bars 1997: EGb 120 mg/day gave a 1.4-point ADAS-Cog advantage over placebo at 52 weeks, with 27% versus 14% achieving at least a 4-point improvement
cards.summary: Le Bars 1997: EGb 120 mg/day gave a 1.4-point ADAS-Cog advantage over placebo at 52 weeks, with 27% versus 14% achieving at least a 4-point improvement
cards.people: 309 mildly to severely demented outpatients with Alzheimer disease or multi-infarct dementia in the intent-to-treat analysis of a 52-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study of the ginkgo biloba extract EGb (EGb 761, described in the record as a particular extract of Ginkgo biloba) at 120 mg/day versus placebo; 202 patients provided evaluable data for the 52-week endpoint.
cards.result: In the intent-to-treat analysis, the EGb group had an Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive subscale (ADAS-Cog) score 1.4 points better than the placebo group (P = .04) and a Geriatric Evaluation by Relative's Rating Instrument score 0.14 points better (P = .004). In the evaluable data set, 27% of patients treated with EGb achieved at least a 4-point improvement on the ADAS-Cog, compared with 14% taking placebo (P = .005). No difference was seen in the Clinical Global Impression of Change, and no significant differences compared with placebo were observed in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A 1.4-point ADAS-Cog difference is modest, about a third of patients dropped out before the 52-week evaluable analysis, and the population again mixed Alzheimer disease with multi-infarct dementia; the global impression measure showed no difference.
cards.source: Le Bars PL et al. A placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized trial of an extract of Ginkgo biloba for dementia. North American EGb Study Group. JAMA. 1997. PMID: 9343463. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Herrschaft 2012: EGb 761 240 mg once daily improved cognition (SKT) by 2.2 points versus 0.3 on placebo in dementia with neuropsychiatric symptoms (p < 0.001)
cards.summary: Herrschaft 2012: EGb 761 240 mg once daily improved cognition (SKT) by 2.2 points versus 0.3 on placebo in dementia with neuropsychiatric symptoms (p < 0.001)
cards.people: 410 outpatients with mild to moderate dementia (Alzheimer's disease or vascular dementia) associated with neuropsychiatric symptoms, scoring 9 to 23 on the SKT cognitive battery and at least 6 on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory, in a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled 24-week trial of Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 at 240 mg once daily (n = 200 treated) versus placebo (n = 202).
cards.result: Patients treated with EGb 761 improved by 2.2 ± 3.5 points (mean ± SD) on the SKT total score, whereas those receiving placebo changed only slightly, by 0.3 ± 3.7 points; the Neuropsychiatric Inventory composite score improved by 4.6 ± 7.1 in the EGb 761 group and by 2.1 ± 6.5 in the placebo group. Both drug-placebo comparisons were significant at p < 0.001, and the EGb 761 group also showed a more favourable course in most secondary efficacy variables. Treatment was safe, with significant and clinically relevant improvement in cognition, psychopathology, functional measures and quality of life as reported by the authors.
cards.watchOut: Enrolment required neuropsychiatric symptoms and mixed Alzheimer's with vascular dementia, so this is the Alzheimer's-predominant dementia population of its era rather than biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's disease; the absolute SKT advantage over placebo is about 1.9 points.
cards.source: Herrschaft H et al. Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761® in dementia with neuropsychiatric features: a randomised, placebo-controlled trial to confirm the efficacy and safety of a daily dose of 240 mg. Journal of psychiatric research. 2012. PMID: 22459264. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Liao 2020: in an Alzheimer's-disease-only meta-analysis (7 studies, 939 patients), ginkgo biloba beat placebo on cognitive response (relative risk ratio 1.98) and global impression (odds ratio 3.12)
cards.summary: Liao 2020: in an Alzheimer's-disease-only meta-analysis (7 studies, 939 patients), ginkgo biloba beat placebo on cognitive response (relative risk ratio 1.98) and global impression (odds ratio 3.12)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Alzheimer disease only (Liao 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to patients with Alzheimer disease treated with Ginkgo biloba preparations, searching English and Chinese databases to July 3, 2019: seven studies with a total of 939 patients were identified and analysed, with efficacy and safety as the main measurement indices.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, Ginkgo biloba showed a higher cognitive-function response (risk ratio = 1.98, 95% CI 1.52 to 2.59, P < 0.001 — a relative measure) and a higher rate of improvement on Clinical Global Impression Change (odds ratio = 3.119, 95% CI 2.206 to 4.410, P < 0.001 — a relative measure). The record does not print the absolute response rates behind these relative measures. Adverse events were mild. The authors conclude that Ginkgo biloba preparation has reliable efficacy for cognitive function and global clinical assessment and safety in the treatment of Alzheimer disease.
cards.watchOut: The pooled preparations are described only as Ginkgo biloba preparations — not necessarily EGb 761 in every included study — and the headline measures are relative response ratios without absolute rates in the record, so the size of the average patient's gain cannot be read from this card.
cards.source: Liao Z et al. Meta-analysis of Ginkgo biloba Preparation for the Treatment of Alzheimer's Disease. Clinical neuropharmacology. 2020. PMID: 32658034. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for Alzheimer's cognition specifically, EGb 761 shows small, consistent placebo-beating gains across three trials and an Alzheimer's-only pooling — a real but modest product-specific effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: for Alzheimer's cognition specifically, EGb 761 shows small, consistent placebo-beating gains across three trials and an Alzheimer's-only pooling — a real but modest product-specific effect
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised placebo-controlled trials of the standardised extract EGb 761 in Alzheimer's-type dementia populations (216, 309 and 410 randomised patients) and one meta-analysis restricted to Alzheimer disease (7 studies, 939 patients). Total randomised participants across the three trials exceed 900, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Cognitive-score advantages over placebo were 1.4 ADAS-Cog points at 52 weeks on 120 mg/day (Le Bars 1997), a significant composite responder advantage at 240 mg/day (Kanowski 1996, p < 0.005), and a 2.2-versus-0.3-point SKT improvement at 240 mg/day in dementia with neuropsychiatric symptoms (Herrschaft 2012, p < 0.001). The Alzheimer's-only meta-analysis found a relative cognitive response ratio of 1.98 versus placebo (Liao 2020). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is confined to the tested standardised extract EGb 761; the fetched records do not name its manufacturer, and other ginkgo products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #3470 holds the broader dementia question and cards the Weinmann 2010 meta-analysis and the Ihl 2012 trial; this shelf's narrower Alzheimer's slice rests on different reports, and none of them enrolled biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's disease.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kanowski S et al. Pharmacopsychiatry. 1996 (PMID: 8741021); Le Bars PL et al. JAMA. 1997 (PMID: 9343463); Herrschaft H et al. Journal of psychiatric research. 2012 (PMID: 22459264); Liao Z et al. Clinical neuropharmacology. 2020 (PMID: 32658034).
